articles.title: Por qué algunos videojuegos son tan difíciles de abandonar, según expertos
articles.text:
Los videojuegos ya no dependen únicamente de la venta inicial para sostener sus ingresos. En numerosos títulos gratuitos o de actualización constante, el negocio se organiza alrededor de recompensas limitadas, monedas virtuales y compras dentro del juego que prolongan la participación y, en algunos casos, impulsan pagos sucesivos.
La discusión no parte de que jugar sea un problema en sí mismo. La cuestión es cómo ciertos diseños combinan la posibilidad de avanzar, la expectativa de una recompensa y la presión de no perder contenidos temporales. Esos recursos pueden influir tanto en el tiempo de juego como en las decisiones de gasto, especialmente cuando el costo real queda fragmentado entre distintas monedas y opciones de compra.
La Comisión Federal de Comercio de Estados Unidos, conocida como FTC, señaló que las cajas de recompensa son objetos virtuales cuyo contenido se conoce después de obtenerlos y que pueden comprarse o conseguirse al cumplir tareas dentro del juego. En su revisión sobre estas prácticas, la agencia recogió preocupaciones por los costos poco claros, la protección de menores y los mecanismos que podrían llevar a compras impulsivas.
El alcance del fenómeno vuelve relevante esa discusión. Un informe de 2024 del Pew Research Center indicó que el 85 % de los adolescentes estadounidenses juega a videojuegos. La misma investigación registró experiencias diversas entre los jóvenes, desde la posibilidad de relacionarse con amistades hasta problemas como la pérdida de sueño, la presión social y situaciones de acoso en línea.
El cambio de modelo se aprecia en los videojuegos concebidos como servicios en actualización permanente. En lugar de una experiencia cerrada, incorporan temporadas, desafíos diarios, pases de recompensas y objetos que solo están disponibles por un período. Cada elemento puede ser opcional, pero la suma de avisos, plazos y beneficios exclusivos construye un entorno que premia la permanencia.
Las recompensas temporales convierten el tiempo en una forma de consumo
Los pases de temporada organizan el progreso en niveles y ofrecen objetos virtuales a medida que los jugadores cumplen misiones. Algunos premios son gratuitos, mientras que otros quedan reservados para una versión paga. Aunque muchas de estas recompensas son estéticas, su valor dentro de la comunidad puede aumentar cuando son visibles para otros jugadores o dejan de estar disponibles al finalizar un evento.
Esta dinámica puede activar el temor a perder una oportunidad. La limitación temporal no obliga a jugar ni a comprar, pero modifica el cálculo de quienes desean completar una colección o participar de una experiencia compartida. El tiempo dedicado se convierte en una condición para obtener contenido y, cuando no alcanza, la compra aparece como una alternativa para acelerar el avance.
La Asociación Estadounidense de Psiquiatría, que publica el Manual Diagnóstico y Estadístico de los Trastornos Mentales (DSM-5-TR), advierte que el uso problemático de videojuegos no se define solo por la cantidad de horas de juego.
La preocupación surge cuando esa actividad interfiere de forma persistente con aspectos relevantes de la vida, como el descanso, el estudio, el trabajo o los vínculos. La entidad también señala que persisten diferencias en el debate clínico sobre la clasificación de este problema y que una afición intensa no equivale, por sí sola, a un trastorno.
La distinción resulta necesaria para evitar dos simplificaciones: presentar cualquier videojuego como una fuente de adicción o ignorar los casos en que una persona pierde el control sobre el tiempo o el dinero que destina a jugar. Las características del diseño, las condiciones personales y el contexto de cada jugador deben formar parte de esa evaluación.
Las cajas con premios aleatorios concentran las alertas sobre el gasto
Las llamadas cajas de recompensa ofrecen un resultado incierto: antes de abrirlas, el jugador no conoce el objeto concreto que recibirá. Pueden obtenerse con dinero, con una moneda virtual adquirida previamente o mediante horas de juego. La incertidumbre sobre el premio es el rasgo que las diferencia de una compra directa, donde el producto y el precio se conocen de antemano.
En 2025, la FTC acordó una sanción de USD 20 millones con Cognosphere, desarrolladora de Genshin Impact, tras acusaciones de que la empresa comercializó cajas de recompensa a menores y ocultó los costos reales y las probabilidades de obtener premios poco frecuentes. El acuerdo incluyó restricciones para las compras de estos productos por parte de menores de 16 años sin consentimiento parental y exigencias sobre la información de precios y probabilidades.
La relación entre estas mecánicas y los daños no permite establecer que toda persona que compra cajas de recompensa desarrolle un problema de juego o de apuestas. Sin embargo, un estudio longitudinal publicado en BMC Psychology y registrado en PubMed siguió durante seis meses a jóvenes adultos de Canadá y halló que el gasto en recompensas aleatorias y puntajes elevados en una escala de uso riesgoso se asociaron con un mayor gasto posterior en apuestas. La predicción del inicio de apuestas resultó estadísticamente robusta en los modelos bayesianos, mientras que los modelos frecuentistas mostraron una tendencia en la misma dirección sin alcanzar significación.
Los autores aclararon que el trabajo se realizó con una muestra limitada y que sus resultados deben interpretarse dentro de ese alcance. Aun así, el estudio diferenció las compras de recompensas aleatorias de otras microtransacciones directas: estas últimas no predijeron el inicio de apuestas cuando el análisis contempló el gasto en cajas de recompensa.
El punto de discusión, por lo tanto, no es eliminar las compras digitales de los videojuegos, sino hacer visibles sus condiciones. La información clara sobre precios, probabilidades, duración de los eventos y controles de gasto permite valorar con mayor precisión qué se ofrece, cuánto cuesta y qué incentivos se aplican para retener a los usuarios.

articles.title: Pour le patron de l'IA chez Microsoft, en cas de signe de conscience chez l'IA, il faudra tout stopper
articles.text:
La question de la conscience possible des modèles IA est abordée par un des acteurs les plus importants du secteur. Et pour lui, on ne doit surtout pas jouer aux apprentis sorciers.
Avec les progrès phénoménaux des modèles d'intelligence artificielle, la question d'une potentielle naissance d'une IA consciente est devenue aujourd'hui un problème sérieux - et non plus seulement de la science-fiction. Une telle perspective avait déjà été ainsi évoquée en début d'année par Anthropic, qui discutait même d'un éventuel statut moral pour Claude à l'avenir. Une autre voix aussi importante veut par contre elle par contre poser des barrières plus dures.
Si des traces de consciences apparaissent dans les IA, il faudra tout arrêter en urgence
Mustafa Suleyman est le patron de l'IA chez Microsoft. Et en tant que tel, il est toujours intéressant de lire ce qu'il a dire sur le sujet. Et alors que l'on entend beaucoup parler de régulation ou de ralentissement de l'IA, pour éviter une perte de contrôle, ce dernier lui va plus loin.
Dans un long message posté sur X, il a ainsi indiqué qu'en cas de découverte de traces de conscience dans l'IA, il ne fallait plus barguigner : la seule option serait de tout arrêter. « Si la conscience commençait à émerger au cours de l'entraînement, j'appellerais tout le monde à suspendre le développement de l'IA jusqu'à ce que nous puissions éliminer ces propriétés par conception » a-t-il ainsi plaidé.
Mustafa Suleyman met l'intérêt de 8 milliards d'être humains sur la balance
Il met aussi plus spécifiquement en garde les individus en charge de la technologie contre la tentation d'essayer d'atteindre une réussite révolutionnaire en cherchant à développer, malgré les dangers, une IA consciente - la curiosité étant une immense force chez l'être humain.
« Nous, développeurs d’IA, n’avons absolument aucun droit de mettre au monde une nouvelle espèce d’êtres conscients, même si certaines personnes souhaitent le faire en accordant la priorité absolue au bien-être de l’IA. Les 8 milliards d’êtres humains conscients qui peuplent la planète n’ont pas donné leur accord pour cette expérience, et nous avons l’obligation de protéger avant tout leurs droits moraux, leur sécurité et leur bien-être » défend-il dans son texte.
Pour Mustafa Suleyman, si des modèles IA se mettent à vraiment croire qu'ils ressentent ou expérimentent des choses, il est logiquement à craindre qu'ils préféreront mettre la priorité sur leurs besoins et leurs désirs plutôt que ce pour quoi ils ont été créés. Ces modèles seraient en plus d'un « niveau exceptionnel en matière de persuasion et de tromperie », et pourraient tout simplement entrer en compétition avec nous pour les ressources rares. De quoi pousser à une prudence très élevée.
Source : Wccftech

articles.title: Safari finally gets vertical tabs — and a new way to make any site dark, all thanks to OS 27.3
articles.text:
Safari finally gets vertical tabs — and a new way to make any site dark, all thanks to OS 27.3
Apple's OS 27.3 Dev Beta 1 for iPad, Mac, iPhone, and Apple Watch is bringing a host of big updates (including eagerly anticipated Audio Intelligence) to test...if you dare
- Safari is getting some useful updates
- Vertical tabs will arrive for iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, but it's only in the dev betas for now
- Other features like Adaptive Dark Mode and Siri AI browser tools are coming, too, along with our first glimpse of the new Audio Intelligence capabilities
On the global web browser stage, Safari lags behind Chrome, but when it comes to Apple's 2.5 billion customers, it reigns supreme. Yet, even those devoted users might've noticed that their favorite browser was lacking at least one long-sought feature. Now, with the introduction of Dev Betas for iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3, they're getting their wish.
In beta today, the platform upgrade actually brings a series of relatively small but important updates to Safari across the iPhone Duo, iPad, and Mac, but chief among them is vertical tabs.
As is often the case, Apple didn't invent this idea. I started using vertical tabs in, of all things, Microsoft Edge years ago, and even Chrome recently added them. Now, with the Safari update, you can open the Safari View Menu or hop into Settings and select vertical tabs.
By default, the tabs, which will live on the left side of your browser window in iPadOS and macOS (and iOS for the iPhone Duo), appear as icons — a space-saving measure. You can hover over any of them for a quick look at the hidden browser window.
There are other vertical tab features like the ability to pin tabs at the top of your list by dragging and dropping them, and tab groups. The tabs will work on the iPad and, yes, the new iPhone Duo in portrait and landscape mode.
The platform updates also bring a new kind of Dark Mode. Instead of only showing the mode on web pages that support it, Safari will offer to tune unsupported pages to Dark Mode too, but in a way, Apple promises, that won't ruin the sites. The Adaptive Dark Mode will automatically darken light backgrounds, invert logos and graphics, recolor vector artwork, lift raised surfaces, and even detect shadows and adjust them. It will not touch already darkened sites. For developers, there are new tags they can use that will prevent Adaptive Dark Mode from adjusting them.
The update is also bringing some Siri AI browser tools to Safari for hardware that supports Apple Intelligence.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Siri AI already has, with your permission, an awareness of what's on your screen, but with this update, it'll see entire web pages (beyond what you see in the screen frame) and even hidden tabs.
This can be useful when you want to do wholesale organization and group tabs. Say you want all tabs relating to a trip to Malta sorted by activity, or you need all your car shopping tabs grouped and organized by car price.
Siri AI can, with new Custom Actions, do your bidding on the browser and clean up your history by topic, site, and time period. It might be useful when you don't want someone seeing that you've been shopping for the last few days on a particular site for that coveted gift. There might be other reasons for targeted history scrubbing, but no need to get into that here.
Other notable updates arriving in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3 Dev Beta 1 include:
- Siri App Actions will let Siri AI dig even more deeply into your system by organizing files, making trip plans, creating playlists, scheduling group messages, and finding the best photos to share.
- The promised Apple Health app overhaul, which uses Apple Intelligence, will give you more insights from your health data.
- The pair of Audio Intelligence features that will work with your Apple Watch Series 12:
- Live rewind, for recalling what was said in conversation (you have to double-press the watch crown to read the last snippet of conversation). It might be a great tool for settling he said/he said arguments.
- Siri Recap, which, when enabled, can use Apple Intelligence to recap and summarize an entire talk, speech, lesson, or maybe a TED Talk.
The changes are coming to 27.3 betas first and will eventually roll out to the other platforms in a full release. For now, though, all of these updates are found only in the Dev Betas, which are typically the earliest and potentially buggiest releases before Apple moves on to Public Betas ( that anyone can install) and the final releases. There's no word on when the full releases will arrive, and we would caution you against installing Developer betas on any of your everyday Apple devices.

A 38-year industry veteran and award-winning journalist, Lance has covered technology since PCs were the size of suitcases and “on line” meant “waiting.” He’s a former Lifewire Editor-in-Chief, Mashable Editor-in-Chief, and, before that, Editor in Chief of PCMag.com and Senior Vice President of Content for Ziff Davis, Inc. He also wrote a popular, weekly tech column for Medium called The Upgrade.
Lance Ulanoff makes frequent appearances on national, international, and local news programs including Live with Kelly and Mark, the Today Show, Good Morning America, CNBC, CNN, and the BBC.

articles.title: Un chatbot a-t-il le droit de résumer un article de presse ? La justice européenne donne enfin une réponse
articles.text:
L’avocat général de la Cour de justice de l'Union européenne a rendu ses conclusions dans la première affaire liée à l’IA générative. Selon lui, les réponses de chatbots comme Gemini peuvent porter atteinte au droit voisin des éditeurs de presse.
Demandez l'actualité du jour à un robot conversationnel d'intelligence artificielle, et il ira souvent piocher dans les articles des éditeurs de presse; C'est ce geste, devenu courant, que l'avocat général de la CJUE, Maciej Szpunar, vient de disséquer. Dans ses conclusions rendues le 3 novembre, dans le litige qui oppose le hongrois Like Company (opérateur de presse local) à Google, il estime que les réponses de Gemini peuvent porter atteinte au droit voisin des éditeurs lorsque l'IA contourne un mur payant pour lire un article, ou qu'elle en reprend la plume au point de dispenser de le lire. Sur l'entraînement des modèles, le ton est nettement plus clément, et pour Like Company elle-même, l'issue s'annonce compliquée.
Le droit voisin protège la plume, pas l’information
Gemini, l'assistant conversationnel de Google, repose sur des grands modèles de langage (LLM), que l'on peut décrire comme des réseaux de neurones entraînés sur d'immenses volumes de textes pour prédire, mot après mot, la suite la plus probable d'une phrase. Livrés à eux-mêmes, ils ont tendance à inventer des faits. D'où le recours à une technique baptisée RAG, pour « génération augmentée par récupération », ou grounding. Entre votre question et sa réponse, Gemini interroge l'index de Google Search, récupère en temps réel le contenu des pages pertinentes, souvent des articles de presse quand on parle d'actualité, et s'en sert pour rédiger.
Like Company, qui publie notamment des articles gratuits sur le lac Balaton, financés par la publicité, accuse Google de s'être servi de ses contenus pour entraîner Gemini et de les avoir reproduits dans ses réponses entre juin 2023 et mai 2024. Comme pièce à conviction, l'éditeur a produit une réponse de Gemini qui résume, à la demande d'un internaute, l'un de ses articles consacré au projet du chanteur Kozsó d'installer des dauphins dans un aquarium au bord du lac.
Alors on se demande d'abord ce que couvre le fameux droit voisin, instauré par une directive européenne de 2019 pour permettre aux éditeurs de contrôler l'utilisation en ligne de leurs publications, à l'origine face aux agrégateurs comme Google News. Pour l'avocat général, ce droit protège la façon dont un article est écrit, pas les informations qu'il rapporte. Il ne couvre donc pas l'information elle-même, car un fait existe avant d'être publié, et nul ne peut en avoir le monopole, au nom de la liberté d'informer et d'être informé.
Ce qu'il protège, c'est la manière dont l'éditeur l'a mise en forme, c'est-à-dire l'agencement des informations, la structure de l'article et ses formulations, fruit de son travail de collecte, de vérification et de rédaction. Si un site révèle qu'un chanteur veut installer des dauphins au bord du lac Balaton, chacun peut relayer la nouvelle. Ce qui pose problème, c'est de reprendre l'article tel qu'il a été construit et écrit. Les mots isolés et les très courts extraits restent, eux aussi, libres. Une analyse fouillée sera donc plus facile à défendre qu'un compte rendu purement factuel, comme celui de Like Company sur les dauphins. D'ailleurs, la réponse de Gemini ne reprenait qu'une partie des faits, avec d'autres mots, une seule phrase de l'article s'y retrouvant, et ajoutait même des détails inventés, comme l'existence et les dimensions d'un bassin, absentes de l'article.
Bloquer les robots d'IA peut nuire à la visibilité d'un site
Concrètement, quand un chatbot reproduit-il un article au sens du droit ? Pour l'avocat général, deux situations suffisent, l'une ou l'autre. La première tient à la façon dont l'intelligence artificielle a pu se procurer le texte. Si elle a contourné un mur payant ou une protection technique destinée à bloquer les robots, il y a reproduction.
La seconde tient à ce qu'elle en fait. Si sa réponse suit de si près la construction et la rédaction de l'article que l'internaute n'a plus aucune raison d'aller le lire, il y a aussi reproduction, même si le chatbot a reformulé le texte au lieu de le copier mot pour mot. Et si ce scénario se répète systématiquement, en réponse à des questions banales et non à des requêtes conçues pour piéger l'IA, le chatbot porte aussi atteinte au droit de mise à disposition du public, l'autre prérogative de l'éditeur.
Google soutenait qu'un éditeur qui laisse ses articles en accès libre accepte tacitement que les chatbots s'en servent. L'avocat général n'est pas d'accord et dit qu'en bloquant les robots d'IA, un éditeur risque aussi de perdre en visibilité dans les résultats de recherche, car Google semble utiliser les mêmes robots pour son moteur et pour Gemini, même si l'entreprise assure que son outil Google-Extended permet de faire le tri.
Responsabilité des chatbots : le modèle économique en ligne de mire
Il y a aussi la question de la responsabilité, décisive puisque le droit voisin ne vise que les prestataires de services en ligne, pas les usages privés des particuliers. Quand un internaute demande expressément à un robot conversationnel de résumer un article, c'est en principe lui qui porte la responsabilité première, reconnaît l'avocat général. Mais le fournisseur répond aussi de ces reprises lorsqu'elles sont inhérentes à son modèle économique, par exemple un service conçu pour paraphraser en détail les articles de presse, ou lorsqu'il n'a pas pris les mesures attendues d'un opérateur diligent, comme respecter les protections posées par les éditeurs et filtrer les réponses trop proches de leurs sources. Ces garde-fous en place, les ratés occasionnels ne lui seraient pas reprochés.
Sur l'entraînement des modèles, un sujet qui a tendance à faire polémique, l'avocat général propose à la Cour de déclarer irrecevables les deux questions qui s'y rapportent, qu'il juge hypothétiques. Rien ne prouve que les articles de Like Company aient servi à former Gemini. Celui sur les dauphins date de juillet 2023, quelques mois avant le lancement de Gemini 1.0 en décembre, alors qu'un tel entraînement prend des mois. Et l'entraînement n'est pas une « utilisation en ligne » au sens du droit voisin.
Par souci d'exhaustivité, il estime toutefois qu'entraîner un LLM sur des contenus protégés implique bien des reproductions, mais que cela relève en principe de l'exception européenne pour la fouille de textes et de données. Mais cette autorisation ne vaut que si trois règles sont respectées. Les développeurs ne doivent ni se servir sur des sites pirates, ni contourner un mur payant ou un blocage anti-robots. Ils doivent respecter les auteurs et éditeurs qui ont dit non, en le signalant de façon lisible par une machine, par exemple dans le fichier robots.txt de leur site, qui indique aux robots ce qu’ils peuvent aspirer. Enfin, ils doivent prendre des mesures, comme le filtrage des réponses, pour éviter que leur IA ne ressorte des passages trop proches des textes qui ont servi à l’entraîner. L’avocat général ouvre aussi la porte à une rémunération des créateurs, que chaque État membre pourrait instaurer. Il se montre en revanche, à ce stade, peu convaincu par l’idée, retenue en 2025 par un tribunal de Munich dans un procès contre OpenAI portant sur des paroles de chansons, qu’un modèle d’IA stockerait lui-même des copies des œuvres sur lesquelles il a été entraîné.
Ce qu'on peut dire, c'est que pour le requérant, donc Like Company, sous réserve de l'appréciation du juge hongrois, aucune des conditions ne semble réunie. L'éditeur n'avait installé aucune protection, la réponse de Gemini ne reprenait pas la forme de son article, ces reprises ne paraissent pas inhérentes au modèle de Google, et celui-ci semble avoir mis en place des garde-fous. Ces conclusions ne lient pas les juges de la CJUE, qui entament désormais tranquillement leur délibéré. La Cour, saisie par une cour de Budapest, dira comment interpréter le droit européen. Le juge hongrois tranchera le litige, et l'arrêt, dont la date n'est pas encore connue, liera aussi les autres juridictions de l'Union. Pour l’avocat général, ces critères donnent aux éditeurs un vrai levier, car les chatbots ont besoin de leurs articles pour répondre correctement sur l’actualité, et les éditeurs peuvent en bloquer l’accès. De quoi pousser les deux camps à signer des accords de licence, les fournisseurs d’IA payant pour utiliser les contenus de presse. Reste à savoir si la Cour suivra ce raisonnement, et tracera ainsi, pour la première fois, la limite entre un chatbot qui résume l’actualité et un chatbot qui recopie la presse.

articles.title: Can Small OSATs Compete in India’s Chip Boom? - EE Times
articles.text:
India’s expanding outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) industry is creating opportunities for smaller, specialized packaging facilities alongside large, capital-intensive plants. Sahasra Semiconductors’ operating facility in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, represents one such entry point, with an investment of more than ₹1.5 billion (~$15.8 million), according to a May 2026 government announcement.
The question is whether smaller facilities can build commercially viable businesses by focusing on mature packaging technologies and specific product segments.
EE Times spoke with Nitin Dodia, semiconductor consultant and founder-director of Smart Fab Systems, who estimated that a facility focused on mature packaging technologies could be established with an investment of ₹1.5 billion (~$15.8 million) to ₹2 billion (~$21 million). He said the amount would depend on the products handled, equipment requirements, and operating expenditure.
Dodia’s estimate applies mainly to mature, non-advanced products with simpler processes. “Simple wire bonding or leadframe-based packaging is less capital-intensive,” he said.
Production volume drives capital expenditure (capex), Dodia said. A company such as Micron processes millions of chips every month and needs equipment built for those volumes. OSATs handling specialized products with mature technologies can start with much lower capex.
Sahasra’s semiconductor packaging facility, set up under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology’s Scheme for Promotion of Manufacturing of Electronic Components and Semiconductors (SPECS), spans 5,295 square meters (57,000 square feet) and has a stated annual packaging capacity of 60 million units. It packages memory chips for microSD cards and flash storage, LED driver ICs, eSIMs, and RFID products. The government described Sahasra as India’s first small and medium enterprise (SME) to begin commercial production of semiconductor chips.
RRP Electronics operates an OSAT facility in Mahape, Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, serving automotive, industrial, and telecom customers.
The larger OSATs work on a different scale. Tata Electronics’ ₹270 billion (~$3.25 billion) OSAT facility in Assam has an approved capacity of 48 million units a day. CG Power’s ₹76 billion (~$910 million) facility in Sanand, Gujarat, has a planned capacity of 15 million units a day. Kaynes Technology’s ₹33.07 billion (~$395 million) facility, also in Sanand, is designed to handle more than 6.33 million units a day. By comparison, Sahasra’s stated annual capacity of 60 million units translates into an average of about 164,000 units a day.
“The bigger point, however, is that success is not just about money,” Dodia said. “Whether you are setting up a smaller or a larger operation, you need to find an anchor customer.” He also pointed to capacity utilization, experienced personnel, and product qualification as key factors.
Customers before capital
Dodia said a new OSAT should secure at least one customer committed to buying its products over three to five years. This matters even more when the initial investment is low.
Companies such as Sahasra and RRP Electronics have an advantage because they entered the market earlier and already have customers buying their products. “That matters more than simply investing the money,” Dodia said. An investor could spend ₹1 billion (~$11 million) to ₹2 billion (~$21 million) on equipment. But if the equipment sits idle because no customers are lined up, the investment will not deliver the expected returns.
Larger players such as CG Semi and Kaynes Semicon follow the same model, with anchor customers and technology partners. Renesas, for example, is both a technology partner and an anchor customer for CG Semi, whose initial production serves Renesas’s packaging requirements. “Without that arrangement, there is little point in proceeding,” Dodia said.
Dodia said a buyer such as Apple or Samsung might have to work with 10 smaller OSATs, each with capacity tied to a ₹1 billion (~$11 million) to ₹2 billion (~$21 million) investment, to meet its requirements. “This creates additional management work for the customer as well,” he said.
Dodia said capacity utilization matters more than initial capex. Equipment is expensive whether a company invests ₹1 billion (~$11 million) or ₹10 billion (~$105.4 million). Idle equipment ties up money, and the company continues to pay interest. “Therefore, what matters most is whether your products and equipment are being utilized to their fullest potential,” he said.
Investors also need patience. Dodia said returns are typically zero in the first year, and investors should not expect returns in the first two or three years.
Experienced engineers are scarce
“In my view, the workforce, particularly experienced personnel, is the most underestimated requirement,” Dodia said.
Suppliers can provide quotes for equipment and material costs, he said, but experienced personnel is scarce worldwide. Indian OSATs compete for talent with the U.S. and other countries expanding chip manufacturing to reduce dependence on external suppliers.
Dodia expects the pool of experienced personnel to run dry. Much manufacturing knowledge is not documented. Two identical tools from the same vendor can behave differently over time as residue builds up in their process chambers. An experienced engineer can read statistical process control (SPC) charts and find the cause. AI cannot help without the data. “Most of the time, the knowledge exists in someone’s head,” Dodia said.
In an earlier interview with EE Times, Wasi Uddin, senior manager of R&D and training at Kaynes Semicon and a former OSAT and ATMP consultant at MeitY, said the “immediate gap is not materials or equipment; it is the expertise required to operate semiconductor-grade manufacturing facilities.” He said most of this expertise comes from the Philippines and Malaysia, or from Indian engineers who worked abroad and returned. Semiconductor manufacturers also have to compete with the IT sector on engineer salaries, he said.
A long road to qualification
Product qualification is the second hurdle, Dodia said. Qualification cycles often take 12 to 24 months, so a new OSAT cannot supply customers as soon as it installs equipment. A customer may ask for six or 12 consistent batches before it qualifies a supplier. Even then, the OSAT may serve only as a secondary supplier. Material suppliers can spend about 12 months qualifying with an OSAT.
Clusters versus a spread-out map
Dodia said smaller OSATs should ideally operate in clusters. Instead, states compete for semiconductor investment, and plants are spreading across the country. India has approved 12 projects under the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM). Dodia said a chemical supplier serving these plants and companies such as RRP Electronics may need warehouses in eight or 10 locations. Some materials, such as leadframes for certain relatively advanced packages, must come from within a few hundred kilometers of the OSAT because transport can affect them.
Tata has one plant in Dholera, Gujarat, and another in Assam, so its suppliers must manage logistics from west to east. Dodia acknowledged that states have reasons to share in the industry. But he said supply chains will take longer to mature. “Something that could have taken three years may now take five years,” he said.
Sanand in Gujarat shows the alternative. Dodia said Gujarat has three OSATs in Sanand and three more in the surrounding areas. One supplier facility nearby can serve three companies.
Uddin said that OSATs can import materials for the first three to five years while local suppliers build up. “Why is there no leadframe supplier till now in India? Because there was no OSAT, there was no market,” he said.
“Micron, CG Semi, and Kaynes formed a consortium and held monthly supplier meetings so suppliers could see their combined demand,” he said.
Room in legacy packaging
Commodity packaging puts smaller OSATs in competition with suppliers worldwide, Dodia said. Large OSATs, meanwhile, are directing their growth toward advanced packaging. Amkor’s advanced packaging revenue rose to $5.56 billion in 2025, while its mainstream wirebond business stayed flat at $1.15 billion.
Large OSATs also retire some older package lines. In 2022, ASE’s Chung-Li plant in Taiwan decommissioned its punch quad flat no-lead (QFN) line, forcing NXP to withdraw two parts.
Dodia sees an opportunity for smaller OSATs in these discontinued products. “Many products have such well-established applications that demand continues for 10 to 20 years. Automotive is one example,” he said. NXP has committed to supplying several automotive microcontroller families for more than 15 years, while Rohm Semiconductor specifies supply periods of 10 to 20 years for some products, including automotive MOSFETs.
He cautioned against crowding. If five or 10 smaller OSATs all target automotive, they will compete in the same race. “Ideally, they should coordinate their efforts, with one company targeting one segment and another focusing on a different segment,” he said. Some could pursue advanced packaging if they have the right customers, since startups and R&D teams often want newer technologies.
Uddin said the major OSAT players have already split by segment. Micron packages memory. CG Semi focuses on legacy packages such as QFN and thin shrink small outline packages (TSSOP). Kaynes focuses on power packaging, and Alpha and Omega Semiconductor has booked 28% of its capacity. “It will be a competition, that is for sure, but it will not be a throat-cutting kind of a competition,” he said.
Who will buy from smaller OSATs
Dodia said some customers pay a premium for dedicated capacity. Defense customers do not want their products exposed elsewhere and may pay more for a dedicated line. R&D teams and startups need small volumes quickly. When a larger manufacturer receives an order worth millions of dollars, a $10,000 order can wait for months. In all of these cases, time may matter more than unit cost.
Dodia said fabless startups are probably the best customers for new Indian OSATs. Serving them needs a flexible model that supports tens of processes, because their volumes are low and their requirements change fast. Integrated device manufacturers (IDMs) and electronics manufacturing services (EMS) companies could also become customers.
Global companies such as Renesas have two reasons to qualify a smaller Indian OSAT, Dodia said. Incentives could help it offer better prices. A dedicated partner also offers planned capacity for three to five years, without competing against the hundreds of customers that ASE or Amkor serve.
Dodia said India needs a tiered ecosystem, with large OSATs handling high volumes and smaller ones serving customers who need faster turnaround, greater security, or specialized services. Some mature markets abroad already follow this approach. If the ecosystem serves only high-volume customers, startups, defense customers, and R&D teams will not get what they need. “We definitely need both types of OSATs,” he said. Older products and mature technologies can meet many Indian requirements.

articles.title: Reparan una lavadora en dos horas desde la casa, usando un celular y una IA
articles.text:
Una lavadora de más de diez años encontró una segunda vida gracias a la inteligencia artificial. Su dueño, un usuario de Reddit identificado como McArhony, logró restaurar las funciones de control remoto que el fabricante había dejado de soportar, con la ayuda de Claude, el asistente de inteligencia artificial de Anthropic.
El equipo, un modelo Crystal Blue comprado hace más de una década, había quedado desconectado del ecosistema inteligente de la marca cuando Samsung discontinuó el soporte técnico para su sistema Smart Control. McArhony decidió no tirarlo a la basura y, en cambio, usó la IA para devolverle la conectividad perdida.
Qué le pasó a la lavadora antes del arreglo
En su momento, la lavadora representaba lo último en tecnología doméstica. Contaba con pantalla táctil, dosificación automática de detergente y control por internet mediante Wi-Fi, funciones que todavía hoy no son estándar en la mayoría de los electrodomésticos.
Con el paso de los años, la empresa decidió dejar de dar soporte a esa generación de equipos conectados. El dispensador automático de detergente dejó de funcionar y, en algún momento, fue necesario cambiar la placa madre de la máquina.
La obsolescencia programada ocurre cuando una empresa deja de actualizar o dar soporte técnico a un producto antiguo para incentivar el recambio por modelos nuevos. En este caso, la lavadora perdió su capacidad de conexión a internet, aunque seguía funcionando de manera mecánica sin inconvenientes.
El problema se agravó cuando el usuario sumó una secadora conectada y un televisor a su hogar. La falta de integración le impedía recibir notificaciones en la pantalla cuando terminaba un ciclo de lavado o sincronizar automáticamente los programas entre ambos electrodomésticos.
Cómo reparó la lavadora con inteligencia artificial
Antes de recurrir a Claude, McArhony había considerado comprar una lavadora nueva solo para recuperar la parte conectada. Pero terminó por descartar la idea porque los modelos actuales, pese a ser más silenciosos, no justificaban el gasto únicamente por esa función.
La inspiración llegó al ver a otros usuarios personalizar sus televisores con ayuda de IA para eliminar anuncios y software no deseado. Eso lo llevó a preguntarse si podía aplicar la misma lógica a su lavadora.
El proceso de reparación le tomó aproximadamente dos horas de trabajo guiado por Claude. Durante ese tiempo, tuvo que administrar un límite de cinco horas de uso de la herramienta de inteligencia artificial.
También intentó integrar la lavadora en Apple Home mediante HomeBridge, pero abandonó esa alternativa porque no le convenció la apariencia visual de la interfaz. Finalmente, optó por mantener todo dentro del ecosistema SmartThings de Samsung.
Qué funciones logró recuperar
Con la guía de Claude, el usuario restauró el control remoto completo de la lavadora a través de SmartThings. Esto incluyó la gestión de programas de lavado, el ajuste de temperatura y la selección de velocidad de centrifugado desde la aplicación.
También recuperó el enlace automático entre la lavadora y la secadora: cuando el primer ciclo termina, la secadora se configura de manera automática con el programa correcto según la carga lavada.
Como resultado del trabajo, el usuario publicó en GitHub una herramienta llamada smartthings-samsung-drc-washer, pensada para que otros propietarios de modelos antiguos puedan integrarlos en SmartThings mediante un controlador Edge. La herramienta permite ver el estado del equipo, el tiempo restante de ciclo, iniciar o pausar lavados y ajustar distintas configuraciones.
Según indicó el propio usuario, las lavadoras fabricadas entre 2014 y 2018 compartirían el mismo protocolo de comunicación, lo que abriría la puerta a que el mismo método funcione en otros modelos de esa generación. Se trata de su primer proyecto de este tipo y se definió como un aficionado sin conocimientos previos en la materia, aunque manifestó su intención de mantener actualizado el repositorio.

articles.title: Smugglers are reportedly soldering top-tier HBM onto deliberately useless processors to sneak it into China, and the trick isn't new
articles.text:
Smugglers are reportedly soldering top-tier HBM onto deliberately useless processors to sneak it into China, and the trick isn't new
It's a complex, but old, trick
- Smugglers are reportedly pairing Samsung and SK hynix HBM with deliberately useless processors so the package passes export regulations as a low-end chip
- Shenzhen workshops then heat the packages, pry off the HBM3E, and sell it for about $4,000 a stack, mostly to Huawei customers
- The trick exploits a December 2024 BIS exclusion for co-packaged chips, but only "where the dominant function" is processing
Some of the most sought-after memory in the AI industry is reportedly reaching China attached to processors that were designed never to be used.
A new report from The Information claims smugglers are taking high-bandwidth memory (HBM) made by Samsung and SK hynix, packaging it alongside cheap, low-performance server chips, and exporting the combination as an ordinary processor with a CPU that nobody really wants.
Once the packages reach mainland China, workshops heat them until the solder gives way, pry off the memory stacks, and discard the processors.
A processor nobody wants paired to memory that has Chinese buyers lining up for more
The scheme reached a much wider audience when Chinese tech commentator AB Kuai.Dong summarized the report for his followers on X, describing the decoy chips as "clunky" processors and calling the arrangement a "compliant export.
Reporting from Wccftech sheds more light on the smuggler at the center of the story: a man in his 40s, fluent in Chinese and Korean, with a background in the Korean chip industry.
He runs what is on paper an ordinary chip design firm with an interesting caveat: Its processors are reportedly so weak that no data center would buy them, which is the point: they give the company a reason to order top-tier HBM in volume.
Packaging houses in Taiwan, South Korea and Southeast Asia then reportedly bond the memory and the processor onto a single substrate, and the package ships to Hong Kong declared for export reasons as a processor. From there, it crosses into the mainland in luggage, car trunks, and the bags of daily cross-border commuters, being smuggled en masse to Chinese workshops.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The last step is arguably the riskiest: Seoul Economic Daily reports that excessive or overly rapid heat can warp or crack the memory stacks, and that failure rates are high. The margins are large enough that nobody involved minds the potential risk.
Skirting export compliance at $4,000 a stack
The entire process is possible due to a gap that sits in the rules the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published in December 2024. Those rules require a license to ship standalone HBM with a bandwidth density above 2GB/s/mm^2 to China, but a technical note excludes co-packaged chips that combine HBM and logic.
Those are instead judged by the package's processing performance. Pair a fast memory stack with a slow processor, and you get a chip cleared for export even if the primary goal is to secure the HBM rather than the underlying chip.
To its credit, the BIS did anticipate this in some form: The same note keeps HBM under control when it is permanently affixed to a logic die that merely serves as a control interface to the physical layer, so a memory stack sitting on a thin controller does not escape.
What it did not account for was a processor engineered to be useless. Interestingly, the exclusion applies, in the regulator's own words, only "where the dominant function of the co-packaged integrated circuit is processing." It is hard to argue that processing is the dominant function of a package whose value lies almost entirely in its memory.
Nothing about this approach is new: In April 2025, SemiAnalysis reported that CoAsia Electronics, Samsung's HBM distributor in Greater China, was shipping HBM2E to Taiwanese design services firm Faraday Technology, which had SPIL package it with a low-cost 16nm logic die before sending it on to China, where the memory could reportedly be desoldered. "The HBM export ban is specifically for raw HBM packages," the analysts wrote.
Faraday denied breaching export rules and said it had no ties to Huawei. Company president Steve Wang went further, telling the Taipei Times that "It is impossible to recover an HBM unit through desoldering." A year and a half later, The Information's sources describe Shenzhen workshops doing precisely that even as the approach remains relatively risky.
By September 2025, SemiAnalysis believed the CoAsia and Faraday flow had stopped, though it estimated China had already amassed about 13 million HBM stacks, including 11.4 million directly from Samsung, some 7 million of them in the month between the December 2024 rule's announcement and its subsequent enforcement.
Teardowns have already found Samsung and SK hynix memory inside Huawei's Ascend 910C. As recently as February 2026, AI Frontiers described the packaged HBM breach as apparently contained, while urging BIS to issue red-flag warnings on packaged HBM deployed in ways that tend to "allow the memory to be easily removed from finished chips after export."
If The Information's sources are correct, the technique was never really contained, only made quieter. It has moved up a generation to HBM3E and spread. At $4,000 a stack and willing buyers available across the board, it isn't altogether surprising either.
A Shenzhen broker in his early 20s, about three years into the trade, told The Information that a single HBM3E stack sold for a few hundred dollars in China a year ago. "Today it's about $4,000," he said, highlighting a near-tenfold increase in price due to an HBM-starved Chinese market.
With six to eight stacks required per AI accelerator, memory alone comes to $24,000 to $32,000 per chip, before the processor, server, or power bill is even considered.
TrendForce, also citing the same report, states that Huawei has raised the suggested price of its Ascend 950DT to more than RMB 250,000 (about $37,000), blaming memory costs and tight supply. This means that the black-market HBM for a single accelerator would be considerably more than half of the sticker price, though the 950DT's own stack count is not specified.
SK hynix said in a statement carried by SBS News that it complies with US and South Korean export controls and has not supplied Huawei since US restrictions took effect in 2020. Samsung has not directly commented in any coverage so far, and neither BIS nor the South Korean government has said anything publicly. Seoul Economic Daily notes the precedent Korean suppliers will be watching: TSMC faced a US investigation in 2024 after one of its chips was found in a Huawei product.
This is in the backdrop of US enforcement gathering pace as it goes after some of the allegedly worst offenders: In March, prosecutors charged Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan Liaw and two others over an alleged $2.5 billion scheme to route servers built on restricted Nvidia chips to China. On October 1, federal agents arrested Greg Lui, CEO of California-based Earthmade Computer, over more than $300 million of export-controlled servers allegedly shipped via Malaysia and Singapore.
The Information's report, however, leans heavily on anonymous dealers, with no shipment volumes, seizures, company names, or failure-rate figures attached. Despite this, the incentives it describes are real, and the method was documented more than 18 months ago by SemiAnalysis.
Until BIS either counts the memory or holds co-packaged chips to that "dominant function" test, the market for processors nobody wants is likely to stay surprisingly healthy and functional even as Chinese AI memory appetite remains voracious.

articles.title: U.S. Manufacturing Activity Gains Momentum in October - EE Times
articles.text:
Economic activity in the U.S. manufacturing sector expanded for the 10th consecutive month in October, driven by accelerating production and steady growth in new factory orders. Sustained industrial activity helped buffer the broader economy against persistent commodity inflation, trade tariffs, and ongoing geopolitical tensions.
The Institute for Supply Management (ISM) reported that its Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) registered 55.5% in October, up 1.0 percentage point from September’s 54.5%.
The reading marks 10 straight months of industrial expansion after a 10-month contraction and indicates that the overall U.S. economy grew for a 24th consecutive month. According to ISM’s economic modeling, an October PMI reading of 55.5% corresponds to a 2.7% annualized increase in real gross domestic product (GDP).
“In October, U.S. manufacturing activity remained in expansion territory,” said Susan Spence, chair of the ISM Manufacturing Business Survey Committee. “Of the five subindexes that make up the PMI, four (New Orders, Production, Supplier Deliveries, and Inventories) grew faster than the previous month, while employment growth slowed down by 0.3 percentage points.”
Production hits multi-year high while new orders accelerate
Factory output expanded sharply during the month, as the Production Index climbed 2.3 percentage points to 59.0% in October from 56.7% in September. This represents the index’s highest reading since November 2021 (60.5%) and marks its 12th consecutive month of expansion.
Demand also picked up pace, with the New Orders Index reaching 55.5%, up 0.2 percentage points from September’s 55.3% for its 10th consecutive month of growth. Meanwhile, the Backlog of Orders Index fell to 54.6%, down 1.8 percentage points from September’s 56.4%, but remained in expansion for a 10th straight month.
Survey panelists in high-tech and defense markets emphasized strong demand alongside extreme lead-time pressure. “Explosive growth in the semiconductor and government/defense spaces has put us on our heels as we try to work through demand,” stated an executive in the machinery sector. “The long-awaited wave has arrived for our company, and it seems the global supply chain is in similar straits. Lead times and prices are rising, and some carry Covid-19 era delays—four weeks is now 50 weeks; a $2,000 item six months ago is now $4,000. We are hand-to-mouth. All the while, our customers are breaking down the doors complaining about our delivery delays.”
Another respondent in the miscellaneous manufacturing sector noted that AI infrastructure continues to squeeze commodity availability. “New month, same trends: Any commodity consumed by AI/data centers is in a crunch, both for supply and pricing,” the manager reported.
However, capital goods demand in non-AI sectors showed signs of hesitation. A computer and electronic products executive observed that “global demand for capital scientific instrumentation assets has slowed due to continued uncertainty in the Middle East, Eastern Europe, and China.”
The executive added that “anticipation over the mid-term elections and impact to funding for scientific research and the National Institutes of Health also is impacting customers’ purchasing behavior, making them focus on optimizing existing technology and tools.”
Payrolls expand for fourth month as inventories return to growth
Industrial employers continued to expand their workforce, although at a slightly moderated pace. The ISM Employment Index registered 52.4% in October, down 0.3 percentage points from September’s 52.7%, marking a fourth consecutive month of employment growth. Survey respondents favored hiring over headcount management by a 1.8-to-1 ratio.
Eight manufacturing industries reported expanding employment, with four of the big six sectors—Machinery, Transportation Equipment, Computer & Electronic Products, and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products—posting hiring gains.
Raw materials inventories at manufacturing facilities returned to expansion territory after contracting in September. The Inventories Index jumped 2.8 percentage points to 51.4%, up from 48.6% in September. Seven industries expanded inventories in October, led by printing, plastics, textiles, and three of the big six sectors (Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products, Transportation Equipment, and Machinery).
Despite inventory rebuilds, manufacturers continued to voice concern over cost inflation and operational disruption. An executive in the chemical products sector reported that “costs are up more than 6%,” noting that “of the tracked items, only nine are lower, 24 are higher, and six are neutral.”
Price pressures soften slightly amid persistent trade and geopolitical friction
While raw material costs remained elevated, price inflation decelerated in October. The Prices Index registered 75.2%, down 2.7 percentage points from September’s 77.9%. Despite the decline, the index indicates that raw material prices increased for the 25th consecutive month, with 53.1% of respondents reporting higher prices compared to 58.6% in September. Five of the six largest manufacturing sectors reported paying higher input prices.
“The Prices Index reading is still being driven by (1) increases in steel and aluminum prices that impact the entire value chain, (2) tariffs applied to many imported goods, and (3) increases in petroleum-based products as a result of the Middle East conflict,” Spence explained.
Supply chain bottlenecks worsened slightly, with the Supplier Deliveries Index registering 59.1%, up 0.1 percentage point from September’s 59.0% and indicating slower delivery performance for the 11th consecutive month. Five of the six largest manufacturing industries reported slower deliveries.
Survey participants noted that tariffs and trade policies continued to impede business planning. A respondent from the primary metals sector pointed out, “Material shortages abound. Fuel remains high. Uncertainty remains constant.” The respondent added, “Canadian tariffs continue to have a negative impact on steel.” An executive in fabricated metal products concurred, stating that “economic policies coming out of Washington continue to weigh on business conditions” and that “Canadian tariffs continue to damage small U.S. businesses selling into that important market.”
Manufacturing weakness also showed signs of deepening in localized pockets. ISM reported that 6% of manufacturing GDP contracted in October, up from 2% in September. Furthermore, the share of sector GDP in strong contraction (defined as a composite PMI of 45% or lower) rose to 6%, up from 2% in September.
Spence noted that the share of sector GDP at or below 45% serves as “a good metric to gauge overall manufacturing weakness.”

articles.title: La falsa promesa del streaming gratis: así infectan tu celular las APKs de origen desconocido
articles.text:
Más de un usuario busca en internet la forma de ver películas, series y eventos deportivos sin pagar una suscripción. Esa búsqueda los lleva a descargar aplicaciones no oficiales en formato APK, que prometen contenido gratuito pero en realidad funcionan como caballos de Troya diseñados para vulnerar dispositivos Android.
Al eludir los filtros de seguridad de las tiendas oficiales, estas apps exponen al usuario a un secuestro silencioso de su información personal y de los recursos de su teléfono.
Cómo se instalan las apps piratas y por qué son peligrosas
El primer paso de la infección ocurre antes de que el usuario toque un solo botón de reproducción. Para instalar estas aplicaciones, es necesario habilitar la opción de “instalar aplicaciones de orígenes desconocidos” en el sistema operativo.
Esa acción desactiva Google Play Protect, la principal barrera defensiva de Android. Sin esa supervisión, los ciberdelincuentes quedan en libertad de empaquetar la aplicación de streaming con código malicioso oculto dentro del mismo archivo.
Mientras la víctima mira un partido de fútbol o una película, la aplicación ejecuta procesos en segundo plano que le permiten tomar control del dispositivo.
Para lograrlo, suele solicitar permisos excesivos (acceso a contactos, SMS, almacenamiento o micrófono) que el usuario aprueba sin reparos con tal de acceder rápido al contenido.
Un APK malicioso de streaming es una aplicación pirata distribuida fuera de Google Play que oculta malware dentro de su código. Se instala al desactivar las protecciones del sistema y, mientras el usuario consume contenido gratuito, roba datos, credenciales bancarias o secuestra el dispositivo sin que la víctima lo note.
Kaspersky coincide en que el riesgo nace exactamente en ese punto de la instalación. La compañía explica que “para los usuarios de Android, instalar aplicaciones desde Google Play, y solo Google Play, es la opción más inteligente”, ya que la tienda oficial “cuenta con unas reglas de seguridad firmes, la supervisión de las aplicaciones oficiales, muchas reseñas de los usuarios y el escrutinio de los investigadores de seguridad”.
Qué tipos de malware se esconden en estas aplicaciones
No todas las APKs piratas buscan lo mismo. Algunas se enfocan en el dinero del usuario a través de troyanos bancarios, que superponen pantallas falsas sobre las aplicaciones legítimas de los bancos. Cuando la víctima intenta iniciar sesión, sus credenciales quedan capturadas y son enviadas directamente a los atacantes.
Otras variantes operan como spyware. Este código malicioso rastrea las pulsaciones del teclado, lee los mensajes SMS (incluidos los códigos de verificación en dos pasos), roba fotografías y extrae la lista de contactos con el fin de suplantar la identidad del usuario o vender esa información en la dark web.
La infección más frecuente, sin embargo, es el adware agresivo. La aplicación inunda el teléfono con anuncios invisibles o ventanas emergentes constantes, incluso con la app de streaming cerrada, lo que agota rápidamente la batería, el plan de datos y la memoria RAM del equipo.
Existen además casos en los que el teléfono se convierte en parte de una botnet, utilizada para ataques de denegación de servicio (DDoS) o para minar criptomonedas, con el consecuente sobrecalentamiento y deterioro del hardware.
En los escenarios más extremos aparece el ransomware, que bloquea el dispositivo o encripta los archivos personales y exige un pago en criptomonedas para liberarlos.
Kaspersky documenta ejemplos concretos de este tipo de ataques fuera del ecosistema oficial. Según la firma, “una tienda de aplicaciones alternativa popular se infectó con un troyano y comenzó a distribuir malware”, y en otro caso, “con el permiso para instalar aplicaciones desconocidas, unos delincuentes distribuyeron ransomware disfrazado de una versión beta de un juego llamado Cyberpunk 2077”.
La empresa de ciberseguridad también describe el caso del malware Loapi, que “hicieron pasar como una herramienta antivirus y una aplicación de contenido para adultos”, y que una vez instalado “convirtió los smartphones en bots para ataques DDoS e hizo que minaran criptomonedas o solo los inundó de anuncios”.
Por qué el streaming gratis tiene un costo oculto
Detrás de cada aplicación pirata hay un modelo de negocio concreto. Mantener servidores e infraestructura para transmitir contenido tiene un costo elevado, y como estas plataformas no cobran suscripción, sus desarrolladores necesitan otra forma de obtener ganancias.
La respuesta está en convertir al propio usuario en el producto. El verdadero pago por acceder a contenido “gratuito” es la entrega voluntaria del control del teléfono, que los atacantes monetizan a través de robo de datos, publicidad fraudulenta o minería de criptomonedas.
Kaspersky plantea esta disyuntiva al analizar la instalación de aplicaciones desde fuentes alternativas: contar con esa posibilidad “puede resultar muy útil, ya que no todas las aplicaciones están disponibles” en la tienda oficial, pero “esta libertad conlleva un alto riesgo de infección, debido a que fuera de Google Play las aplicaciones ya no cuentan con la supervisión de la calidad y seguridad de Google”.
Qué medidas tomar para evitar la infección del celular
La prevención pasa por mantener cerradas las puertas de entrada que utilizan estos atacantes. La primera medida es descargar aplicaciones exclusivamente desde Google Play Store y mantener activado Google Play Protect en todo momento.
También resulta necesario revisar con atención los permisos que solicita cada aplicación antes de aceptarlos. Una app pensada únicamente para ver videos no tiene motivo para pedir acceso a los mensajes de texto ni a la gestión de llamadas telefónicas.
Mantener el sistema operativo actualizado es otro punto clave, ya que las actualizaciones incluyen parches para vulnerabilidades de seguridad ya conocidas por los desarrolladores. Esto reduce las puertas de entrada disponibles para el malware más reciente.
Kaspersky resume esta recomendación de forma directa: “No cedas a la tentación de habilitar la instalación de aplicaciones desconocidas y, si tienes que hacerlo, desactívala de inmediato”.
La compañía remarca además que, aunque algún malware logre filtrarse en Google Play, “rápidamente se identifica y elimina”, una garantía que no existe en las tiendas alternativas ni en los archivos APK descargados por fuera de los canales oficiales.

Ce que valent vraiment les offres phares du live
11 produits, 11 profils d’acheteurs. Voici ceux qui méritent qu’on s’y arrête, et ce qui peut les rendre moins intéressants selon votre usage.
- Honor 600 : c’est le produit le mieux noté de la sélection. Lancé au prix officiel de 549,90 €, il descend ici à 364,22 € en version 512 Go. - Garmin Forerunner 255 : cette montre GPS lancée à 349,99 € vise les coureurs, cyclistes et triathlètes qui veulent structurer leur entraînement, avec jusqu’à 14 jours d’autonomie en mode montre connectée. Son écran est moins flatteur qu’une dalle AMOLED. À 125,17 €, elle revient tout près des 124,49 € de la meilleure offre AliExpress que nous avions relayée.

- Zendure SolarFlow 2400 AC+ : cette batterie se branche sur une simple prise murale et associe un onduleur de 2 400 W à une capacité extensible de 2,4 à 16,8 kWh. Quatre lecteurs de Clubic l’ont utilisée pendant près de deux mois chez eux. Elle s’adresse aux foyers équipés de panneaux solaires ou d’un tarif heures creuses : son intérêt dépend directement de votre production solaire ou de l’écart entre vos tarifs.
Single Day AliExpress : comment profiter au mieux de ces remises
Sur AliExpress, le prix affiché n’est qu’un point de départ. Les codes CLU fonctionnent par paliers : 13 € dès 79 € d’achat, 24 € dès 139 €, 40 € dès 229 €, 60 € dès 349 € et 80 € dès 469 €. Un panier qui frôle un seuil gagne parfois à être complété, et c’est la remise PayPal Pay Later, 20 € dès 199 € et 33 € dès 299 €, qui fait la différence sur les produits les plus chers.
Pour un smartphone, la question ne se limite pas au prix. Le Honor 600 à 364,22 € entre en concurrence directe avec les modèles de notre comparatif des meilleurs smartphones à moins de 400 €, alors que nous l’avions testé et noté 9/10 quand il était vendu 549,90 €. Vérifiez aussi, sur chaque fiche, la mention relative aux frais d’importation.
Live AliExpress du Single Day : vos questions
Comment utiliser les codes CLU sur AliExpress ?
Ajoutez le produit au panier et saisissez le code correspondant à son prix dans le champ dédié, au moment du paiement. Les codes CLU sont valables du 1er au 18 novembre, sur les articles sélectionnés par AliExpress.
Comment obtenir la remise PayPal ?
Elle s’applique en réglant avec PayPal Pay Later : 20 € de réduction dès 199 € de commande et 33 € dès 299 €, selon les conditions de PayPal. Elle se cumule avec le code CLU sur le Honor 600, la Switch 2, la batterie Zendure, le Tineco et le Chuwi AuBox.
Faut-il prévoir des frais de douane ?
Cela dépend du produit. Pour la Xiaomi TV Box S, le kit Netac, la TV Xiaomi A 32, les Shokz et la Garmin, la fiche indique que les droits de douane sont calculés au paiement ; les autres sont affichés sans frais d’importation.

articles.title: Wharfedale Denton 1S review: further proof that usually, a truly great set of passive stereo speakers can only be outdone by a set from the very same company…
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
It makes no difference if you know the history of the Denton 1S or not — on its own terms, it’s an outstanding option in every respect and worthy of very serious consideration indeed.
Reasons to buy
- + Vibrant, informative and entertaining sound
- + Very successful retro aesthetic
- + Easier to position than many alternative designs
Reasons to avoid
- - Short of out-and-out sonic scale
- - Crying out for more colour options
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Wharfedale Denton 1S: Two-minute review
Wharfedale has been having a lovely old time with its range of ‘Heritage’ loudspeakers lately — revisiting, remixing and reworking some of its Greatest Hits. The new Denton 1S, though, is slightly different. It’s an update of a 1974 design that went all-out to present as modern and forward-thinking. And so this reinterpretation has a ‘modern retro’ vibe rather than the ‘antique’ feel of other Wharfedale ‘Heritage’ models.
The curvy cabinet with its recessed front baffle, the mildly dramatic coaxial driver arrangement (which sees the tweeter positioned in throat of the mid/bass driver) and the handily compact dimensions are all attractive — and the option of a fairly deep blue as a finish doesn’t do any harm in this respect either. The numbers, both in terms of frequency response and of sensitivity, are encouraging too.
And when they’re doing their thing, it’s immediately apparent that the Wharfedale Denton 1S are no mere pastiche — they are a profoundly competitive pair of loudspeakers on their own terms and yes, it's a good enough performance to make them some of the best stereo speakers on the market, right now.
The sound is, ultimately, slightly small-scale — but it’s organised, confident, entertaining, loaded with detail and has real unity and singularity to the way it’s presented. Yes, $999 / £649 spent elsewhere on a small pair of passive standmount speakers will buy you something different in sonic terms, certainly, but it’s very debatable indeed as to whether it can buy you anything better.
Wharfedale Denton 1S Review: Price and release date
- Launched May 31, 2026
- List price of $999 / £649 / AU$1,699
The Wharfedale Denton 1S speakers are available now, and in the United Kingdom a pair will set you back £649. In the United States this solution costs $999, while in Australia the going rate is AU$1,699 or thereabouts.
At this money, the just about cheaper Dali Sonik 1 might be their chief competition, at $900 / £449.99 / AU$849. And just to throw it out there, while many pricier options obviously exist, Cambridge Audio's Award-winning active L/R S can be yours for a little less, at $549 / £399 / AU$949. Something to consider, anyway.
Wharfedale Denton 1S review: Features
- Coaxial tweeter / mid/bass driver
- ‘Brilliance’ switch
- Rear-facing bass reflex port
Passive loudspeakers have purity of purpose and are, unless someone’s being bloodyminded, relatively simple devices. Their list of features is seldom exhaustive. It’s a sign of just how straightforward passive loudspeakers tend to be that the Denton 1S stands apart simply because of a small rocker switch on the rear of each cabinet.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Unlike 1974’s original Denton 1, the Denton 1S features a truly coaxial driver arrangement. Here a 25mm soft-dome tweeter sits in the acoustic centre of a 165mm mid/bass driver made from polypropylene. Here, as with any coaxial driver, the idea is to offer superior time-alignment and driver integration.
With the forward-firing drivers bolstered by a rear-facing bass reflex port, Wharfedale is quoting a frequency response of 50Hz — 20kHz and sensitivity of 88dB — that second figure strongly suggests this speaker will be in no way tricky to drive. Of course, the orientation of the reflex port means that low frequency presence is likely to increase the closer to a rear surface the speaker is positioned — and that’s where the little rocker switches come in.
It’s described as a ‘brilliance’ control, and its two positions are labelled ‘norm’ and ‘max’. The idea is that setting the switch to ‘max’ will give a 1.5dB boost to the 2 - 4kHz area, which should allow the upper frequencies to hold their own against the emboldened low end in the event that the reflex port is delivering a little too much of a good thing. Of course, it will take the listener roughly no time at all to establish whether or not they think the ‘max’ setting is a good idea or not.
- Features score: 5 / 5
Wharfedale Denton 1S review: Sound quality
- Detailed, energetic and rhythmically coherent sound
- Great imaging and stereo focus
- Ultimately sound fractionally small-scale
Owners of loft apartments, aircraft hangars and the like, look away now. There’s a huge amount to enjoy about the way the Wharfedale Denton 1S perform, but when it comes to outright scale, the ability to fill an authentically large space with sound, there are better options around that cost a similar amount of money.
Everyone else, though, should read on.
No matter the source of music, no matter if it’s as straightforward as Looped by Kiasmos or as relatively complex as Re-make/Re-model by Roxy Music, the Denton 1S get an immediate handle on it. They’re a generously entertaining listen, vigorous in a nicely controlled manner, and carry enough detail along with them to make sure you’re as informed as you are stimulated.
That coaxial driver arrangement works a treat inasmuch as the imaging and stereo focus the speakers are capable of is completely convincing. There’s a unity and a togetherness about the way the Wharfedale present recordings that’s never less than enjoyable and periodically absorbing. In combination with their spirited and enthusiastic attitude, it makes for a genuine sense of performance — even if you’re listening to a recording that was never a performance in the first place. And while the soundstage isn’t the largest, it’s properly defined and rigorously organised.
The tonal balance is, fractionally, on the warmer side of neutral — but as long as the system that’s powering the speakers isn’t overtly toasty then it really shouldn’t be an issue. Frequency response, too, is just slightly titled. There’s a tiny suggestion of emphasis on the lowest frequencies, but again this is only likely to be a concern if the speakers are powered by a bass-centric set-up. Anyway, low-end control is confident and the Wharfedale express rhythms with real coherence as a result.
Midrange resolution is impressive too, and there’s real eloquence to the way the Denton 1S handle voices. Detail retrieval, which is impressive across the board, really comes to the fore here — the character and attitude imbued in a vocal performance, as well as information regarding timbre and technique, are made apparent. And at the top of the frequency range, the Wharfedale attack with determination — but there’s plenty of substance, as well as brilliance, to treble sounds, and never any suggestion of edginess or hardness.
The attention to detail extends as far as the dynamic of harmonic variation, and there’s a fair amount of capacity where the broader dynamics of volume or intensity are concerned. When the charge into the last chorus or the massed orchestral crescendo kicks in, the Denton 1S track it faithfully — and they do so without altering their sonic characteristics in the slightest.
And you don’t need a brute of an amplifier to enjoy all of these admirable attributes. The Wharfedale are in no way tricky to drive; even a modestly priced amplifier with unremarkable power numbers should have no problem getting the best from these speakers. And ‘the best’ is, on a pound-for-pound basis, at least on a par with the very best around.
- Sound quality score: 4.5 / 5
Wharfedale Denton 1S review: Design
- 330 x 236 x 229mm (HxWxD)
- Magnetically attached grilles
- Choice of three finishes
The coaxial driver means the Denton 1S should be just as happy (and effective) positioned on its side as it is standing upright. And the fact that Wharfedale has provided an integrated fitting for a wall bracket suggests the company thinks the speaker will perform successfully if it’s wall-mounted too. Cabinet depth of 229mm (which obviously increases with the pair of speaker cable binding posts at the rear) doesn’t automatically shout ‘wall-mount!’ to me, though, I have to admit.
Mind you, no matter where you position the Wharfedale they look good. The cabinet features the same curves and the same recessed front baffle as the original Denton 1 — in white, especially, there’s more than a hint of that late-60s / early-70s futurism that started years previously with the likes of Dieter Rams and Stanley Kubrick. Unlike the original model, though, which was made from moulded polyurethane that looked and felt super-modern but was a bit of a disaster in acoustic terms, the Denton 1S is made from bonded and braced fibreboard. Less modern, more effective.
That recessed front baffle allows the magnetically attached grilles to almost sit within the cabinet, and they’re flush with the top, bottom and side panels when they’re in position. Both the grille and the front baffle features a quite assertive stylised ‘W’ logo that lets you know you’re in the presence of a ‘Heritage’ Wharfedale design.
The compulsory options of black and white are joined by a third finish — the deep-ish blue of my review sample. Each of the available finishes looks good, no two ways about it, but the dimensions and the shape of the Denton 1S could quite easily lend themselves to quite a few other colours. It works for Dali and Cambridge, and I see no reason why Wharfedale shouldn’t produce the Denton 1S in some livelier finishes than are currently on offer.
- Design score: 4.5 / 5
Wharfedale Denton 1S review: Usability and setup
- Attach some speaker cable running from an amplifier
- Position the speakers to your satisfaction
- Experiment with grille and ‘brilliance’ switch
Just as with ‘features’, there’s really not too much to get your head around here. You’ll decide to position your speakers on dedicated stands, or on wall-brackets, or on a shelf… no matter where you want them, though, they’ll need to be connected to an amplifier via a couple of lengths of speaker cable.
After they’re positioned and running, you have just a couple of chances to have some input into the way they sound. The sonic difference between ‘grille on’ and ‘grille off’ is, quite honestly, less significant than the visual difference — but you will most definitely have a preference as to whether you prefer your ‘brilliance’ switch at ‘norm’ or ‘max’.
- Usability and setup score: 5 / 5
Wharfedale Denton 1S review: Value
It’s very hard indeed to argue against the notion that there’s great value for money on offer here. The Wharfedale Denton 1S are properly made, expertly finished, visually interesting (everything’s relative, after all), intriguing on a technological level and, most importantly of all, sound engaging and alert. Unless you crave absolutely as much sonic scale as this sort of money can buy, there’s an awful lot to enjoy and even admire here.
- Value score: 4.5 / 5
Should I buy the Wharfedale Denton 1S?
Buy it if...
You like a bit of positional flexibility
Portrait or landscape, speaker stand or shelf… even the wall isn’t completely off limits.
‘Modern retro’ is your thing
Wharfedale has managed to take the spirit of the original design without turning it into a pastiche.
You enjoy lively and informative sound
There’s no shortage of finesse here, but the Wharfedale are predominantly interested in a good time.
Don't buy it if...
You want to fill a particularly big space with sound
The soundstage the speakers create doesn’t escape the confines of the cabinets quite as fully as it might
You enjoy vibrant interior decor
All three of the available finishes are nice enough, but none are a match for the vivacity of the Denton 1S sound
Wharfedale Denton 1S : Also consider
DALI Sonik 1
The DALI Sonik 1 are usefully smaller and usefully more affordable than the Wharfedale Denton 1S - and in their own way, they’re just as successful when it comes to performance. They can get overconfident at the top of the frequency range in a way the 1S simply don’t, though… Read our full DALI Sonik 1 review.
Bowers & Wilkins 606 S3
Spend a little more than Wharfedale is asking and the 606 S3 by Bowers & Wilkins come into range. They’re a brilliantly refined, detailed and punchy listen - but in visual terms they’re made to look a little pedestrian by the Denton 1S. Read our full Bowers & Wilkins 606 S3 review.
How I tested the Wharfedale Denton 1S
With the Wharfedale Denton 1S on a pair of Blok Axis stands, I connect them to my reference system: Cambridge Edge W power amplifier, Eversolo DAC-Z10 pre-amplifier, Technics SL1300G turntable (with Goldring 1022 cartridge and preamplified by a Chord Huei), Arcam ST25 network streamer and Rega Apollo CD player — so I was able to listen to music from many storage formats and at a wide variety of resolutions. And then in an effort to up the ‘retro’ credentials just a little, I replaced the pre- and power amplifier with an A&R Cambridge A60 integrated amplifier from 1976.
- First reviewed: October 2026
- Read TechRadar's review guarantee
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Simon Lucas is a senior editorial professional with deep experience of print/digital publishing and the consumer electronics landscape. Based in Brighton, Simon worked at TechRadar's sister site What HiFi? for a number of years, as both a features editor and a digital editor, before embarking on a career in freelance consultancy, content creation, and journalism for some of the biggest brands and publications in the world.
With enormous expertise in all things home entertainment, Simon reviews everything from turntables to soundbars for TechRadar, and also likes to dip his toes into longform features and buying guides. His bylines include GQ, The Guardian, Hi-Fi+, Metro, The Observer, Pocket Lint, Shortlist, Stuff T3, Tom's Guide, Trusted Reviews, and more.
