articles.title: Google: LLMjacking attacks rack up $1 million in cloud AI charges
articles.text:
Large language model hijacking attacks, also known as LLMjacking, are generating large fraudulent cloud charges, with some organizations losing more than $100,000 per day.
Companies can record costs as high as $1 million due to fraudulent calls using stolen API keys, researchers at Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant in analyzed incidents.
Based on their observations, there are "two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure."
The researchers identified two categories of threat actors: those who scan for publicly exposed LLM endpoints and those who steal valid API keys from unprotected machines.
After gaining initial access, the attackers sell it to services known as LLM mixers, which provide their subscribers with unauthorized access to LLMs.
Once access is resold, request volumes can spike suddenly, sometimes exceeding 1,000 requests per second. The service provider records the requests as legitimate consumption and charges the victim organization for the tokens.
GTIG and Mandiant observed an increase in this type of activity this year, with fraudulent charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, and cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1,000,000.
LLM mixers offer access to AI resources at very low prices, using their proxy infrastructure to relay customers' prompts to hijacked services through stolen API keys.
The researchers found several examples of such relaying infrastructure, including Jet Night, which sells “unlimited access plans” for $60/month, and the newapi[.]pro service.
“Another threat actor that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours leveraged stolen third-party API keys to power the token routing service jet-night.com,” Google says.
“Jet Night passed nearly one million dollars in token costs to the victim organization.”
Google also identified the threat cluster UNC6993, which appears to use gateway tools to aggregate stolen keys and distribute requests, and likely sells access via underground forums.
The attackers gain access via exposed or compromised cloud credentials, service account keys, GitHub tokens, active session tokens, and LLM API keys.
Attackers search the compromised environment for credentials, logs, databases, and secret managers, and try to create backdoor accounts or inject SSH keys to maintain persistent access.
The researchers have also observed threat actors exploiting CVE-2026-40217, a vulnerability in LiteLLM that allows running arbitrary code on the server by leveraging the custom-code guardrail testing endpoint.
In some cases, Google says that attackers used the victim's cloud infrastructure to host unauthorized proxy endpoints and agentic workloads.
"For example, one threat actor enabled agents, deployed publicly accessible reverse proxies, and used custom Node.js proxy bundles to expose endpoints compatible with multiple frontier LLMs rebranded under a persona known as D1337-KAIROS," the researchers say.
Google recommends several actions to protect against LLMjacking attacks, which start with prioritizing Identity and Access Management (IAM) and securing the supply chain.
Companies should use centralized secrets platforms to enable the rotation and management of sensitive keys and secrets. Users should not have extended privileges unless required by their role and tasks.
"Deny all permissions that are not explicitly required, including access to Cloud LLM services," Google recommends.
Enforcing phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA), ensuring monitoring tools provide comprehensive visibility across the environment to identify unauthorized LLM and AI services (shadow AI), and setting API usage and spending limits can help organizations detect LLMjacking attacks early, limit their impact, or prevent them altogether.
Furthermore, cloud audit and inference logs should be enabled and monitored for unauthorized service activation, suspicious credential checks, unusual usage, and attempts to disable logging.

articles.title: Brett Adcock, CEO de Figure AI y joven gurú de la IA: “Estamos creando una nueva especie”
articles.text:
“Estamos creando una nueva especie”, dijo Brett Adcock, fundador y CEO de Figure AI. Lo decía en una conversación que mantuvo con Marc Benioff (Salesforce) en la que hablaban de los robots humanoides. “Estamos creando una nueva especie”.
Esto fue en Dreamforce 2025. En 2026 hemos vuelto a ver este video. Y además, Figure ha sacado algunos resultados posteriores.
El desarrollo de Figure 03
En concreto, han mostrado el proyecto denominado Figure 03. Se trata de la tercera generación de humanoides de la empresa. También cuentan con una inteligencia artificial llamada Helix (que abarca visión, lenguaje y acción). El objetivo es que el robot haga trabajos que hacen los humanos y aprenda de ellos.
Para el ámbito doméstico hay varias cosas interesantes. Por un lado, han incluido materiales blandos (textiles y espuma) para evitar riesgos de pellizco, tienen cámaras en las palmas de las manos y, además, tienen sensores táctiles en los dedos. Estas cámaras son útiles para cuando las cámaras principales están ocultas (por ejemplo, al alcanzar algo en un armario).
De esta manera tenemos pruebas visuales de robots que organizan las habitaciones o hacen operaciones con la vajilla. Es importante saber que el hecho de que el robot pueda hacer una tarea en un entorno conocido no implica que sepa hacerlo en entornos nuevos.
En nuestra cobertura de junio de 2025 de Genbeta ya comentábamos el acuerdo entre Figure y BMW. En términos prácticos, hay que pensar en qué pueden hacer y bajo qué circunstancias.
En junio de 2026, BMW anunció que estaba desarrollando un proyecto con el Figure 03 en Spartanburg. La idea es que recoja los componentes (que llegan desordenados) y los coloque en los carros en el orden adecuado para el montaje. También han confirmado que el Figure 02 ha sido útil para la fabricación de más de 30.000 BMW X3 en 10 meses. En concreto, han usado el robot para poner piezas de chapa (para luego soldar).
Las pruebas de Helix 2.5 en viviendas
El 17 de septiembre de 2026 presentaron la versión 2.5 de Helix. También han llevado a cabo pruebas en entornos domésticos (30 casas en la bahía de San Francisco). En estos casos, el sistema no había visto antes estas casas. Han probado tres tipos de tareas (recolectar juguetes, doblar toallas y hacer camas).
Han publicado un 56 % de éxito (con el sistema preentrenado con Index, su dataset de comportamiento humano), comparado con el 9 % de éxito con el modelo entrenado desde 0. Para que contase como un intento correcto, tenía que completarse la tarea totalmente.
Los datos de entrenamiento se habían recogido en otro sitio, pero lo nuevo eran las casas y objetos de evaluación. Lo que debemos tener claro es que un 56 % no quiere decir que pueda hacer más de la mitad de cualquier trabajo doméstico; es el resultado de estas pruebas.

articles.title: Intel réoriente une partie de sa production vers les CPU serveurs face à une demande IA record
articles.text:
Moins de processeurs Intel pour le grand public ? De toute façon, avec les prix de la mémoire vive et des SSD qui peut encore se monter un PC ?
Refrain entendu déjà des centaines de fois, l'intelligence artificielle cannibalise la production en matière de RAM et de SSD, mais elle nécessite aussi de nombreux processeurs pour animer les serveurs. Dans ce contexte, Intel a décidé de revoir sa stratégie.
Recul du PC personnel, croissance de l'IA
Ce n'est une surprise pour personne avec les prix actuels, le secteur du PC grand public recule chaque trimestre un peu plus et les prévisions en la matière ne sont guère optimistes pour l'ensemble de l'année prochaine.
Pourtant grand fournisseur de CPU pour le grand public, Intel ne semble cependant pas trop s'inquiéter de ce recul et ses principaux dirigeants estiment que la croissance du secteur de l'intelligence artificielle fera plus que compenser ces « pertes » sur le marché des ordinateurs personnels. C'est en ce sens qu'une importante réorientation de la production a été décidée.
Évoquant la demande croissante de l'IA, Lip-Bu Tan – le PDG d'Intel – a ainsi déclaré au cours d'une conférence téléphonique sur les résultats du groupe : « Le secteur continue de faire face à l'une des pénuries d'approvisionnement les plus importantes de son histoire, alimentée par une demande sans précédent en matière de superintelligence. »
« Dans ce contexte, je suis satisfait des progrès réalisés au troisième trimestre en matière d'augmentation de notre production de serveurs. Je reste néanmoins conscient des défis que nous devrons relever dans les prochains trimestres pour répondre à la demande croissante. »
Réorientation de la production Intel 18A
Une augmentation de la production en matière de CPU serveurs qui est passée par l'agrandissement de l'usine Intel Fab 24 située en Irlande, mais également par l'installation de nouveaux équipements dans l'usine Fab 62 en Arizona.
Cette réorientation de la production d'Intel ne surprend pas les analystes dans la mesure où la demande en processeurs pour serveurs continue de dépasser l'offre, malgré les augmentations évoquées précédemment. Ainsi, la division DCAI (Data Center and AI) du groupe américain a généré 7,3 milliards de dollars de chiffre d'affaires sur le seul troisième trimestre 2026, soit une progression de 17 % par rapport au trimestre précédent et de près de 80 % sur un an.
Intel anticipe donc une demande soutenue – voire en augmentation – sur les prochaines années et entend donc y répondre par un accroissement de la production de processeurs Xeon 6 « Granite Rapids », fabriqués avec la technologie de gravure Intel 3. L'agrandissement de la Fab 24 irlandaise ne suffira cependant pas et Intel entend également convertir une partie des ressources de son usine située en Oregon.
Une usine qui devait être avant tout destinée à la production de puces selon le plus récent procédé du groupe, l'Intel 18A, et qui donc va être en partie convertie vers l'Intel 3. « Pour installer Intel 3 en Oregon, nous mettons hors service des wafers de 18A, qui servent généralement à fabriquer des produits Panther Lake », a précisé Dave Zinsner, directeur financier d'Intel. « La libération de cette capacité nous permettra de produire davantage de wafers pour les centres de données ».
Clairement, Intel entend « profiter » de la baisse du marché du PC personnel et de la croissance que connaît l'activité intelligence artificielle. Pour autant, les travaux d'agrandissement et de réorientation ne produiront pas immédiatement leurs effets, on parle du second semestre 2027. Enfin, Intel entend profiter des optimisations réalisées sur le processus Intel 3 pour augmenter ses marges : il est question d'une baisse des coûts de fabrication d'environ 15 % depuis le premier trimestre 2026.
Source : Tom's Hardware

articles.title: Windows 11: Darum friert der Taskmanager immer dann ein, wenn man ihn braucht
articles.text:
Windows 11: Darum friert der Taskmanager immer dann ein, wenn man ihn braucht
Wenn Programme hängen oder abstürzen, wird der Taskmanager zum wichtigen Werkzeug für Windows-Nutzer:innen. Schließlich lassen sich darüber die betroffenen Anwendungen schließen, auch wenn sie nicht reagieren. Doch manchmal braucht die Systemfunktion dann selbst lange zum Laden. Woran das liegt, erklärt Microsoft-Entwickler Raymond Chen in einem Blogbeitrag.
„Wenn ein System unter CPU-Mangel leidet, sind alle Prozesse davon betroffen“, schreibt er. „Das gilt auch für die Taskleiste und den Taskmanager – ausgerechnet jene Werkzeuge, die man eigentlich nutzen möchte, um den Prozess zu beenden, der das System in die Knie zwingt.“
Warum eine höhere Priorität das Problem nicht löst
Um das Problem zu verstehen, muss man wissen, dass eine CPU nur eine begrenzte Anzahl von Threads gleichzeitig verarbeiten kann. Windows legt die Reihenfolge der Ausführung mithilfe von Prioritätsstufen (0 bis 31) fest. Wenn eine rechenintensive Anwendung die CPU vollständig beansprucht, müssen alle anderen Prozesse warten – auch der Taskmanager. Dieser benötigt jedoch selbst CPU-Zeit, um sein Fenster zu zeichnen, die Prozessliste zu aktualisieren und auf Benutzereingaben, wie etwa Mausklicks, zu reagieren.
Liegt es dann aber nicht nahe, dem Taskmanager eine möglichst hohe Priorität einzuräumen? Laut Chen würde das Vorgehen das Problem nicht lösen, denn ein Thread mit hoher Priorität kann ebenfalls blockiert werden. Und zwar dann, wenn er auf eine Ressource wartet, die von einem anderen, langsameren Thread belegt wird.
Die Priorität bestimmt demnach lediglich, welcher Thread als Nächstes CPU-Zeit erhält. Sie ermöglicht es einem Thread jedoch nicht, eine Sperre, eine Datei oder eine andere gemeinsam genutzte Ressource zu umgehen, die bereits von einem anderen Thread belegt wird. Ein Thread, der auf eine solche Sperre wartet, befindet sich laut Windows Latest gar nicht erst in der Warteschlange für die CPU.
Tech-Nostalgie aus den 90ern
Das könnt ihr tun, wenn der Taskmanager nicht mehr reagiert
Chen vergleicht dies mit einer Situation im Supermarkt. „Mit einem ‚Priority Checkout Pass‘ (einem Vorrang-Ticket für die Kasse) gelangst du zwar an den Anfang der Schlange, aber wenn die Person vor dir einen voll beladenen Einkaufswagen hat, musst du eben warten, bis sie fertig ist – erst dann bist du an der Reihe.“ Keine noch so hohe CPU-Priorität könne ein langsames Netzwerk dazu bringen, schneller zu reagieren. Chen erklärte auch, warum Microsoft den Taskmanager nicht „unverwundbar“ machen kann: „Das Problem ist, dass es schwierig ist, ein außer Kontrolle geratenes System von innerhalb eben dieses Systems zu reparieren“, schrieb er.
Was ihr tun könnt, wenn der Taskmanager oder die Taskleiste nicht mehr reagieren: Drückt die Tastenkombination Strg+Alt+Entf. Der Sicherheitsbildschirm läuft so auf einem eigenen, geschützten Desktop und ermöglicht es euch, den Taskmanager zu starten, sich abzumelden oder das System neu zu starten. Allerdings kann es auch hier zu Verzögerungen kommen, wenn Windows schwerwiegend blockiert ist.
Did you switch it off and on again?

articles.title: Another child dies of measles as CDC reportedly holds up health alert
articles.text:
A child in New York has died of measles, health officials in the state announced late Monday. It marks the first reported measles-associated death in New York in more than 30 years. It is the seventh measles-linked death reported in the US this year; all six of the other deaths were reported in Pennsylvania, which is experiencing a dramatic measles outbreak that has stricken over 1,430 people this year. Prior to the deaths, Pennsylvania hadn’t seen a measles-related death in 35 years.
The boom in vaccine-preventable outbreaks, cases, and tragic deaths is being fueled by slipping vaccination rates nationwide as health misinformation and anti-vaccine sentiments have taken hold. One of the most prominent anti-vaccine activists in the US currently serves as the US health secretary; Robert F. Kennedy Jr. spent decades prior to taking office attacking vaccines and spreading misinformation. He and his anti-vaccine organization, Children’s Health Defense, have been one of the most prolific sources of anti-vaccine content.
Since taking office, Kennedy has waged a multi-front war on vaccines that has included dismantling and obstructing federal vaccine recommendations; launching dubious studies to look for alleged, unspecified harms of vaccines; promoting alleged vaccine injuries; and continuing to spread misinformation about vaccines and vaccine-preventable illnesses.
In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul directly tied the state’s death to Kennedy’s policies and anti-vaccine activism. She called the child’s death “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.” She also said she was “heartbroken” by the death, sending her condolences to the family. “As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through,” Hochul said. Overall, New York has reported 170 measles cases in over a dozen counties.

articles.title: Samaila Zubairu: AI alone can’t formalise Africa’s economy
articles.text:
Speaking alongside the heads of AfDB and Afreximbank at AFIS 2026 in Luanda, Angola, Samaila Zubairu, chief executive officer of Africa Finance Corporation (AFC), warned that artificial intelligence and digital apps cannot formalise the continent’s shadow economy without massive investment in basic physical infrastructure. GODFREY GEORGE reports
The persistent belief across Africa’s technology ecosystem that digital platforms and artificial intelligence can leapfrog traditional industrialisation collided with hard realities on Tuesday inside the plenary halls of the Africa Financial Summit (AFIS) in Luanda, Angola.
Addressing financial leaders on his panel, “Capital Architecture: A New Age for African Finance,” Zubairu warned that tech alone cannot formalise the continent’s massive informal economy.
Software applications, Zubairu argued, are rendered practically useless when businesses lack fundamental physical utilities like electricity, storage, and transport networks.
Responding to panel discussions on digitisation and emerging technological disruption, Zubairu noted that while artificial intelligence presents tangible risks to current labour markets, it cannot operate in a vacuum.
For technology to drive real economic formalisation, it requires foundational enablers that cannot be coded.
“AI is a threat, but it will not work in isolation,” Zubairu said. “It requires other supporting elements, including digital service provision, accessible land titles, effective tax systems, training systems, digital access to government services, and the infrastructure needed to support businesses.”
Zubairu pointed out that economies such as China managed to formalise vast informal sectors not merely by deploying administrative mandates or digital tools, but by building the physical infrastructure that drastically lowers the cost of doing business.
In Africa, where the informal sector accounts for about 83% of total employment, attempting to digitise small enterprises without reliable electricity, warehousing, cold chains, and telecommunications networks will not lift productivity.
According to the AFC chief, African policymakers and investors must step back from isolated interventions and embrace comprehensive industrial master planning.
Rather than treating infrastructure developments as stand-alone engineering projects, Zubairu argued that policymakers must deliberately plan entire regional ecosystems around them.
He pointed to the multi-billion-dollar Lobito Corridor—a strategic railway project connecting the mineral-rich belts of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia to Angola’s Atlantic port—as a prime example of an asset that must serve a broader economic purpose.
Instead of functioning merely as another extractive conduit for shipping unrefined raw materials to overseas buyers, Zubairu insisted that the corridor be leveraged to anchor regional processing, local agricultural distribution, and cross-border energy trade.
“We should be thinking about agricultural value chains, the mining sector, and the other industries that can develop around it,” Zubairu said.
“We should be thinking about the amount of energy that will be required within that economic zone and whether we should be creating an integrated energy hub. We should consider how electricity generated in Angola can reach the wider region, and we should also ensure that the minerals extracted are processed within the region, rather than simply exporting raw materials.”
Zubairu added that industrial planning must also extend to urbanisation, cautioning that large-scale infrastructure projects will inevitably attract human migration.
Without proactive planning, emerging transport and mining hubs risk turning into unplanned urban slums rather than structured, productive commercial centres.
The debate underscored a broader institutional dilemma, as highlighted by the panel’s moderator: the divergent speeds at which African development is currently moving.
While tech entrepreneurs operate on an accelerated digital timeline and development financiers coordinate cross-border capital, bureaucratic state machinery often operates at an excruciatingly slow pace.
As the AFC, AfDB, and Afreximbank attempt to build a unified African Financial Architecture for Development, the consensus delivered in Luanda was uncompromising.
For Africa’s technology sector, the lesson is clear: apps and algorithms cannot substitute for power plants, freight rails, and factories.
Until the hard, physical back end of the continent’s economy is built, the promise of digital formalisation will remain unfulfilled.

articles.title: Refrigerator cyberattack spreads to many European countries, spoiling food worth thousands
articles.text:
What we know so far: Last month's cyberattack on French grocery store refrigerators became an expensive reminder of the risks of relying on the Internet of Things for critical infrastructure. New attacks this week show that several European countries face the same vulnerabilities, with lax security practices and obsolete systems the likely culprits.
A cyberattack on internet-connected refrigeration systems ruined food at grocery stores in at least seven European countries on Monday, with one Belgian Delhaize store estimating its losses at €100,000. The attack mirrors the one that hit French grocers in mid-October, exposing gaping security holes.
Grocery stores and chains in Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia reported that refrigerators had been set to defrost, in some cases raising temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit), spoiling food and leaving many shelves empty. The French attack set cooling systems to the same temperature and caused damages estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
An ICA store manager in Stockholm told Reuters on Monday that employees didn't notice the attack, which hit at 2am local time, until hours later, by which point "everything" was destroyed. Other targeted businesses include Delhaize in Belgium and Luxembourg, Carrefour and De Laet & Van Haver in Belgium, Coop in Sweden, and more.
It remains unclear who was responsible for the attacks. No one has claimed responsibility, and at least some affected stores have security vulnerabilities so deep that practically anyone could have accessed their systems.
The refrigerators attacked in France were operated by Danfoss, and the incident came two months after security researchers at Claroty warned of multiple vulnerabilities in the company's controllers. Danfoss also supplied the affected units in at least some of Monday's attacks, though Belgian installer Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's refrigeration, was also involved.
Security researcher Kevin Beaumont says several thousand Danfoss management systems are directly reachable from the internet with essentially nonexistent login security. In his words, the username is "admin" and the password changes daily to the current date. Claroty's research points to a hidden daily code derived from the date that bypasses the real password, a flaw Danfoss has since patched.
Furthermore, many affected systems were running outdated firmware, and some can't receive patches at all because they are end-of-life, a common risk with IoT devices. Shodan.io shows thousands of exposed Danfoss units, more than half in France, with others in South Africa and elsewhere.
Whether a sophisticated state actor or a bored individual was behind the attacks, they serve as another lesson in IoT pitfalls. Some also fear that similar incidents could form part of a broader effort to destabilize a country's infrastructure.

This is also the painter's experience where over time you keep using that paintbrush, and then there's some legacy there, and then there's a brittleness from the dried paint. This is our experience as well, where we see maybe some things that became overly constrained or overly defined over time, we kept adding to it, now became brittle, so our code becomes brittle, or we have the legacy, we have things like that that are lying around that we're unaware of, or really need to be able to address and detect that arises.
Then tin cans flung in disarray, anarchy from side to side. This is part of it, this is part of creation, is the messiness. In this poem, Mira's embracing it. Then, finally, view this mental storm from the out, to see not the unfinished canvas, not an end or a start, but a beautiful masterpiece that has become your art. Essentially, what this is saying is, step back, look at what you've created, and yes, it is unfinished, just like our products are unfinished, and over time, we collectively work on it, it becomes a piece of art. Then, any constraints. There's a palette of paint, colors that are already chosen beyond which you would not want to go to other color schemes. These are types of constraints that we may also have for when we're establishing any structural type of constraints for our agents as well. Then, finally, validations. What might be some things that we've already learned along the way, any prototyping and small experimental forms and things like that that then lead and become context to the paint and the canvas that we're about to put together. Structurally there might be our type systems. We might have sandboxes for our agents, things like that. That still allowed bounded autonomy for the agents, but we're providing these types of boundaries. Reactive, we might have backpressure. We might have rate limits, things like that, and linters, and so forth that we also have our agents leverage. Then you have dynamism. You have some dynamic feedback guardrails as well. Those might be things that you want to be able to assess from a guardrail standpoint. Like, what are those drifts? What are those architecture drifts? What are those drifts from, the spec said this, but you're actually implementing this, things like that. If there's any budget runs, if there's any cost optimizations, things like that that we're going beyond. We have to be able to step back and see that. Finally, reflective, some reflective feedback. We dive deep and we're going in the rabbit hole and working through this. Wait, let's step back. Is this where we want it to be? Let's do any postmortems and retrospectives on how things are and so forth. This is all part of that experience, and hence the canvas experiences that we have. That was the what. That was talking about harness engineering, the evolution towards that, the verbiage, the taxonomy for that, and now also starting to think, what if we think about it as a system? What if we think about it as a canvas for creativity, but still with bounded autonomy?
Why?
Now let's go a little bit into the why. Why bother with this and why are we doing this? Some of this, I think we're all experiencing. The first thing, of course, is just the industrial pressures that exist in our own organizations. It's like, whether you want to or not, if you are in this industry, it is coming to us and has already entered our own goals and requirements coming from leadership. This is coming from McKinsey, of course, is one of the consulting firms, also consulting leaders in organizations on this whole AI movement. It starts with where we were, let's say, status quo. Then once GitHub Copilot, for instance, came in, and now you have developers always using AIs as an assistant or pairing with AI, maybe you might result in 1.2x if things are good, improvements in productivity. Then when you start having coding agents, so beyond just GitHub Copilot's assistant mechanism, but a coding agent with that harness and things like that, then maybe you might see 2x improvement.
Then, really, where people are looking to go, and this is where leadership are seeing this type of slide. They're saying, we can do even more because we can have a whole swarm of coding agents, and now everybody as developers, we elevate, and each of us become architects and so forth. That might be a 20x improvement. This is one of the whys. We've been learning as we've been experimenting with these coding agents. This one is coming from LangChain, Viv's blog post that I mentioned earlier. Here, what they found was that, if they take a model and all they do is change the harness and improve on the harness, they were able to have real improvements. They went from top 30 to top 5 on the Terminal-Bench 2.0's benchmarking. There is credibility around this way of thinking about leveraging harnesses.
I'm curious, have any of you experimented with harnesses? There are some starter kits and things like that on GitHub. This just came out in February. Still, this is something that we're experiencing. When we hear from people like LangChain, OpenAI, and these bigger companies, allows us to learn from them. This is definitely interesting, worth looking at their blog post on some of their learnings. OpenAI, as I mentioned, a million lines of code in five months. One of their lessons was just that we need to have continuous garbage collection, because now that we are going faster we can't wait to have that maybe a sprint zero or a sprint just for cleaning. Sometimes teams do that. We need to have continuous garbage collection. What they did was they launched separate agents where their role just was to do garbage collection. That garbage collection could be anything from code that's not used or detecting drift, feature toggles unused, anything like that as well.
This one, there's quite a few industry learnings here about not constraining agents. If we constrain the agents too much, then you get context bloat because you're saying all of these things, and then there's cognitive misunderstanding and communication interaction failures with the agent because it doesn't know what to follow. Those issues arise. Then, also, what we might be creating as agent skills, they might become brittle because there's too much complexity. We're saying do this and do that and do that. It's such micro-optimizations that any little change, the agent is not able to self-heal and recover because it's been told too many things. I think those are some learnings for us to consider.
In the article that I mentioned earlier by the team in China, they had a whole taxonomy of failures from their experiences. They talk about, for instance, it's possible that the context itself, the agent doesn't have the context that it needs. Maybe the tool that it's trying to fetch doesn't have access to it. There's any access issues to the tool, or it doesn't know which tool to discover, things like that. Maybe the feedback mechanism that we may have put into play becomes unavailable or is not accessible for any reason, or the agent doesn't understand it. The models themselves might have some failures that were unexpected. Then on the bottom row we have things that agents may not be able to verify for whatever reason. Entropy is going to continue to be there. That's just part of law of thermodynamics. Regardless of what we do, there's always going to be entropy.
When it comes to architecture, we're always managing entropy. That's going to be part of whatever we build. Even today without machine agents or in the past without machine agents, these were things that we would run into. Recovery, so maybe there is an issue in production or issue with some tests and whatever, and agents not able to recover from that. These are different types of agentic issues. Sometimes we don't really know the root cause. I do want to say while, for instance, models will continue to improve and the harnesses provided by our coding agent providers, they might focus more on the top and be able to bridge the gap between what they provide and what we're able to do today. However, the things on the bottom, like they're always going to be there. They always have been there even without machine agents. Just want to share that these types of failures, we're not here to control and prevent.
Instead, the alternative model is, how do we make ourselves resilient? Like the DevOps model, if something's going to fail and has failed, try to make it happen more often so that you have a much more resilient system so you know how to recover from those failures. Then, finally, another industry learning also comes from Birgitta, and she was sharing that a lot of the work today up to now has been more on the coding tasks related stuff and maintainability of code and things like that. What's a gap right now is behavioral stuff. Like, what about the product standpoint? What are those behavioral, functional requirements? How do we work with our coding agents to support those?
How?
That's what I'm going to talk about actually in this next section, because we've been doing this. We have been working on functional requirements. Right now, our focus is on all the non-functional requirements. How do we now apply functional requirements to the coding agent world? Where I would like to start, this is actually coming from 2020, this is coming from my architecture experience earlier. I looked back at this, remember I said it feels very deja vu-ish, to like say, this is the product engineering operating model that we used at edX. Can this now be applied here where we're thinking about agents? I'm working with some life science clients right now, and we're trying to put together an operating model as we're working with agentic code and stuff like that. I looked back at this to see how might we do this. Then, whatever canvas we might develop for the agents, how might we leverage from here?
Let's take this one by one of what we're talking about. You'll see overall, even then, we were thinking about, and this is just the human world, the define phase, the build phase, and review phase. As a product organization, when we're defining, we're thinking about what's the overall strategy, product strategy, what are the opportunities, what are those hypotheses that we might want to test and experiment with. We might do things like Lean Value Trees. We might do some opportunity mapping and so forth. Then the output of that could be things like the opportunity trees, the strategy documents, and so forth. Then when we're building and we're iterating, continuous iteration, lean startup type of style, we might experiment as we do this, so continuous discovery as we're building. Then there, those outputs are specifications as well as any other compliance reports and things like that that we generate from our CI/CD pipelines and so forth.
That was always something that we also did. Then there's the review aspect. This part is interesting. I did want to call it out. I don't think the visual does it justice. There is a time aspect to reviews. Then there's the people or the who aspect to reviews as well. Who is doing which reviews, and then when? Because not everything needs to happen all the time. There's microfeedback loops as well as macrofeedback loops. Then the team themselves would do reviews of their builds and do that in their own sprint demos and so forth. Maybe with their stakeholders and the customers. Then there might be some opportunity reviews that we might do with the product leader or the product organization that requested the change in the first place. Then there might be some strategic reviews. Those strategic reviews are not just with the business organization, but also the engineering leaders. Your VP of engineering, your CTO, whatnot, may want to be able to see, we said that we want to have these metrics, everything for value, flow, quality of our work. Where are we on those? Those are reports that we would generate along the way. I wanted to share that.
The other thing that comes in the build phase are decision records. You're also generating architecture decision records. Proposal here is to also generate product decision records as you go along the way. Those then become artifacts. Those are the traces or the pheromones that we leave behind. Then it doesn't matter which agent is there. It doesn't matter if we have cognitive gaps. We can pick it up as we go, depending on the quality of those decisions. Then the other aspect I want to share, this is also coming from past work, not even in the agentic era, but where we were thinking about, strategically, what are all the different ways that we think about providing context to our teams? Going from right to left, so at the organization level, we have our mission and our values and our vision. These don't change as frequently, so there's less volatile.
Then, as you go from right to left, it becomes more volatile. The context is also handed down from right to left. Then information is forwarded from left to right. You'll see goals and outcomes and key results and problem statements and all of that providing the why as well as what are we trying to do, any guidelines about the how we do it, but then also very valuably is how we're going to measure. How we measure, I know right now, I think there were other talks around metrics and stuff too, and it comes up a lot. I wasn't going to go into it too detail in this talk. I think that's a whole other talk and a whole other exploration of what measures are most impactful and don't constrain us and don't become vanity metrics or have unintended consequences, but also thinking about metrics as also evolving.
It's not just a one-time thing but things that would evolve. Here too, if you go right to left, the metrics that are more on the right-hand side may not change as frequently, like KPIs, key performance indicators for your organization don't change as much, because those are ongoing observations. It might be your customer satisfaction. It might also be your code quality, things like that. The key results are things that you're going to do for a particular initiative, for a particular moment in time for a product. Going from the organization to a product to initiative to a task.
How does this apply to agentic coding? The organization here is essentially your agentic team topology, however you may choose to design that. Could be 100 agents working together. It could be five or one. That's something that you would design for yourself, depending on the size of your problem space. I wanted to bring this because I'm not seeing this applied so far as much right now in our conversations because we're talking a lot more about coding. The point is how might we apply things from product engineering there. You'll see here, for instance, the example that we were working with from the life science company. This is just a screenshot coming from basically providing as context to the agent about what we just talked about. Then, actually leveraging the agent to define what is the mission, what are the goals, and so forth. Providing the agent basically the overall structure here and how we want to go about it.
Then you still use the agent to assist you with whatever context you have to accelerate this. Then the agent themselves are creating these documents, these are all Markdown files, for this type of thing. What is going to be the product's KPIs, goals, and so forth? Then you'll see here, it's also developing those decision records, architecture ones, and product decision records. It's part of its now its process as it's working through this canvas that we designed. There's an example decision record around designing a control port for human in the loop. You'll see things like, I've asked it to really think about decay and drift and think about panels, control panels, where I can look at the measures and the metrics and so forth. Then also number five, there is adversarial input. I want to be able to, as a human, actually go ahead and destroy things, remove things, take away things, take away code, or take away a tool that it expected and make sure that it's resilient and recovering.
You'll see some of this output from a dashboard that we had created. It's able to show the decay, the staleness, and so forth. Any drifts that it's able to find. Even adversarial probes, for instance being able to make sure that what we expected, if we do go ahead, and this is talking about patient keys and stuff like that because this is from the life science example I was talking about. You'll see that some of these outcomes are therefore reviewable.
Summary
In summary, some of the takeaways that we talked about. These mental model shifts, consider those. How might they actually enable us evolve our thinking as the industry changes, as we change. Let's not over-constrain ourselves, but at the same time, of course, be responsible with the right bounded context. We talked about a bounded canvas, how you still want to do boundaries but still provide the autonomy so that agents and the generative capabilities of agents can be leveraged. Then, when it comes to stigmergy, leaving traces behind. Whether it's a human agent or a machine agent or whoever changes hands. We're able to also do traceability, be able to understand what it did. In terms of product engineering models, a lot of that work that we did for our own human topologies, how might we leverage that to our machine topologies? Let's think back to it so that the behavioral outcomes are also there, not just the cross-functional ones. Let's design for change and design for failures.
Does this resonate, whether you're a lead architect or a senior leader or a manager or a technologist, this type of way of thinking about bounded autonomy, these are things that we've experienced in many different ways.
Questions and Answers
Participant 1: It definitely resonated with me, a lot of what you had to say. I have two thoughts. One is more of a comment, but it's an insight from a friend. You showed this picture of a dog weighed down by 100 rules. One of the things my friend has been drilling into me is this idea of the model captures all the possibilities that it's been trained on. That when you imagine, like if you were in a situation and someone gave you 100 rules, what kind of response you would have? It's not to be creative and capable. You're asking for a mindless automaton, and that's what you get. A not very skilled junior engineer, where you're treating it like a junior engineer, and that's what you get. If you want a senior engineer, you have to treat it like a senior engineer, and show respect. It just makes sense. Then you're putting yourself more in the probability space of the conversations it's seen with senior engineers where they're very capable, and that's what you're more likely to get out. I thought that was a really interesting way of thinking about it.
One of the things that really has been troubling me is how to keep a view of the architecture as I'm lifting up. You mentioned decision records. I have similar things where it's like, ok, I've got a lot of documents describing things I did and the way I thought about it at the time. The integral of that over time is the architecture, and that is much more challenging to keep up to date, I find.
Nimisha Asthagiri: One of the things maybe I went through is maps. Maps are as critical, I think. Once again, let's take our learnings from architecture and things like that and how it might be applied here. Decision records is very key, and they're too, not all decisions are equal. One of the other guidelines I had provided the agents were also which decisions require human review, which ones don't, which ones require decision records, which ones maybe, so the reversibility of the decisions are there. The other guideline is about drawing maps and keeping those maps up to date. Those maps, we have to be very intentional about which ones matter, and which ones are ok to drift, which ones do we want to keep up to date. By maps there, I'm talking about, it could be the C4 diagrams and the simplicity of that, but don't go all the way down to level 4, not needed anymore. Just level 0, level 1 of C4 diagrams might be sufficient. There might also be maps that sometimes we create from a product standpoint as well. The product strategic maps, lean value tree maps, Wardley mapping, so those things. Just for that context sharing.
Another thing here is that before, people used to put a lot of things in README files, or even in like CLAUDE.md and things like that. The recommendation now is don't, like that's too much, because those CLAUDE.md type files go into the agent's context every single time. It gets too noisy for them. Why do I have to keep hearing that over and over again? It's not applicable for what I need to do now. Really just keep a map of the folder structure. That's enough. Things like that.
One other comment I wanted to make, which I forgot, which is important too, is one of my learnings is also I had all of those strategy docs and all of that. I think I may have overengineered it, because I think there was a little bit of feedback when I was working with the agent about where to start. I do think that's another recommendation here too from the field as well is, don't over-constrain it. You want to be able to build up that. Then over time your harness or your canvas will get better.

articles.title: How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search
Your professional reputation now lives online first. Recruiters check LinkedIn before returning a call. Clients review your digital presence before booking a first meeting. For ambitious professionals, that shift is an opportunity: a well-crafted online voice can open doors that a résumé alone never could.
But standing out takes more than content generation. It takes real-time awareness of what’s happening right now. A professional building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader needs to react to today’s breakthroughs, not last week’s headlines. And with feeds flooded by AI-generated noise, audiences reward authenticity and timeliness more than ever.
Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore made that possible. We built Norton Revamp, a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform. At its heart is an AI-curated News Engine, powered by AgentCore Web Search, that grounds every content suggestion, goal recommendation, and news feed item in current, cited web knowledge. The platform launched in March 2026, built by a small group of engineers.
In this post, we show you how the Gen team builds an AI-curated News Engine in Norton Revamp with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search to help customers turn ideas into engaging social media posts.
The challenge: Real-time grounding for professional content
Unlike chatbots that rely on static knowledge bases, Norton Revamp needs to understand what’s trending right now in each user’s professional domain. A cyber security expert needs today’s threat intelligence. A marketing leader needs this week’s industry shifts. Traditional approaches (custom web crawlers, third-party news APIs, static content databases) each carry trade-offs: infrastructure overhead, stale data, vendor complexity, or data egress risk.
We evaluated three alternatives before choosing AgentCore Web Search. Custom crawlers require ongoing maintenance and lag real time. Third-party news APIs added vendor contracts, API key management, and data leaving our AWS environment. Static knowledge bases were perpetually stale. AgentCore Web Search eliminated these concerns. It’s fully managed with zero infrastructure overhead, operates entirely within AWS with zero data egress, and returns cited sources with URLs and publication dates. This makes personalized, real-time news feeds viable at scale.
How AgentCore Web Search powers Norton Revamp
Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a fully managed web search capability, compliant with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It’s available as a managed connector on the AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Our agent sends a natural-language query, and Web Search returns relevant snippets, source URLs, titles, and publication dates that the model uses to produce grounded responses.
This capability powers three core features:
AI-curated news feed
Every user gets a personalized content stream surfacing the latest articles and trending topics tied to their goal. If you’re building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader, your feed prioritizes AI breakthroughs, industry analysis, and emerging use cases, sourced in real time through AgentCore Web Search. Unlike a static RSS aggregator, the feed is a goal-aware discovery engine that refreshes with every session.
Smart content suggestions
Users receive AI-generated content ideas tailored to trending topics in their space, written in their own authentic voice, with optional AI-generated visuals. AgentCore Web Search grounds every suggestion on what’s happening today. A three-step coaching flow (Analyze, Refine, Post) walks users from initial ideas to published content on LinkedIn and X, with a feedback loop, so the AI gets sharper with every iteration.
Trend-aware goal setting
Users define a goal. The AI builds a personalized roadmap with weekly themes and milestones. AgentCore Web Search feeds real-time trend data into goal generation, so weekly themes reflect current industry movements. The system learns from the past four weeks of activity, refreshing recommendations as users grow.
Architecture and tech stack
The integration follows an event-driven architecture. When a user sets or updates their professional goal, Amazon Nova (through Amazon Bedrock) generates targeted search queries based on the goal, recent activity, and engagement patterns. The agent sends these queries to AgentCore Web Search, which returns cited results entirely within our AWS environment. Our AI Learning System ranks the results for relevance, recency, and source credibility. The ranked results then serve as grounding context for Amazon Nova Lite to generate content suggestions in the user’s authentic voice. Engagement data feeds back into query generation, making the News Engine progressively smarter.
Generative AI and machine learning stack:
- Amazon Bedrock – Core generative AI engine for content generation, personalization, post analysis (batch mode), and content coaching.
- Amazon Nova (Nova Lite) – Primary large language model (LLM) powering content generation, goal creation, and trend analysis.
- Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Real-time web retrieval powering the News Engine, content grounding, and trend discovery through an MCP-compliant managed connector.
- Stability AI – Image generation.
- Claude (through Amazon Bedrock) – Additional LLM capabilities for complex reasoning tasks.
Infrastructure: React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS on the frontend. Node.js, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB (multi-table with composite key patterns), Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon EventBridge, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS Secrets Manager on the backend. Infrastructure managed through Terraform with blue-green deployment for zero-downtime releases.
Processing pipeline: The platform runs four pipeline stages:
- Full Scan – Pull up to 1,000 historical posts, store in Amazon S3, run Amazon Bedrock batch analysis for reputation impact.
- Daily Scan – Amazon EventBridge-triggered incremental analysis.
- Weekly Goal Generation – Lambda generates goals considering past engagement data plus real-time trend data from AgentCore Web Search.
- Content Coaching – Synchronous Amazon Bedrock calls through the Analyze, Refine, Post flow, each step grounded with AgentCore Web Search results.
Engineering with an AI-native development mindset
We embedded generative AI from day one, as both the product and the development methodology. The human-AI responsibility split was deliberate: human-owned architecture decisions, security reviews, business logic, and personalization algorithms. AI handled code generation, documentation, test scaffolding, refactoring, and UI component creation.
With Claude, we produced 10 or more design variants per concept, compressed design-to-prototype time from weeks to hours and generated 70 percent of UI code with AI. We tested five pricing models in the time previously needed for one. The gamification system went through eight iterations before launching.
The measurable impact: 3x faster feature implementation, boilerplate generation accelerated by 90 percent, documentation by 80 percent, test creation by 70 percent, and UI component generation by 65 percent. The trade-off: AI output review consumed 20–30 percent of our time.
AI helped with personalization algorithms, the DynamoDB multi-table architecture (which needed experience-based judgment), security implementation, and Amazon Bedrock batch processing optimization. The key insight: AI accelerated implementation, but humans designed how the AI Learning System should adapt to user goals. Product generative AI (Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova, AgentCore Web Search) and development generative AI served different purposes, and we kept them separate.
Testing, security, and quality assurance
We achieved 85 percent code coverage through automated test generation. Critical test areas included content generation quality, AgentCore Web Search result relevance and freshness validation, engagement tracking accuracy, gamification logic, and news feed relevance to user goals.
For a product carrying the Norton brand, compliance is non-negotiable. Security checks spanned static code analysis, dependency vulnerability scanning, authentication flows, user data encryption, access control logic, generative AI model output validation, and content filtering. Our security team reviewed all AI-generated recommendations: AI accelerated identification, and humans made final decisions.
The result: 99.9 percent uptime since launch with real-time monitoring of generative AI content quality and user satisfaction.
Best practices for AgentCore Web Search integration
For teams considering AgentCore Web Search for real-time grounding:
- Invest in query generation – Well-structured queries yield better results than open-ended ones, so we focused on our prompt engineering there.
- Cache strategically – Real-time freshness is the point, but some queries don’t need to re-execute every session. We cache results with time-to-live (TTL) values that match freshness requirements.
- Build feedback loops – Track which web search results users engage with and feed that signal back into query generation. Our News Engine’s relevance improved over the first 90 days.
- Validate source quality – AgentCore Web Search returns source URLs and publication dates. We built a lightweight credibility scoring layer to prioritize authoritative sources.
Conclusion
Building Norton Revamp proved that a small, generative AI-augmented team can deliver enterprise software in months. It also proved that Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can serve as the real-time intelligence backbone for products that need to stay current with the world.
We launched a generative AI-native professional reputation management platform in months, with personalized goal setting, AI-driven content suggestions, real-time curated news feeds grounded by AgentCore Web Search, adaptive learning, gamification, and Norton-grade security. A small group of engineers achieved 99.9 percent uptime.
Generative AI doesn’t replace engineers. It amplifies them. Pairing that amplification with fully managed services like AgentCore Web Search removes entire categories of infrastructure complexity. Humans designed the vision. Generative AI through Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova, and AgentCore Web Search accelerated bringing it to life, grounded in real-time, cited web knowledge.
        “Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore eliminates the complexity of building and maintaining our own web retrieval infrastructure. It lets our Norton Revamp News Engine deliver real-time, personalized content grounded in what’s happening in each user’s professional domain, with zero data egress and Norton-grade privacy. We went from concept to production in months, and AgentCore Web Search was a key enabler.”
To learn more about Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, visit the AgentCore documentation. Check out Norton Revamp.

articles.title: Goldman Sachs restricted Claude Code for bankers — but made one surprising exception
articles.text:
Goldman Sachs restricted Claude Code for bankers — but made one surprising exception
Replit CEO Amjad Masad is warning that AI coding agents running on employee devices are becoming a security risk for enterprises and governments, as financial institutions begin restricting access to tools such as Claude Code.
“AI agents running on employee endpoints are becoming a systemic security risk for enterprises & governments,” Masad writes on X, Tuesday. “Some are responding by restricting tools like Claude Code, as Goldman Sachs reportedly has.”
“Some are responding by restricting tools like Claude Code, as Goldman Sachs reportedly has.”
Why finance restricts coding agents
His comments follow a Bloomberg report that Goldman Sachs has restricted access to Anthropic’s Claude Code and Microsoft’s GitHub coding tools to engineers. The restrictions apply to bankers and traders, but certain quantitative employees known as strats are exempt.
Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra told Bloomberg the bank weighs productivity gains against potential risks when deciding which employees can continue using AI tools.
Masad suggests Goldman Sachs is not alone.
“This is widespread in finance. The ban hammer is coming down,”
“This is widespread in finance. The ban hammer is coming down,” he writes, responding to a post about the bank’s restrictions.
When asked what was driving the crackdown, Masad points to “Supply chain attacks etc.”
The credential exposure problem
Running coding agents directly on employee machines raises concerns about credential exposure, malicious instructions and compromised dependencies, each of which has already surfaced well beyond the finance sector.
The credential question has been pushing vendors toward short-lived tokens for months, a shift Vercel recently forced on its own suppliers by setting a deadline to abandon the long-lived keys that an agent operating on an endpoint could quietly read and reuse.
When asked on X whether banks were more worried about code leaving their environments or a lack of audit trails, Masad says, “So many things.”
He offered no examples of security incidents that prompted Goldman’s restrictions or other financial institutions adopting similar policies.
Isolating agents in the cloud
Alongside his comments, Masad shares a security advisory published by Replit on Monday. Written by Luis Héctor Chávez, Replit’s chief technology officer, and engineering lead at Replit, Manish Mehta, it recommends keeping AI agents off employee devices and running them in company-controlled cloud environments instead.
“AI agents should operate in dedicated, organization-controlled environments with limited access to the resources each task requires,”
“AI agents should operate in dedicated, organization-controlled environments with limited access to the resources each task requires,” Masad writes.
Replit recommends running agents in isolated environments, with credentials, audit logs, and approvals managed separately.
The advisory points to recent security incidents, including a compromised Claude Code extension distributed through the Cursor marketplace, as an example of how attackers can exploit developer tools.
That pattern has played out repeatedly across the ecosystem this year, including an attack in which intruders hijacked roughly 1,900 GitHub accounts before moving against some 30,000 repositories, a reminder that a single poisoned link in the chain can reach far past the machine where it started.
Controlling what agents can access
But restricting AI coding agents to engineers doesn’t necessarily solve the problem. Even experienced developers can run agents that follow malicious instructions or pull in compromised software, and research has shown how little it takes to knock an agent off course, with one team finding that stripping a single line from Claude Code’s instructions sent its out-of-scope actions climbing. Replit argues that companies need to control what agents can do, not just who gets to use them.
What this means for enterprise AI adoption
Goldman’s restrictions suggest companies may be rethinking how widely they allow employees to use AI coding tools. Giving non-developers the ability to build software has been a major selling point, but that becomes harder to justify when agents have access to sensitive corporate systems.
Masad argues that companies don’t need to stop using agents. They need to keep them off employee devices and put tighter controls around what they can access.
Whether financial institutions broadly adopt that model remains to be seen. Masad has described restrictions as widespread, but has not provided public evidence establishing how many organizations have introduced them.
The New Stack has reached out to Replit for additional comment on the reported restrictions, the security concerns driving them, and whether financial institutions are changing their approach to AI coding agents.

articles.title: Canva is announcing changes and layoffs affecting 22 percent of its staff
articles.text:
Canva is making significant changes affecting 1,271 people, which is 22 percent of its staff, co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins announced today. “For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs,” says Perkins. “Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today.”
Canva is announcing changes and layoffs affecting 22 percent of its staff
Some Canva workers may have different roles, be asked to relocate, or be laid off.
In her note to staff, Perkins says that:
After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough. To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community.
Canva’s changes include bringing its Product, Growth, and Platform teams together into one product organization, “simplifying layers” and “consolidating overlapping responsibilities,” and making Sydney the “primary home for more of our product teams, as well as roles in other Specialties where shared context and close collaboration are especially important.” Starting in January, Canva will also “expect” most hybrid employees to spend 2 to 3 days in an office each week “depending on what makes sense in your area.”
Employees leaving Canva will get benefits including at least six months of salary, twelve months of healthcare coverage, and career support resources.
Yesterday, Squarespace announced layoffs affecting 19 percent of its staff.

articles.title: 10 European bootstrapped startups who are crushing it in 2026 | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Europe’s startup ecosystem is often associated with major funding rounds, venture capital and ambitious expansion plans. However, some of the continent’s most interesting companies are taking a different approach, building their businesses without relying on external investors. From AI-powered software to sustainable mobility solutions, these startups are demonstrating that significant progress doesn’t always require significant venture capital.
Bootstrapping allows founders to retain greater control over their businesses, prioritise profitability and develop products around the needs of paying customers. While this approach comes with its own challenges, including limited resources and the pressure to generate revenue early, it can also encourage leaner operations and more sustainable growth.
Across Europe, entrepreneurs are applying this model to a wide range of industries, including legal technology, construction, customer service, sustainability and digital marketing. Their businesses highlight the diversity of opportunities available to founders willing to grow on their own terms.
With that in mind, we’ve put together a list of 10 promising bootstrapped startups in alphabetical order. All founded from 2021 onwards, these companies are developing practical solutions to everyday business challenges while carving out their own paths in increasingly competitive markets.
Chatarmin (Austria)
Founded in 2022 in Vienna, Chatarmin is helping eCommerce businesses improve how they communicate with customers through WhatsApp and AI-powered customer support. Its platform integrates with popular eCommerce tools such as Shopify, Klaviyo and Shopware, enabling brands, retailers and franchise businesses to manage customer interactions and marketing campaigns more effectively. Through automated messaging and personalised communication, the company aims to strengthen customer engagement and help businesses build lasting relationships.
Blulinc (Belgium)
Belgium’s Blulinc, established in 2021, is making electric vehicle charging more accessible and manageable for businesses. Its smart charging solutions help companies oversee their charging infrastructure, manage electricity consumption and simplify the administrative processes associated with electric vehicle fleets. By combining charging management with energy optimisation and billing capabilities, Blulinc is supporting businesses as they transition towards more sustainable mobility.
CENDAS (Germany)
Since its founding in 2021, Bochum-based CENDAS has been developing digital tools for construction sites, helping tradespeople and construction businesses manage projects more efficiently. Its software supports the entire construction process, from initial preparation and task allocation to project execution, documentation and progress monitoring. By connecting office-based planning with on-site activities, CENDAS aims to reduce administrative workloads and improve collaboration between construction teams.
Freda (Sweden)
Emerging from Stockholm’s technology ecosystem in 2025, Freda is developing an AI-powered platform designed to simplify legal and regulatory compliance for businesses. By automating complex processes and organising regulatory requirements, its technology aims to reduce the administrative burden associated with compliance and make it easier for companies to navigate changing regulations. Its approach brings AI-driven automation to an industry traditionally dependent on manual processes and extensive documentation.
Herodesk (Denmark)
Founded in 2023 and headquartered in Aarhus, Denmark, Herodesk is helping small and medium-sized businesses improve customer service through an AI-powered support platform. Its software brings customer conversations from different communication channels into a shared inbox, allowing teams to manage enquiries, collaborate on responses and provide more consistent support. By combining customer service management with AI-powered automation, Herodesk helps smaller businesses handle growing support demands without significantly expanding their teams.
Nimber (Portugal)
Portugal’s technology consulting landscape welcomed Nimber in 2022, when the Lisbon-based company was established to help businesses navigate increasingly complex digital challenges. Its services span technology recruitment, cybersecurity, quality assurance and AI-related consulting, supporting organisations that need experienced professionals and practical solutions for their digital projects. By combining specialist talent with technical consulting, Nimber aims to help businesses strengthen their digital capabilities and access expertise across emerging technologies.
North ESG (Denmark)
Copenhagen-based North ESG entered the sustainability technology space in 2024 with a mission to make ESG reporting more manageable for small and medium-sized businesses. Its AI-powered accounting platform helps companies collect, organise and document environmental, social and governance data, reducing the time and resources needed to prepare sustainability reports. Through automated workflows and AI-supported documentation, North ESG helps smaller businesses respond to evolving regulatory requirements and growing expectations around sustainability transparency.
Senja (United Kingdom)
Launched in London in 2022, Senja is helping businesses turn positive customer experiences into valuable marketing assets. Its platform simplifies the process of collecting, organising and displaying customer testimonials, allowing companies to showcase feedback across websites, landing pages, emails and other digital channels. With support for written and video testimonials, Senja makes it easier for creators, startups and growing businesses to build credibility and strengthen customer trust through authentic feedback.
Submagic (France)
France’s Submagic has been simplifying short-form video production since its launch in Paris in 2023. Its AI-powered editing platform helps content creators, marketers and businesses automate time-consuming elements of video production, including caption generation, editing and turning longer recordings into shorter clips designed for social media. By making professional-looking videos easier to create without advanced editing skills, Submagic is helping users produce engaging content more efficiently.
Vaskeladden (Norway)
Established in Oslo in 2022, Vaskeladden is bringing an AI-driven approach to Norway’s cleaning industry, using technology to improve how cleaning services are priced, sold and managed. Its platform connects customers with cleaning providers while automating important parts of the business, including customer acquisition, operational coordination and customer support. By centralising these processes, Vaskeladden is applying AI and automation to modernise traditional cleaning services and make everyday operations more efficient.
Building European startups on their own terms
These 10 startups demonstrate that Europe’s entrepreneurial landscape extends well beyond venture capital-backed technology companies. From digitalising construction and improving customer support to simplifying regulatory compliance and modernising traditional services, they are addressing challenges that businesses encounter every day.
Their different approaches also highlight an important aspect of bootstrapping: success is not necessarily defined by how much funding a company can attract. Developing a useful product, building lasting customer relationships and maintaining control over business decisions can be equally important measures of progress.
As Europe’s technology ecosystem continues to evolve in 2026, companies like these offer a reminder that ambitious ideas can take shape through different financing models. Whether they are building specialised SaaS products or applying AI to established industries, these startups show how founders can pursue growth while maintaining greater independence.

articles.title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
articles.text:
Google’s Threat Intelligence Group says it has shut down a massive botnet called x.cpe. At its height, x.cpe ran on more than 1.3 million Android TV devices, and unusually, these were Google-certified boxes. Google says its screening process missed the malware due to “obfuscation techniques” employed by Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology.
In a detailed blog post, the Threat Intelligence Group explains how the x.cpe botnet evolved quickly from a single-stage dropper into a modular three-stage malware platform that sold access to third parties. Manufacturers must have their devices certified if they want access to Google apps and branding, a process that is supposed to catch threats like this. However, Videostrong’s compromised boxes, mostly sold under the MECOOL brand, evaded detection by using a backdoor to remotely install the malware after the devices were set up and online.
After devices appeared online, a stub application called x.cpe or com.oemservice would phone home. This package did not have any malicious capabilities of its own, but it had the system-level permissions necessary to install malware modules at the operator’s behest. It also disabled Play Protect, which would have otherwise flagged the silently installed packages as malicious.
Google found most of the boxes were running residential proxies for routing large volumes of nefarious traffic or modules that engaged in ad fraud schemes. Selling access to this botnet was probably a big business. Videostrong also had full access to the devices, allowing operators to run terminal commands, capture the screen, and probe other devices on the local network. Google reportedly observed Videostrong doing this in real time.

articles.title: Critical Node-RED Flaw Exploited in Attacks
articles.text:
Hackers have started exploiting a critical-severity vulnerability in Node-RED to deploy various payloads, vulnerability intelligence company VulnCheck reports.
Node-RED is a low-code, flow-based programming tool that supports the creation of event-driven applications through a browser-based editor. It is used in products across various sectors, including commercial ICS/OT devices.
Tracked as CVE-2026-58115 (CVSS score of 10/10), the bug is described as a missing authentication issue on the Node-RED HTTP interface that could enable attackers to access programming nodes that can execute system commands.
Siemens disclosed it on August 11, after finding it in its SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed. SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced version 4.3.4.1 and later contain patches for the security hole.
According to Siemens, CVE-2026-58115 “could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to create malicious flows and execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with maximum privileges.”
On Sunday, VulnCheck warned that it had observed successful in-the-wild exploitation of the vulnerability on October 30. The attack came from an IP in AS8075, Microsoft’s network, and delivered a complete exploit.
“It deployed a Node-RED flow, triggered it automatically, and pulled a binary from an attacker-controlled server, all behind three layers of encoding,” VulnCheck says.
The payload was a Linux bot, and the execution command did not check if the installation succeeded. Based on the file’s name, the company believes the attackers had built payloads for multiple architectures.
By November 1, VulnCheck observed 15 additional attacks from the same IP address, delivering additional payloads, including persistent webshells that would allow the hackers to run arbitrary commands on the compromised servers.
According to the company, the attacks show that threat actors are actively scanning for Node-RED instances without adminAuth and exploiting them automatically with a single HTTP request.
“If you run Node-RED anywhere, including embedded in your ICS/OT environment, check whether it can be reached from outside your network today. Also review deployed flows for unexpected exec nodes or HTTP endpoints, since some attackers are leaving webshells rather than bots,” VulnCheck notes.
