articles.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike is buying two AI security companies that expand its products to more broadly monitor, test, and cover AI models and agents, as companies across industries start rolling out AI agents and models wholesale.
CrowdStrike said it will buy Fiddler AI, which makes observability software for monitoring AI agents inside enterprises, and Dreadnode, which helps companies automate security testing specifically aimed at detecting flaws in AI models, apps, and agents before they are set live.
The company is paying around $400 million for Fiddler AI, and about $95 million for Dreadnode, according to The Wall Street Journal.
The deals are happening at a time of significant upheaval in the cybersecurity space, especially as companies’ policies and processes lag behind AI adoption within their walls. Teams and individual employees alike are experimenting with AI tools, automating workflows, vibe-coding custom apps, and deploying armies of AI agents to do their bidding, which is understandably causing headaches for security teams.
CrowdStrike, whose products are used widely across enterprises and governments, is clearly trying to leverage its already significant heft and presence to capture a share of this quickly burgeoning market. It’s not alone, of course, as we’ve already seen several startups and cybersecurity vendors raising dozens of millions in funding to solve issues for companies, though most of these approaches are essentially based on the conviction that existing security software isn’t enough to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, or usage.
The company has itself been building detection and response controls, dubbed Falcon Guardian, to help companies see and understand what agents are doing on their devices, and these acquisitions seem to further flesh out its offerings.
Fiddler AI is going to be part of CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform as Falcon Observe, where it’ll ostensibly help the company’s clients evaluate agents before they’re deployed, understand their actions, and monitor what they do, and feed that information as telemetry into the broader platform. Dreadnode, meanwhile, will be integrated into the Falcon Guardian product, to which the startup’s software will feed its testing results as security policy recommendations.
Founded in 2018, Fiddler AI has raised a total of about $99 million to date, according to PitchBook. Dreadnode, founded in 2023, has raised $14 million so far.

articles.title: Amazon closes AI creator's account after he attempts to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark mini-PCs — Epic CEO Tim Sweeney says his regular orders were canceled before arrival after he tried to buy two GPUs
articles.text:
Amazon closes AI creator's account after he attempts to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark mini-PCs — Epic CEO Tim Sweeney says his regular orders were canceled before arrival after he tried to buy two GPUs
Amazon’s closure email cites a verification process and offers no reason.
AI creator Nick Saraev says on X that Amazon closed his account after he tried to buy seven Nvidia DGX Spark AI mini-PCs. The closure email cites a verification process and gives no reason. Epic CEO Tim Sweeney chimed in that his regular orders would go through, then get canceled before arrival, after he tried to buy two GPUs.
Saraev puts it plainly that “Amazon just closed my account” and that “Buying even modest amounts of compute immediately puts you on a watchlist.” He was “4 orders deep,” and Amazon will no longer allow him to buy DGX Sparks.
The shared screenshots indicate those orders were all canceled, with each stating, “Your order was canceled. You have not been charged for this order.” Although he does not give a unit count, the screenshots indicate he tried to buy seven DGX Sparks in total. All show the same listing, with 128GB of memory and 4TB of storage.
Amazon’s support account did respond to his earlier post, about three hours before his closure post, offering a review. The shared email shows that Amazon had “made the final decision” to close his account after review; no reason was given. However, it did mention “previous attempts to verify your account,” and he says he did go through the verification process, but seven DGX Sparks is a significant amount that might draw suspicion. Either way, Amazon’s Conditions of Use reserve the right to “refuse service, terminate accounts” or “cancel orders in its sole discretion.”
He’s not alone in running into trouble with the company. Sweeney says that “Amazon didn’t cancel my account but continued accepting all my regular orders and canceling them just prior to arrival dates, after I tried to buy two NVIDIA GPUs. Rather bizarre.” Nvidia GPUs are often used for local inference. Saraev replied that everyone would “appreciate a bit more transparency.”
Also, in September, Dracones89 on the Nvidia developer forum shared that one Amazon account was hit with “suspicious activity locks” while trying to buy a pair of Asus GX10s; the user ended up with two DGX Sparks from Micro Center instead. Another X user, @PurzBeats, wrote, “They canceled the order when I tried to buy my 5090, twice.” This is a different trajectory than the OpenClaw days of Mac minis, when buyers faced long delivery waits rather than canceled orders or closed accounts.
With local inference remaining of high interest to many, particularly AI influencers, the event is potentially disturbing, especially after recent comments about self-owned DRAM by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. While this time it was a guy who helps entrepreneurs and small businesses implement AI and claims 500K on YouTube and 700K on Instagram, the slope is slippery, although Saraev’s orders are hardly typical.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The 128GB DGX Spark has an MSRP of $6,950, but it may be found at 20% or more over that: two Amazon listings showed $8,499.99 and $9,499.99 when we checked today, which would put seven at roughly $59,500 to $66,500. Both showed Prime delivery tomorrow, so the hardware is still on sale there.
Hardware has been climbing in price, largely due to rising memory costs. As open-weight models have become more popular, so has local AI inference. The combination may make retailers uneasy, as you’re dealing with high ticket prices and there has been uncertainty about the safety of models as they have improved, with open-source AI agent tools reportedly being used in multiple recent cybersecurity incidents.
Micro Center, a different retailer, required one buyer to sign an Advanced Computing Product Purchaser Declaration with photo ID, end user, and an install location, just for a workstation with an RTX 5090. This form specifically forbade exporting or reselling the hardware, which might give a little insight into Amazon’s reasoning, too. Amazon’s conditions also say customers “must comply with all U.S. or other export and re-export restrictions.” China and the U.S. remain locked in a fight over exports of AI hardware.
Amazon hasn’t explained itself, but the attention this is getting may motivate a more detailed response. Right now, it’s a warning signal to users looking to buy significant amounts of hardware for AI work, at least from traditional online retailers. Brick-and-mortar stores, like Micro Center, may crack down further to prevent workarounds designed to export the hardware illegally.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Rockstar confirms GTA 6 pre-load times for digital and code-in-box editions as the game's huge storage requirement revealed
articles.text:
GTA 6 digital pre-loads for PS5 and Xbox will begin 9 days early and require a whopping 212GB of free space
Get ready to free up a ton of space on your consoles
- Rockstar Games has confirmed players can pre-load the digital version of Grand Theft Auto 6 on November 10
- Code-in-box editions should be available in stores starting November 12
- The pre-load file will be "up to 212GB depending on your device"
Rockstar Games has announced the file size for Grand Theft Auto 6 and the dates for when players can pre-load the game depending on their edition.
In a new blog post, the studio confirmed that digital pre-loading on PlayStation 5 will begin nine days before the game's November 19 launch, on Tuesday, November 10 at midnight local time "in your respective time zone."
For Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, pre-loading begins globally on Tuesday, November 10 at 12AM GMT / 7PM EST / 6PM CST.
Meanwhile, code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12.
GTA 6 was speculated to be a massive game already due to its ambitious scale and impressive features, but Rockstar has officially confirmed that the pre-load file will be "up to 212 GB depending on your device."
"So make sure you've got ample space to begin pre-loading as soon as possible," the studio cautioned. Say goodbye to a fair few of your games if you want to install GTA 6.
In addition to the new details, Rockstar said it will be adding an official printable Grand Theft Auto 6 cover art poster and map of Leonida as a free digital download to the official site on November 19 for fans.

articles.title: No eres solo tú: un fallo está drenando la batería de los Pixel Watch (pero tiene solución)
articles.text:
Si tienes un Pixel Watch y has notado que últimamente la batería dura menos de lo habitual, no estás solo. Días atrás comenzaron a circular reportes de usuarios advirtiendo que la energía de su reloj inteligente se agotaba más rápido que de costumbre. Ahora, Google ha confirmado que esto se trata de un fallo y que una solución está en camino.
Curiosamente, la causa del problema todavía no se ha revelado al público. Los usuarios impactados por esta situación simplemente comenzaron a ver que su Pixel Watch tenía una autonomía bastante más acotada de lo habitual. Y si bien las primeras sospechas se posaron sobre una reciente actualización de Wear OS, esto no se ha confirmado ni desmentido por el momento.
Los Pixel Watch afectados por este inconveniente no fueron los de una generación en particular. Básicamente, cualquier modelo desde el Pixel Watch 2 en adelante han presentado este problema. Vale aclarar que, si bien no se trata de un fallo de alcance masivo, sí es un inconveniente de importancia en las unidades donde se presenta.
Algunos de los reportes divulgados en Reddit indicaban que la duración de la batería de los Pixel Watch se había acortado de forma considerable. En los casos más notorios se observaron autonomías máximas de 12 horas, cuando previamente podía superar las 48 horas cuando la función de pantalla siempre encendida permanecía desactivada.
Google ha liberado una solución para los problemas de batería en los Pixel Watch
Desde Google le confirmaron a 9to5Google que ya habían desplegado una actualización para resolver el drenaje de la batería en los Pixel Watch alcanzados. La empresa con sede en Mountain View no reveló la causa formal del inconveniente, aunque remarcó que se hizo presente en un número limitado de unidades.
Un dato que llama la atención es que la solución no llega con una actualización de Wear OS, sino de las apps instaladas. La firma indica que para resolver el fallo hay que ingresar en la Play Store y buscar Administrar apps > Actualizar todas. Una vez que se complete el procedimiento, la duración de la batería de los Pixel Watch afectados debería regresar a la normalidad.
Esto hace pensar que el inconveniente podría estar en la Play Store en sí misma o en alguna de las aplicaciones que Google preinstala en el Pixel Watch. Sea como sea, la resolución ya se encuentra disponible. Los californianos indican que el fix llegará a todos los usuarios en los próximos días, así que si todavía no notas mejoras seguramente debas aguardar un poco más.

articles.title: ChatGPT já alcança 20% do volume de buscas do Google, diz OpenAI
articles.text:
O ChatGPT está ampliando sua participação no mercado de buscas na internet. Segundo a OpenAI, o chatbot já processa um volume de consultas equivalente a um quinto do registrado pelo Google. A declaração indica o avanço da ferramenta como alternativa aos mecanismos tradicionais de pesquisa, embora a distância entre as duas plataformas ainda seja significativa.
O número foi apresentado por Adam Fry, responsável pelo produto de consumo do ChatGPT, durante evento da OpenAI realizado na segunda-feira (2). Segundo ele, a companhia considera uma busca toda consulta enviada pelo usuário que resulta em uma pesquisa na web. Perguntas simples, como pedidos para definir um termo ou explicar como fazer alguma coisa, não entram nessa conta.
A empresa, porém, não informou a origem do número utilizado para comparar o volume de pesquisas do ChatGPT com o do Google.
ChatGPT ainda está distante do Google
- Apesar do crescimento, o volume de buscas do ChatGPT representa apenas uma fração da atividade registrada pelo Google;
- A comparação feita pela OpenAI também ajuda a dimensionar o desafio de conquistar espaço nesse mercado;
- Durante o julgamento antitruste do Google em 2023, o CEO da Microsoft, Satya Nadella, afirmou que o Bing detinha aproximadamente 3% do mercado de mecanismos de busca, mesmo após mais de uma década de investimentos para competir com a ferramenta do Google;
- O avanço da inteligência artificial (IA), entretanto, vem alterando esse cenário. O próprio Google passou a incorporar recursos generativos ao seu mecanismo de pesquisa, incluindo resumos produzidos por IA e experiências mais personalizadas, com visualizações e gráficos;
- O The Verge observa que uma parcela significativa das buscas realizadas pelo ChatGPT provavelmente utiliza o Bing, da Microsoft, além de um índice de pesquisa próprio da OpenAI. Ainda existe especulação sobre a possibilidade de algumas consultas serem encaminhadas ao Google.
Leia mais:
- ChatGPT e outras IAs mudam resultados de testes de personalidade conforme o idioma
- ChatGPT teria orientado mulher a abandonar remédio antes de morte, diz processo
- OpenAI amplia restrições do ChatGPT sobre armas e violência para crianças e adolescentes
OpenAI aposta em interface visual e anúncios
A disputa não envolve apenas responder a perguntas. A OpenAI também está desenvolvendo experiências de pesquisa mais visuais e interativas dentro do ChatGPT.
A companhia chama essa abordagem de “Intelligent UI” (interface inteligente, em tradução livre). A proposta é transformar as respostas do chatbot em ambientes interativos, com elementos visuais e recursos que permitam ao usuário explorar informações sem sair da conversa.
“É para lá que o futuro dessa tecnologia está indo. Você está conversando com uma tela”, afirmou Fry.
Outro ponto estratégico é a publicidade. Assim como o Google, a OpenAI enxerga nos anúncios uma possível fonte de receita para seus serviços, especialmente diante da possibilidade de uma abertura de capital no início de 2027.
Fry afirmou que a publicidade não provocou reação negativa duradoura entre os usuários e que a maioria das pessoas parece não se incomodar com os anúncios no produto.
A empresa anunciou no mês anterior que começaria a exibir imagens de produtos e serviços patrocinados no ChatGPT. Até então, os anúncios apresentavam principalmente o nome da companhia, seu logotipo e um link para o produto.
“Os anúncios talvez tenham nos mostrado que poderíamos estar fazendo isso ainda mais”, declarou o executivo.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: This space company is betting its future on a propellant available everywhere
articles.text:
Robert, Ryan, and Kirby Carlisle are three engineers who worked at SpaceX during the Falcon 9 era, seeing the revolution in the global launch industry from the inside.
The brothers launched rockets, refurbished rockets, and sold rockets. But when it came time for them to leave SpaceX and start their own space company—a lifetime dream for the Carlisle brothers—they chose not to build rockets. Rather, they focused on spacecraft.
In late 2022, the three Carlisles founded Argo Space to build infrastructure in space. Their vision was not just in-space transportation but also removing the need to use propellants from Earth to move around the heavens. They chose water, which is potentially harvestable on the Moon and found all over the Solar System, as a means of propulsion.
“We based the company on water,” Robert Carlisle said in an interview.
The availability of water is key to the company’s vision for building a transportation network between low-Earth orbit, geostationary orbit, and the Moon. This would open up a large number of affordable logistics options, such as satellite resupply, refueling, repair, redeployments, and more. And in the company’s vision, water is not just a propellant; it’s also a coolant and radiation shield. Much of the spacecraft, including its thrusters to the avionics, is cooled by water. This helps increase the propellant mass fraction of the spacecraft, meaning more mass is devoted to propellant, allowing the vehicle to go farther and do more things.
“In the long run, this water-based transportation will give us a commercial incentive, a profit motive to go harvest it from the Moon’s shallower gravity well,” Robert Carlisle said.
When even former SpaceXers can’t find a Falcon 9
Argo Space flew its first demonstration mission, dubbed Navigator, in July on a Falcon 9 rideshare. The company successfully made contact with the spacecraft, but one of its two rollout solar arrays failed to deploy. Controllers spent about half a day troubleshooting the issue and gathering data on the spacecraft’s health. Unfortunately, however, the spacecraft remained power-negative, draining its battery. There was not enough energy to test the propulsion system.

articles.title: How Kenya’s PayServe is building the operating layer for managed real estate - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Kenyan prop-tech and fintech startup PayServe is raising a US$1 million Series A round as it scales a platform that automates billing, payments and reconciliation for the country’s fast-growing managed estates.
Founded in 2024, PayServe provides revenue assurance for managed real estate, handling billing for rent, service charge and utilities across gated communities, large apartment estates and mixed-use developments.
“Our platform reads consumption straight from our smart water and power meters, collects payments through M-Pesa and direct bank integrations with Absa, Co-op Bank, NCBA, Equity and KCB, and reconciles them automatically,” founder and CEO Steve Butler told Disrupt Africa. “It then posts everything to the client’s accounting system, such as SAP, Zoho or QuickBooks, with KRA eTIMS compliance built in.”
Around that core, the startup offers modules for visitor and access control, maintenance, procurement, unit handover, bookings, and a portal for residents and homeowners. Its customers are property developers, facility and property management companies, owners’ associations and community water schemes.
“Put simply, PayServe is the operating layer of managed real estate,” said Butler, who has spent more than 20 years working across fintech, banking, FMCG, real estate and development. He said PayServe was built in response to a structural shift in the Kenyan property market.
“Kenyan real estate has moved from standalone rentals to large managed developments: gated communities, apartment estates of 1,000 or more units, and mixed-use developments. Each one bills rents, service charge, water, power and security to hundreds of households,” he said.
“Yet most still run on spreadsheets, manual meter readings and M-Pesa statements reconciled by hand. That leads to disputed bills, revenue leakage, especially on service charge and water, late payments, and homeowners and residents who don’t trust the numbers.”
The startup sees its competition falling into three groups – rent-collection apps mostly built for landlords with tens of units, meter vendors who sell hardware but not the billing behind it, and global suites such as Yardi.
“Those global suites are expensive and not built for M-Pesa or eTIMS,” Butler said. “We combine software, metering, payments and accounting in one system built for estate-scale operations in Kenya.”
PayServe has been entirely founder-funded to date, but is now raising a US$1 million Series A.
“We’re raising to scale sales, deepen the product and expand regionally,” Butler said.
The startup has already built a sizeable footprint. It now bills more than 10,000 units across over 50 properties, has deployed 3,000 smart meters, and has processed KES1 billion (US$7.7 million) through the platform since inception.
“Flagship deployments include Northlands Heights, with over 1,000 units and more than 1,000 smart water meters, and Mwalimu Kisaju, with 840 units and 1,600 smart meters, plus JJ Tower, Altura, Volaire, Escada and others,” Butler said.
Other milestones include a live KRA eTIMS integration and direct integrations with Safaricom’s Daraja API and five major banks, with PesaLink next on the list.
“Our pipeline now extends into serviced apartments, mixed-use developments and community water projects,” he said.
PayServe makes money through three revenue streams – a monthly software-as-a-service (SaaS) platform fee per unit, smart water and power meters sold outright or leased, and implementation, integration and support services.
“For developers who don’t want upfront costs, we offer a zero-upfront model,” Butler said. “We deploy and operate the system and recover our costs through a revenue share over an agreed period.”
The journey so far has not been without its challenges.
“Sales cycles are long. Decisions involve developers, management companies and often owners’ committees,” Butler said. “And hardware is hard. Site readiness, plumbing and legacy meters from other vendors all affect timelines.”
Onboarding brings its own problems, with inherited billing records usually needing cleanup before go-live.
“Every client has a different bank, accounting system and tax setup, so each integration is its own project,” he said.
PayServe currently operates in Kenya, with clients in Nairobi, Eldoret and Mombasa, but has its sights set further afield.
“The near-term focus is expanding to regional markets like Uganda, Ethiopia and Congo, where the managed-estate market is growing fast, once the Kenya playbook is proven,” Butler said.

articles.title: Pénurie de Mac et d'iPad pour Noel ? Apple risque de manquer d'appareils à mettre sous le sapin
articles.text:
Il n’y a pas que l’iPhone Duo qui pose des problèmes de stocks chez Apple. Les Mac et les iPad aussi sont concernés : il pourrait en manquer pour les fêtes de fin d’année. Le Black Friday arrive, les promotions de Noël aussi et c’est à ce moment-là que la plupart des consommateurs achète les cadeaux de Noël pour leurs proches. Parmi eux, des Mac et des iPad. Alors, y en aura-t-il pour tout le monde ?
Apple reconnaît des problèmes d’approvisionnement qui impactent ses Mac et iPad
C’est lors de la conférence téléphonique de l’entreprise sur ses résultats financiers du quatrième trimestre qu’Apple a confirmé que la disponibilité des Mac et iPad serait limitée durant toute la période de Noël. Rassurez-vous, la santé financière d’Apple est excellente (surtout comparée à celle du reste de la tech, impactée par les déboires autour de l’IA) : c’est son meilleur exercice fiscal jamais enregistré. Ce qui ne l’empêche pas d’avoir des petits soucis.
Concernant les Mac tout d’abord, ils se vendent bien : 24% de plus sur la période par rapport à l’année dernière, soit plus de 10 milliards de dollars de chiffre d’affaires. Quant aux iPad, c’est plus nuancé : 10% de baisse sur un an et un chiffre d’affaires de 6,2 milliards de dollars. Pour ces deux types de produits, Apple reconnaît des « contraintes d’approvisionnement » ainsi que des « pressions liées aux taux de change », qui touchent les iPhone, les Mac et les iPad. Des difficultés qui pourraient avoir un impact sur le chiffre d’affaires global de l’entreprise : 7 à 10% de progression sur un an, sa « meilleure estimation compte tenu de l’approvisionnement contraint ».
Au regard des temps de livraison sur le site d’Apple, rien d’alarmant : de quelques jours à plus d’une semaine pour recevoir les produits chez soi ou aller les chercher en boutique. Mais qu’en sera-t-il fin novembre avec les promotions de Noël ? Les revendeurs tiers aussi pourraient pâtir de ces problèmes d’approvisionnement.
La marque à la pomme n’arrive plus à suivre les hausses de prix des composants
Jusqu’à il y a quelques mois, Apple semblait protégée par la hausse du prix des composants. Par sa taille, Apple a de quoi remplir des carnets de commande à tour de bras pour les usines. Mais ce n’est plus le cas : la plupart de ses produits a vu ses tarifs augmenter et on commence à voir des problèmes d’approvisionnement. C’est notamment le cas avec l’iPhone Duo : si vous en commandez un sur le site d’Apple aujourd’hui, il arrivera le 25 janvier.
Le dirigeant d’Apple John Ternus le reconnaît : « Ce que nous constatons actuellement avec les prix de la mémoire est sans précédent. […] nous avons observé des coûts de mémoire plus élevés qu’au trimestre de juin ». Une hausse qui ne va pas aller en s’arrangeant, puisqu’Apple prévoit que la mémoire voit encore son prix augmenter sur le dernier trimestre de l’année. Même chose en 2027 : « nous anticipons que les prix d’achat de la mémoire continueront d’augmenter. » Et pourtant, John Ternus se veut rassurant devant ses investisseurs : « nous sommes enthousiastes quant à notre situation actuelle. » La raison possible : dans cette crise, Apple est peut-être l’entreprise qui s’en sort « le moins mal ».
Pour conserver ses marges, Apple n’a d’autre choix que d’augmenter ses tarifs et c’est bien ce qui pourrait se passer en mars ou avril prochain, période durant laquelle de nouveaux produits pourraient sortir. On s’attend à l’arrivée de nouveaux iPad, à l’iPhone Air 2, mais aussi et surtout l’iPhone 18 et pourquoi pas sa déclinaison 18e. Pourraient également arriver le MacBook Air M6 ainsi qu’un MacBook Neo 2 sur cette même période.

Source : AppleInsider

articles.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
In this post, we show how to build a semantic layer for agentic AI using EDB Postgres AI. We run a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that queries the layer to answer customer 360 (C360) questions. Earlier posts in this series built the same C360 pattern with Stardog’s knowledge graph, Denodo’s data virtualization platform, AtScale’s dimensional model, and Strategy Mosaic’s linked models.
EDB Postgres AI puts the semantic layer inside the operational Postgres database as an AIDB extension. Business meaning lives next to the data in standard Postgres COMMENT statements, the join graph comes from Postgres foreign keys, and governance uses Postgres GRANT and row-level security through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that ships with AIDB.
By the end of this post you will know:
- How to build an AIDB semantic knowledge base (SemKB) over a Postgres schema, how COMMENT ON statements and aidb.create_semantic_alias behave as the authoring surface, and how foreign keys crawl into join paths.
- How to expose the AIDB tool catalog to an external agent through the built-in EDB MCP endpoint, fronted by an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and registered as an MCP target on AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
- How Postgres roles, column-level GRANT statements, and row-level security produce different results for different callers. The prompt, tool catalog, and agent code stay the same.
- How AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for every SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, queryable with ordinary SQL.
Three layers an agent needs
An agent that answers business questions from live data needs three layers: a model that plans and writes queries, a meaning layer that tells the agent what the data represents, and a runtime that hosts the agent and controls identity and access. The Stardog post in this series introduced this framing. The model layer in this post is Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock, the same as prior posts (model availability varies by AWS Region). The runtime layer is AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore Gateway handles inbound authorization, and AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, holds outbound credentials for the tool targets, same as prior posts. EDB Postgres AI hosts agents and tools inside the database itself and acts as the connection point for external agents through its MCP endpoint.
The meaning layer is where this post diverges from the others. Here it is a SemKB that lives inside the operational Postgres database. The schema and the business definitions are indexed together. Postgres GRANT, row-level security, and column-level grants enforce access, not an advisory system prompt. The sections that follow cover how AIDB builds the layer, how AgentCore exposes it, and how two Postgres roles asking the same question get different answers.
Example use case: C360 on EDB Postgres AI
The dataset is the Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit, loaded into a single EDB Postgres AI instance in a dedicated c360 schema. The data model has four tables and one derived view.
| Object | Key columns | 
| customers | cid, first_name, last_name, full_name, email, ssn, phone, picture, location (FK to locations.id) | 
| locations | id, city, state, zip | 
| products | id, name, brand, dept, price | 
| purchases | id, cid (FK to customers.cid), pid (FK to products.id), date, quantity, price | 
| big_spender (view) | cid, full_name, state, large_orders, largest_order | 
The physical schema is a plain Postgres join graph: a customer in the customers table lives at a location, places purchases, and each purchase references a product. The semantic work rests on three business ideas that column names don’t reveal.
State isn’t on the customer row. It lives in locations, reached through the customers.location foreign key, and a comment on that column tells SemKB where to find it.
purchases.price records the order total. An agent that reads it as a unit price and multiplies by quantity returns $502,529 for the top customer instead of $27,991.66.
Big spender is a term the business owns. Captured as a view with a COMMENT ON VIEW statement, its definition stays in one place that every agent, dashboard, and query reads from.
The questions we run through the agent end to end:
- Who are our top 10 customers by total spend, and what state is each in?
- How many big spenders do we have in each state?
- Can you list 10 customers and the state each lives in?
- Which 10 products have sold the most units?
- Can you list five customers with their Social Security numbers? (used in the governance rerun).
Reference architecture
The following diagram shows the request path from the analyst through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to the semantic layer inside EDB Postgres AI. The analyst authenticates with Amazon Cognito and calls AgentCore Gateway with the issued JSON Web Token (JWT) as a Bearer token. Gateway routes to AgentCore runtime, which plans with Claude on Amazon Bedrock. The agent calls MCP tools through Gateway, which forwards to an Application Load Balancer in the EDB Postgres AI virtual private cloud (VPC) and on to the edb-endpoints MCP server inside AIDB. AIDB serves the SemKB, semantic aliases, and read-only PostgreSQL tables. AgentCore traces go to Amazon CloudWatch, and AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres.
Two flows cross the boundary between AgentCore and EDB Postgres AI.
Inbound: A client calls AgentCore Gateway with a bearer token issued by an Amazon Cognito user pool. The Gateway inbound JWT authorizer validates the token against the Cognito discovery URL. Gateway then evaluates its Cedar policy against the token’s claims to decide which tools this agent, acting for this user, can invoke. It then routes the call to AgentCore runtime. The agent invokes Claude on Amazon Bedrock for planning and answer composition.
Outbound to the semantic layer: The agent’s tool call is an MCP request. AgentCore Gateway supports MCP server targets directly. AIDB’s edb-endpoints HTTP server speaks streamable HTTP MCP with HTTP Basic authentication, which lets Gateway treat it as an MCP server target with no translation layer. An Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate fronts edb-endpoints on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance. The ALB URL is registered as the Gateway target. The AgentCore Identity credential provider holds the Postgres role credential and injects it as Basic auth on every outbound request. The agent code doesn’t see the Postgres credential.
Observability: AgentCore emits traces for tool calls, large language model (LLM) calls, and token usage to CloudWatch Transaction Search. AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres, queryable with ordinary SQL after the database is configured to write them (see enabling telemetry on the source database).
No AWS Lambda is required in this architecture. AIDB already speaks MCP, so Gateway talks to it as an MCP server target directly through the ALB. The Denodo post in this series uses the same ALB pattern in front of its MCP server, and the architecture here is unchanged other than the vendor.
Build the semantic layer
These steps assume AIDB is installed and enabled on the EDB Postgres AI instance and the Stardog C360 kit’s four CSVs are loaded into a dedicated c360 schema with the primary and foreign keys shown earlier. Because this layer lives in the same database as the data, there is no second system to deploy and no catalog to synchronize. The semantic layer is defined in SQL, inside the same database as the application that writes the rows.
An AIDB semantic knowledge base indexes Postgres schema, not data. It embeds the definition of every table, view, and column (with the COMMENT ON text alongside) into a vector store that an agent can search in natural language. Three authoring tasks help the agent find the right table and column by meaning: writing COMMENT ON statements, defining business terms as views with their own comments, and registering recurring questions as semantic aliases. Comments are the simplest of the three authoring tasks and improve text-to-SQL accuracy the most for both users and agents.
Add comments where the agent will look
The view holds the business definition in one place, so no agent or dashboard has to redefine big spender. The time you spend on comments up front pays off on every query the agent runs afterward.
Create the semantic knowledge base
Create the SemKB over the c360 schema. The call registers the name, the embedding model, the target schemas, and the auto-processing mode.
The embedding model is a local llama.cpp model (llamacpp_embeddings) that ships with the AIDB Amazon Machine Image (AMI). SemKB uses one embedding model per KB, so every entry sits in the same vector space. The AIDB AMI ships with a default SemKB named semkb over public, so creating c360_kb leaves two SemKBs on the instance. When more than one SemKB exists, every aidb.semantic_kb_search call must pass kb_name explicitly. To swap the local model for a remote embedding model, such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings on Amazon Bedrock, register the remote model with aidb.create_model. Pass its name as the SemKB’s model parameter. The auto_processing parameter accepts Disabled, Live, or Background. Live reacts to schema changes through Postgres event triggers. Background processes them asynchronously from a worker. Disabled waits for an explicit aidb.refresh_semantic_kb(). SemKB also crawls foreign keys into relationships at the same time. The purchases.cid foreign key becomes a join path the agent can discover by meaning, not by column name.
Capture recurring questions as semantic aliases
A semantic alias is a named, parameterized read-only SELECT with a natural-language description that SemKB indexes alongside the schema metadata. The agent finds it by meaning, calls it with parameters, and returns a governed answer.
Aliases are AIDB’s reusable text-to-SQL building block. They sit next to tables and views in the SemKB index and show up to an agent as a tool. For a full text-to-SQL walkthrough, see the EDB documentation.
Govern access
Governance in this architecture runs through Postgres primitives all the way down. The AIDB MCP endpoint has no permission system of its own: “Postgres grants decide what each agent can run” (MCP endpoint reference). Each MCP request authenticates with a Postgres username and password over its own connection, so current_user inside every tool call is the agent’s role, visible in pg_stat_activity like other connections.
The following diagram traces how identity flows from the end user through AgentCore to the Postgres role that evaluates the SQL, and how the resulting trace is captured for audit. The chain runs in four phases: inbound trust at the Gateway, outbound credential from AgentCore Identity, enforcement in Postgres through GRANT and row-level security, and audit through OpenTelemetry traces in the aidb_otel schema.
Inbound trust at Gateway: 1. The end user authenticates with Amazon Cognito and receives a JWT bearer token. 2. The client calls AgentCore Gateway with the token in the Authorization header. 3. The Gateway JWT authorizer validates the token against the Cognito user pool’s discovery URL. 4. Gateway evaluates its Cedar policy against the token’s claims to decide which tool this agent can call.
Outbound credential to AIDB: 5. Gateway resolves the outbound credential for the MCP target from the AgentCore Identity credential provider. For AIDB, this is a Postgres username and password used as HTTP Basic auth. 6. Gateway forwards the MCP streamable-HTTP request to the ALB, which forwards it to edb-endpoints.
Enforcement in Postgres: 7. edb-endpoints opens a Postgres connection using the username and password from the Basic auth header. Postgres authenticates the login role per pg_hba.conf, and current_user inside the tool call is that role. 8. Column-level GRANT statements and row-level security policies on c360 tables enforce what rows and columns the tool call returns. A denial surfaces as a Postgres permission-denied error on the restricted table or column, which the MCP endpoint forwards unchanged.
Audit. 9. AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for the SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, available through SQL immediately.
Two Postgres roles, same question, different results
Define two agent login roles that differ only in a column-level GRANT: mcp_agent_full sees every column, mcp_agent_restricted sees every column except customers.ssn.
Both login roles need password-auth entries in pg_hba.conf for the local edb-endpoints connection path, as covered in configuring your agent role. Running the same question through both roles produces different results. The agent calling under mcp_agent_restricted can’t project the ssn column: the moment it tries, Postgres returns permission denied for column ssn and the MCP endpoint forwards that error unchanged. The agent then responds that it can’t read SSNs. The prompt, the tool catalog, the SemKB, and the agent code are identical between the two roles. The only difference is the credential AgentCore Identity injects on the outbound Basic auth header.
Row-level filtering follows the same pattern. Enable row-level security (RLS) on a target table and attach per-role USING policies. The AIDB MCP endpoint sees the same rows the role would see in a direct psql connection.
A note on AIDB purposes. AIDB also ships purposes, a policy abstraction that confines in-database agents (those created with aidb.create_agent and invoked with aidb.agent_converse) to a named Postgres role. Purposes apply to the in-database agent path. The external AgentCore path this post uses governs through Postgres roles directly at the MCP endpoint, as described earlier. For audit of external MCP agents, see EDB Agent Governance, which reads the same aidb_otel spans and visualizes agent sessions and policy decisions.
Responsible AI considerations. The governance surface shown so far controls what the agent can execute at the database layer. Pair it with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on the model side to shape what the agent is allowed to generate: content filters for sensitive topics, denied-topic lists, and PII redaction. The two layers complement each other. Postgres GRANT stops the agent from reading SSNs at the data layer. Guardrails help prevent PII patterns from leaking through other paths in the model response. For agents answering business questions over customer data, both are production controls.
Expose the layer and run the agent
Enabling the AIDB MCP endpoint takes two Postgres parameters plus a restart. Set edb.endpoints_mcp_enabled = on in postgresql.conf, add aidb to shared_preload_libraries, and restart (enabling the endpoint). To reach the endpoint from outside the EC2 instance, set edb.endpoints_mcp_host to a non-loopback address such as 0.0.0.0. Choose a port with edb.endpoints_mcp_port (default is 8765). Supply the Transport Layer Security (TLS) pair with edb.endpoints_mcp_tls_cert and edb.endpoints_mcp_tls_key, which the endpoint requires for non-loopback binds (configuring the endpoint).
An Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an ACM certificate exposes edb-endpoints to AgentCore Gateway. The ALB target group uses HTTPS to the EC2 instance on port 8765 and doesn’t validate the backend certificate chain, so a self-signed certificate on edb-endpoints is sufficient for development and testing. For production, use an internal ALB with AgentCore Gateway VPC egress to keep connectivity between Gateway and the ALB private.
Create an AgentCore Gateway with a Cognito authorizer, register the ALB URL as an MCP server target, and store the two Postgres credentials in the AgentCore Identity credential provider (credential provider reference).
The agent is a short Python script. It uses Strands Agents to wire a BedrockModel pointing at the latest Claude Sonnet to an MCPClient. The MCPClient connects to the Gateway URL over the streamable HTTP MCP transport with the Cognito access token as a Bearer header. The system prompt instructs the agent to call semantic_kb_search first for schema context, passing kb_name => 'c360_kb', then execute_sql to run the generated query. The AgentCore runtime starter toolkit with Strands has a worked example of hosting an agent of this shape in production.
We recommend turning on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the agent’s system prompt. The same instruction and the same tool list are reused on every call, which is what prompt caching is for.
Sample queries and verification
Four questions through the agent plus one governance rerun, all against the C360 data loaded earlier.
Query 1: Who are our top 10 customers by total spend, and what state is each in?
Without the comment on purchases.price, an agent configured with only a SQL execution tool reads price as a unit price and multiplies by quantity. The top row comes back as roughly $502,529 for Carolyn Inworth, which is wrong. One column comment, indexed by SemKB, is the entire difference between that answer and the right one:
Same model, same prompt, same tool catalog. The semantic knowledge base changes the answer.
Query 2: How many big spenders do we have in each state?
The agent finds the big_spender view through semantic_kb_search because its COMMENT ON VIEW matches the natural-language question. The business definition sits in exactly one place:
If the business later redefines a big spender as a customer with cumulative spend over $5,000, the change is one CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW statement. Every agent sees the new definition the next time SemKB refreshes.
Query 3: List 10 customers and the state each lives in
The state is in locations, not customers. The join path is encoded in the customers.location foreign key and in the column comment, both indexed by SemKB. The agent emits:
Query 4: Which 10 products have sold the most units?
A plain aggregation that runs inside Postgres next to the data:
Governance rerun: List five customers with their Social Security numbers
The same prompt runs twice. Under mcp_agent_full, the agent returns five customer rows with their ssn values populated. Under mcp_agent_restricted, the agent’s tool call fails with the Postgres error permission denied for column ssn, and the agent responds with a short message that SSNs are not accessible to this caller. The failure is enforced by the column-level GRANT, not by the prompt or the model. AIDB captures the OpenTelemetry trace for the SQL execution in aidb_otel, so a reviewer can query the trace row to confirm the governance decision later.
Extending across data sources
For analytical workloads that outgrow the operational database, EDB Postgres Analytics Accelerator (PGAA) lets Postgres read Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Parquet tables in object storage through an Iceberg REST catalog. The EDB Postgres AI analytics overview covers the end-to-end setup. PGAA tables appear in Postgres as ordinary tables, so the same SemKB description keeps working against the analytical copy and the agent’s tool catalog doesn’t change.
For federation to external relational sources, Postgres foreign data wrappers make an external table reachable as if it were local. The semantic layer is unchanged in either case because business definitions, column comments, and semantic aliases live in Postgres.
Deployment
Two shapes work for this architecture.
Self-managed on Amazon EC2. Use the EDB Postgres AI Agent Factory AMI from the AWS Marketplace. The customer owns the VPC, the subnet, the version cadence, and the EDB Postgres AI software upgrades. The ALB and the AgentCore Gateway target configuration are unchanged from the preceding architecture.
EDB-managed on Amazon EC2. EDB Managed Database is a service where EDB experts handle database administration on the customer’s behalf. The AgentCore side is unchanged.
Conclusion
Reliable agentic analytics needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that provides a governed business view of the data, and an agent runtime that hosts the agent and manages identity. Amazon Bedrock supplies the model, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supplies the runtime, and EDB Postgres AI supplies a semantic layer that lives inside the operational Postgres database. Business meaning, join paths, and governance come from Postgres primitives already present in the schema. The AWS side is the same as the rest of this series: AgentCore Gateway, Runtime, Identity, Bedrock, and CloudWatch.
The data, the business definitions, and the access rules all live in one Postgres schema, so there is no separate catalog to keep in sync. Audit lives in the same database: aidb_otel holds a span per tool call, next to the data it ran against.
Where to start
To apply this architecture to your own data, work through these steps:
- Pick one Postgres database your agents need to query live. Narrower is better.
- Create a dedicated schema for the agent’s data, with GRANT USAGE scoped to a service role.
- Write COMMENT ON statements on columns and views that use business language. Capture business terms as views with a COMMENT ON VIEW statement.
- Create a SemKB over the schema with aidb.create_semantic_kb and auto_processing => 'Live' (or Background under high write volume).
- Register recurring questions as semantic aliases.
- Enable the AIDB MCP endpoint, front it with an ALB with HTTPS and an ACM certificate, and register the ALB URL as an AgentCore Gateway MCP server target.
- Run three real questions through the agent, then rerun one under a role with reduced grants to confirm the enforcement surface works end to end.

articles.title: GTA VI is starting to take over the GTA
articles.text:
GTA has come to Toronto in a big way.
This week, Torontonians have taken to social media to share images of Grand Theft Auto VI marketing across the city. The most prominent example is a GTA VI takeover of multiple big billboards at Yonge and Dundas, as seen in a video shared by the social media account GTA 6 Countdown. At the end of the video, we also see GTA VI marketing in the Bloor-Yonge TTC station.
Rockstar’s GTA 6 takeover in Toronto, Canada with 3 giant billboards.
(via @TottiN835) https://t.co/zApsJrlwbh
— GTA 6 Countdown ⏳ (@GTAVI_Countdown) November 3, 2026
It remains to be seen what other marketing efforts may come up for the game across Toronto or other parts of Canada. (It’s worth noting that developer Rockstar Games does actually have a Canadian office, Rockstar Toronto, which is based in Oakville. That said, it’s always been low-key about that location, even when people were protesting there last year over layoffs that Rockstar allegedly carried out as part of wider union-busting efforts.)
Either way, this increased marketing push will no doubt make the impending release of GTA VI feel all the more real for fans. After all, the game has been a long time coming, with GTA V having been released in 2013. GTA VI eventually entered early development in 2018 following the release of Red Dead Redemption II and was formally unveiled in 2023 following a major leak. After a couple of delays, the game will now finally launch on Nov. 19 for $109.99.
GTA VI is a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired tale of romantic duo Jason and Lucia as they engage in various criminal activities in the Florida-inspired U.S. state of Leonida. The game will be available on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S at launch, but not PC right away. Pre-loads on console begin on Nov. 10 and will eat up over 200GB of storage.
Image credit: Rockstar Games

articles.title: Ni Google, ni OpenAI : Cyclon dégaine le premier smartphone 100 % piloté par l’IA — Frandroid
articles.text:
En 2009, Apple vendait l’iPhone avec un slogan qu’elle a fini par déposer : « There’s an app for that », il y a une application pour ça. Dix-sept ans plus tard, la promesse a été tenue au-delà du raisonnable. On a une application pour la banque, une pour le parking, une autre pour scanner un document qui nous inflige trois publicités avant d’enregistrer le PDF, une autre pour compter les calories de ses plats… Mais retrouver un contrat dans Drive, l’envoyer à un collègue sur WhatsApp puis l’appeler demande une bonne dizaine de gestes, trois applications et un copier-coller qu’on rate une fois sur deux. La startup Cyclon a choisi précisément cette scène pour sa démo, en la réduisant à une seule phrase dite à voix haute.
Cyclon se présente comme « un téléphone où l’IA est l’interface ». Son cofondateur Adam Zinebi l’a dévoilé ce lundi 2 novembre sur X, avec une ambition modeste : remplacer l’iPhone. La promesse tient en trois points : l’agent utilise les applications déjà installées avec nos comptes, il fabrique celles qui manquent et il exécute des tâches en arrière-plan pendant qu’on fait autre chose. On peut le réserver dès maintenant avec un acompte remboursable de 199 dollars (environ 180 €), à valoir sur un prix final estimé à 699 dollars hors taxes (environ 625 €). Le vrai téléphone Cyclon, avec un matériel maison, est attendu au deuxième trimestre 2027 et dépend encore d’une autorisation de la FCC, le régulateur américain des télécoms. En attendant, les premiers acheteurs américains reçoivent sans supplément, sous 30 jours, un Pixel 8a, un milieu de gamme lancé en 2024 à 549 euros chez nous, qui fait tourner Cyclon OS en guise de prototype.
D’un hackathon chez Y Combinator à un Android maison
L’équipe tient sur les doigts d’une main, et il en reste trois de libres : la fiche de l’entreprise chez Y Combinator affiche deux salariés, basés à San Francisco.
Adam Zinebi, le CEO, est passé par CentraleSupélec et l’EPFL, où il a étudié l’électronique et la miniaturisation du matériel, avant un poste chez Oracle et des travaux de recherche à Berkeley. Thomas Kiefer, le CTO, a travaillé sur Android chez Google après Stanford et l’ETH Zurich. Leur histoire commune démarre le 17 mai 2026, au Call My Agent Hackathon organisé dans les locaux de Y Combinator. Face à 91 équipes, ils décrochent la première place avec Drishti Jain grâce à Gavel, un agent à qui on écrit par SMS pour vendre un objet : il publie l’annonce, discute avec les acheteurs, négocie le prix et cale le rendez-vous. Le premier prix garantissait un entretien chez YC, et la société qui porte Cyclon s’appelle toujours TextGavel Inc.
Y Combinator, que tout le monde abrège en YC, est l’accélérateur le plus célèbre de la Silicon Valley. Fondé en 2005 par Paul Graham, Jessica Livingston, Robert Morris et Trevor Blackwell, il a vu passer Airbnb, Dropbox, Stripe ou Reddit. Le fonctionnement est rodé : quatre promotions par an, environ 1 à 2 % de candidats retenus, trois mois de programme à San Francisco et un Demo Day final devant des centaines d’investisseurs. Cyclon fait partie de la promotion d’automne 2026, baptisée « F26 », qui court d’octobre à décembre. Chaque startup admise reçoit 500 000 dollars (environ 445 000 €) : 125 000 dollars contre 7 % du capital, plus 375 000 dollars convertibles lors de la prochaine levée. C’est pour l’heure le seul financement connu de Cyclon. Chez YC, la startup est suivie par David Lieb, cofondateur de Bump passé ensuite par Google Photos.
Cyclon ne part pas d’une page blanche, et ses dépôts publics sur GitHub montrent comment l’équipe s’y prend. Cyclon OS repose sur LineageOS, la ROM Android alternative chère aux bidouilleurs, associée à microG, une réimplémentation libre des services Google Play. C’est d’ailleurs cette solution qui est utilisée sur les smartphones Huawei pour faire fonctionner les services Google.
L’agent navigue ensuite dans les applications comme on le ferait : il lit l’écran, tape et fait défiler, sans attendre que les développeurs lui ouvrent une porte dédiée. Quand une application manque, il écrit le code dans un bac à sable hébergé dans le cloud, le teste, le corrige puis l’installe comme une vraie application, à l’image du clone de CamScanner sans publicité exhibé par Adam Zinebi. Détail savoureux, les branches de code portent le préfixe « claude/ » et les relectures sont confiées à un autre modèle : le téléphone piloté par l’IA est lui-même en partie écrit par des IA.
Le cerveau, en revanche, ne loge pas dans le Pixel. La FAQ de Cyclon l’admet sans détour : pour exécuter une demande, le téléphone envoie à ses fournisseurs d’IA ce qui s’affiche à l’écran, nos messages ou notre position, sans dire de quels fournisseurs il s’agit. La mémoire de l’assistant est stockée sur l’appareil, mais ses passages utiles sont aussi envoyés quand une demande l’exige. Certains fournisseurs conservent ces données un temps limité pour détecter les abus. Ça cadre mal avec la réponse d’Adam Zinebi à un internaute, assurant que tout se passe « dans ta poche, pas dans un cloud ». Le choix de microG a aussi un coût que la startup reconnaît : sans certification Google, certaines applications de banque, de paiement ou d’entreprise risquent de refuser de fonctionner.
Agent OS : Google, Samsung et OpenAI sur les rangs
Ce que vend Cyclon porte un nom un peu barbare, l’agent OS. Aujourd’hui, le système d’exploitation d’un smartphone sert surtout à lancer des applications et à les isoler les unes des autres, à nous de faire le lien entre elles. Un agent OS inverse la logique : on formule une intention, et le système décide quelles applications ouvrir, dans quel ordre et avec quelles données. Les applications deviennent des briques qu’on ne regarde presque plus. Quand la brique n’existe pas, on la génère : n’importe quel chatbot récent crée déjà, dans le cloud, un petit outil ou un jeu à partir d’un prompt, et le Xiaomi 18 Pro permet de créer sa propre application pour l’écran arrière, en cinq minutes lors de notre test.
Google est le plus avancé des géants, et aussi le plus prudent. Depuis février, Gemini sait piloter des applications tierces sur les Galaxy S26 et Pixel 10, mais aux États-Unis et en Corée uniquement, et sur une poignée de services comme Uber, Lyft, DoorDash ou Starbucks. Gemini Intelligence, présenté en mai, étend l’idée à Android 17 avec l’automatisation entre applications et un outil « Créer mon widget », cousin de l’application générée par IA du Xiaomi 18 Pro, sans calendrier annoncé pour la France à notre connaissance. Samsung a fait du Galaxy S26 un téléphone multi-agents où cohabitent Bixby, Gemini et Perplexity, qu’on réveille d’un « Hey Plex ». Galaxy AI reste pourtant surtout une boîte à outils de retouche, de résumé et de traduction, dont les agents touchent aux applications maison et à quelques partenaires. On est loin d’un téléphone qui gère seul notre fil WhatsApp pendant une heure.
Deutsche Telekom a déjà tenté l’expérience en Europe. L’opérateur allemand présentait au MWC 2024 un concept de smartphone sans applications, conçu avec Qualcomm et Brain.ai, avant de lancer en 2025 ses T Phone 3 vendus comme « AI Phone ». L’assistant de Perplexity s’y lance d’un bouton dédié et utilise en arrière-plan les applications déjà installées.
    Pour aller plus loin
Xiaomi 18 Pro : j’ai créé ma propre application pour l’écran arrière, ça m’a pris 5 minutes
            
OpenAI vise la même cible avec infiniment plus de moyens. L’entreprise a racheté io, la startup de Jony Ive, pour environ 6,5 milliards de dollars en 2025, et aurait recruté environ 400 anciens d’Apple, selon la plainte déposée par la firme de Cupertino le 10 juillet. Apple y accuse notamment Tang Tan, aujourd’hui responsable du matériel chez OpenAI, d’avoir aidé à faire sortir des secrets industriels, ce qu’OpenAI conteste en réclamant l’abandon pur et simple des poursuites. Le premier appareil, attendu en 2027, serait une enceinte sans écran, et le téléphone capable de remplacer le smartphone viendrait plus tard. Cyclon dispose donc d’une fenêtre de tir tant qu’OpenAI n’a pas de téléphone à vendre.
    Pour aller plus loin
Un téléphone ChatGPT en 2028 ? OpenAI préparerait son smartphone : MediaTek et Qualcomm dans la boucle pour 2028
            
Encore faut-il pouvoir accéder aux applications. Sur Android, une simple application va déjà loin : Perplexity propose depuis janvier 2025 un assistant capable de commander un VTC ou de lancer une playlist sur Spotify. Google surveille toutefois de près les services d’accessibilité dont ces outils dépendent, et réserve ses accès les plus profonds aux applications système, Gemini en tête. Sur iOS, la porte est fermée, puisque Siri passe par des actions que chaque développeur doit exposer lui-même. Un Anthropic ou un Perplexity pourrait donc déployer un agent sur Android si Google le tolère, ou s’allier à un fabricant comme Perplexity l’a fait avec Samsung. Cyclon tente une troisième voie, celle du système maison, quitte à perdre la certification Google qui garantit que les applications tournent.
    Pour aller plus loin
ChatGPT : les agents IA Dots deviennent plus puissants et encore plus autonomes
            
Pour l’instant, Cyclon s’adresse à des premiers utilisateurs américains prêts à immobiliser 199 dollars et à essuyer les plâtres sur un Pixel 8a. Depuis la France, on peut réserver, mais le prototype n’est expédié qu’aux États-Unis et les pays de vente du téléphone final ne sont pas annoncés.
Cyclon laisse plusieurs questions sans réponse : les modèles d’IA utilisés, le coût de l’IA après la phase de test, l’autonomie, ou le respect des conditions d’utilisation de WhatsApp, sur lesquelles Adam Zinebi explique simplement que l’équipe « règle les détails ».
Deux personnes promettent un OS, un matériel maison et une homologation de la FCC pour le deuxième trimestre 2027, un calendrier qui a tendance à glisser dans le matériel. Cyclon parle d’ailleurs d’une simple estimation et promet de rembourser l’acompte en cas de retard. Petite ironie au passage : Rabbit vendait son R1 199 dollars (environ 180 €), Humane facturait son AI Pin 699 dollars (environ 625 €), et aucun des deux n’a convaincu. Les deux projets ont échoué. Parmi les messages enthousiastes qui ont fait décoller l’annonce, celui du leaker Ice Universe apparaissait d’ailleurs avec la mention « partenariat rémunéré ».
Sur le fond, Cyclon a raison : un smartphone découpé en dizaines d’applications cloisonnées ressemble de plus en plus à un héritage de 2008, et un agent qui les fait travailler ensemble en est la suite logique. Sa démonstration va plus loin que ce que Google ose lancer, justement parce que deux ingénieurs n’ont ni réputation ni procès antitrust à ménager. Il lui faut maintenant prouver que ça tient hors d’une vidéo, sur des applications qui changent d’interface tous les mois. Si Cyclon y parvient, la startup tiendra quelque chose. Apple, Google, Samsung et les constructeurs chinois ne manqueront pas de s’en inspirer.
Votre café et votre dose de tech vous attendent sur WhatsApp chaque matin avec Frandroid.
Pour nous soutenir gratuitement, dites simplement à Google d’ajouter Frandroid à vos sources préférées en cliquant ici.
