articles.title: How Anju turned a personal food experiment into a snack brand expanding to 41 retail stores
articles.text:
How Anju turned a personal food experiment into a snack brand expanding to 41 retail stores
After a 20-year corporate career, Anju Kalhan ventured into entrepreneurship and built Bliss by Anju, a plant-based food brand offering snacks without added oil, ghee or dairy.
A 20-year corporate career, an events business and eight marathons may not seem like the usual starting points for a food entrepreneur.
But Anju Kalhan's journey to building a healthy snacking brand has taken an unconventional route.
A graduate in Business Economics from the University of Delhi, Anju spent two decades working in corporate and industry organisations.
She served as a Senior Economist at ASSOCHAM and Deputy Director at the Hotel Association of India, where she also worked with SSH Rehman, former Managing Director of ITC Hotels.
She eventually left her corporate career to start an events company, organising FICCI events and corporate workshops. Alongside her professional commitments, she pursued fitness, completed eight marathons and trained as a yoga professional and fitness coach.
But it was a personal health experience that eventually led her towards the food business.
Today, she is the founder of Bliss by Anju, a food brand making plant-based snacks without added oil, ghee, dairy or refined ingredients.
What began with experiments in her home kitchen has grown into an operation with an in-house manufacturing facility and a retail presence across 41 stores in India.
A personal journey sparks a business idea
Anju says she had lived with high blood pressure for nearly 30 years, along with severe migraines and sinusitis. Health complications within her family, including diabetes and high blood pressure among her parents, also made her reconsider their everyday food habits.
During the Covid-19 pandemic, she began exploring plant-based whole-food diets, learning from coaches and studying the role of food in health.
She gradually removed ghee, cooking oil and highly processed packaged foods from her kitchen. According to Anju, she noticed significant improvements in her blood pressure and migraines within 90 days. Her mother, who was over 80, also experienced improvements in her diabetes and blood pressure after changing her diet, she says.
The experience encouraged Anju to look beyond her household and examine what was available in the market.
She visited organic stores, large retail outlets and shops selling artisanal products to find snacks that aligned with her new food choices. However, she found that many products marketed as healthy still contained palm oil or other added oils.
This exposed a gap she wanted to address.
"The healthy food is not tasty, and the tasty food is not healthy," was how Anju described the problem she encountered.
She decided to create snacks that could offer both. Rather than depend on oil and ghee for flavour, she began experimenting with Indian spices, nuts and seeds.
The company's earlier journey began with home-kitchen experiments in 2018-19, followed by selling at farmers' markets in 2019-20. As her understanding of whole-food eating evolved, she reworked the product range in 2023-24 to remove ghee and added oils.
From kitchen experiments to an in-house factory
Building a food business without a background in professional cooking or bakery operations meant learning several things along the way.
Anju says she is neither a trained chef nor a nutritionist. Instead, she approached product development through research, experimentation and a willingness to learn.
The brand's philosophy is built around plant-based whole foods and familiar ingredients. Its range includes granolas made with nuts and seeds, cookies prepared using chickpea flour, sattu and almonds, biscotti, sweets and savoury snacks such as matthi.
One of its products, tangy dates, uses dates, spices and lemon, offering an alternative to conventional packaged aam papad.
For Anju, spices are central to making the products flavourful without added fats. Cinnamon, cardamom and nutmeg, she explains, can bring aroma and flavour to snacks without relying on oil or ghee.
The company also pays attention to how its ingredients are prepared. Anju says nuts and seeds are washed, soaked and dried before being used in its products.
What started in her kitchen has now moved into manufacturing. The company operates an in-house factory in Okhla industrial area, where it makes its products.
Its approach is to cover different snacking occasions throughout the day, from morning granola to cookies with tea, biscotti with coffee and savoury snacks in the evening.
Taking the brand to more consumers
Bliss by Anju has expanded its distribution to 41 stores across India and is also available on Amazon and Blinkit.
The company has entered its third year of operations in its current phase of growth, according to Anju. It remains bootstrapped, and she says she is looking for investment to support the next stage of the business.
Building awareness remains one of the challenges. As a relatively small brand, Anju says she cannot afford large celebrity endorsements or extensive marketing campaigns. She is looking to reach consumers by communicating the thinking behind the products and the ingredients used to make them.
The brand's products can also be relatively expensive because of their use of nuts, seeds and other whole-food ingredients. Anju believes consumers should understand food labels and make informed choices about what they eat.
Her efforts extend beyond selling packaged snacks.
Through her association with the SHARAN community, she participates in cooking demonstrations and classes that teach people how to prepare food without oil and ghee. Many of these sessions are free or offered at a nominal charge.
She is also careful about how she positions her products. Anju says the snacks are not intended to replace fresh meals. Instead, they are meant for people who need convenient options while travelling, working in offices or packing food for children.
At 60, Anju is building a food business around an idea that emerged from her own experiences. Having moved from a corporate career to entrepreneurship and then into food manufacturing, she is now looking for investment and opportunities to expand Bliss by Anju.
For women considering entrepreneurship, her advice is simple: pursue the idea, even when the circumstances are not perfect. As she puts it, one should not be afraid of taking the plunge. Something worthwhile can emerge from the effort.

articles.title: Barracuda warns of critical flaws allowing root access to devices
articles.text:
Cybersecurity company Barracuda Networks warned customers to patch two vulnerabilities that can let attackers run commands with root privileges.
The first is a critical flaw (CVE-2026-116606) stemming from an Email Security Gateway (ESG) authentication weakness that attackers can exploit to modify an appliance's global configuration, while the second (CVE-2026-111560) lets threat actors with admin permissions inject OS commands that run as root.
However, Barracuda said successful exploitation also requires access to the administrative interfaces of targeted devices and advised customers to use appropriate network access controls and restrict access to trusted internal networks to limit exposure.
"Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product. If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device," the company explained.
"Barracuda immediately initiated a comprehensive remediation process and released security patches for affected products. Customers should review the affected products and remediation guidance [..], ensure their systems are running the latest firmware version, and have all security patches applied."
A complete list of all affected devices and available security patches is available in the table below.
| Affected Product | CVE-2026-116606 | CVE-2026-111560 | Patch | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Email Security Gateway (ESG) | Yes | Yes | BNSF-40425 (9.4.017+), BNSF-40430 (<9.4.017) | 
| Load Balancer ADC | No | Yes | BNADC-16586 | 
| Message Archiver (BMA) | No | Yes | BNMA-32468 | 
| WAF Control Center (WCC) | No | Yes | BNWF-60060 | 
| Web Application Firewall (WAF) | No | Yes | BNADC-16586 | 
| Web Security Gateway (WSG) | No | Yes | BNYF-24789 | 
Three years ago, Barracuda also patched an Email Security Gateway flaw (CVE-2023-7102) that the UNC4841 hacking group exploited in zero-day attacks to execute arbitrary code on unpatched appliances.
The same year, UNC4841 hackers abused another zero-day (CVE-2023-2868) to target Barracuda ESG appliances as part of cyber-espionage attacks.
Barracuda later revealed that the vulnerability had been exploited for at least seven months, since at least October 2022, to deploy previously unknown SeaSpy and Saltwater malware and steal data from compromised systems.
Almost a third of appliances hacked in the 2023 campaign belonged to government agencies worldwide, most of them breached between October and December 2022, according to cybersecurity firm Mandiant.
Founded in 2003, Barracuda has more than 200,000 customers worldwide, including small- to medium-sized businesses (SMBs), large enterprises, and managed service providers (MSPs).

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft promet des PC à 8 Go de RAM "jusqu'à 40 % plus rapides" — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pavan Davuluri, vice-président exécutif chargé de Windows chez Microsoft, a publié ce mardi 3 novembre un billet sur le blog officiel de Windows sur les PC qui n’ont que 8 gigaoctets de mémoire vive. Ces machines reviennent dans les rayons, et Microsoft répète depuis juin que 8 gigaoctets suffisent. Il y a déjà eu une première mise à jour à la mi-octobre pour alléger Windows 11. Cette fois, l’éditeur détaille ce qu’il a changé, avec des chiffres qu’il a mesurés lui-même.
Une histoire de compression
Microsoft a annoncé avoir réglé autrement la compression de mémoire, qui tasse les données peu utilisées pour les garder en RAM. D’après l’éditeur, Windows peut ainsi garder en mémoire jusqu’à 2 gigaoctets de données actives en plus. Windows met aussi en pause des tâches de fond, comme l’indexation de la recherche, pendant qu’on utilise le PC.
Les applications de Microsoft ont aussi été retouchées. Sur les PC à 8 gigaoctets ou moins, les Widgets ne se chargent plus qu’à l’ouverture, ce qui libère environ 200 mégaoctets quand le panneau est fermé. Edge met en veille les onglets inactifs au bout de 15 minutes par défaut, contre deux heures jusqu’ici. Teams passe dans un mode qui consomme moins de ressources et se lance jusqu’à 20 % plus vite.
Au total, Microsoft annonce jusqu’à 900 mégaoctets de mémoire réservée en moins pendant une séance de multitâche, dont 360 mégaoctets grâce à Word, PowerPoint, Excel et Outlook.
Des gains mesurés par Microsoft, sur un seul PC
Les 20 % de réactivité viennent de la télémétrie, ces données que les PC envoient à Microsoft. Elles portent sur six gestes : ouvrir le menu Démarrer, lancer une recherche, faire un clic droit, ouvrir les Paramètres, l’Outil Capture et l’Explorateur de fichiers. La comparaison se fait avec la version de Windows 11 de janvier 2026.
Les 40 % en multitâche, eux, sortent d’un seul scénario en laboratoire, sur un HP OmniBook 3 à puce Snapdragon X Plus. Microsoft écrit lui-même, en note de bas de page, que ce résultat ne vaut que pour ce scénario et cette machine. Précisons qu’un test comparatif publié en octobre sur Windows 11 26H2 allait déjà dans le même sens.
Le billet met aussi en avant un Dell XPS 13 de 2026 avec 8 gigaoctets, 94 % plus rapide en multicœur qu’un modèle de 2021. Ce test a été fait par le cabinet Principled Technologies, à la demande de Microsoft. Microsoft reconnaît quand même que la 3D ou le montage vidéo poussé demandent 16 gigaoctets ou plus.

articles.title: Scream 8 : Sidney Prescott est de retour ! Neve Campbell rempile pour le prochain film
articles.text:
Scream 8 : Neve Campbell de retour dans le prochain volet de la franchise culte
L'actrice qui a incarné Sidney Prescott dans six des sept films de la franchise Scream a confirmé son retour dans le prochain opus.
Sidney Prescott sera de retour dans le prochain volet de la saga Scream. L'actrice Neve Campbell a en effet confirmé la nouvelle au micro d'AP Entertainment.
Sidney Prescott toujours face à Ghostface
Neve Campbell campe le rôle de Sidney Prescott depuis le premier film Scream sorti en 1996. Elle a depuis repris le rôle dans tous les films de la franchise à l'exception de Scream VI en raison d'un différend avec Paramount au sujet de son salaire. Elle est ensuite revenu pour Scream 7 et a maintenant confirmé qu'elle répondra à l'appel de Scream 8.
"Je serais dans Scream 8," a déclaré Campbell en réponse à une question sur le futur film lors de l'avant-première de la saison 2 de la série Black Doves, dans laquelle elle apparaît.
Au-delà de cette confirmation, l'actrice s'est gardée d'en dire plus sur ce prochain film de la franchise horrifique. On sait cependant déjà qu'il sera écrit par Lilla et Nora Zuckerman, les soeurs scénaristes derrière la série Poker Face.
Kevin Williamson, qui imaginé la saga Scream et réalisé le dernier film, va se contenter de produire le prochain opus et passe la main à un réalisateur qui n'a pas encore été choisi.
Pour rappel, Scream 7 a généré 208 millions de dollars au box-office mondial pour un budget de 45 millions de dollars. Comme quoi, même si elles ont maintenant 30 ans, les aventures de Ghostface continuent d'attirer les spectateurs dans les salles obscures.
En attendant de savoir quand Scream 8 sortira en salles, vous pouvez voir ou revoir la quasi-totalité des précédents slashers de la franchise (à l'exception de Scream 4 et 7) en streaming sur la plateforme Paramount+.

articles.title: IFC bets on cash-flow lending for African MSMEs
articles.text:
African enterprises are being strangled by short-term dollar debt, over-leveraged balance sheets, and administrative red tape, threatening the continent’s ability to generate employment for its fast-growing youth population.
Delivering his address at the Africa Financial Summit (AFIS) in Luanda on Tuesday, Makhtar Diop, Managing Director of the International Finance Corporation (IFC), issued a blunt assessment of Africa’s structural capital mismatch.
Addressing central bank governors, finance ministers, and commercial bank executives, Diop argued that while the continent’s projected 4.5% economic growth is notable amid global headwinds, it remains insufficient to absorb millions of young entrants into the labour market.
With advanced economies cutting foreign aid budgets and domestic fiscal space severely constrained by inflation and public debt, Diop warned that Africa can no longer depend on external development assistance. Instead, domestic and international savings must be mobilised into productive enterprise through local-currency credit, long-term debt, and equity.
“When we talk to leaders across the continent, they all raise the same challenge: how can we create jobs for our very young population?” Diop said. “If we do not create those jobs, we risk the kind of situation we are already seeing today, fueled by anxiety over climate change, geopolitics, mental health, regional and global pandemics, and other pressures. These challenges weigh heavily on young people, who may take to the streets and demand change. So we need to focus totally and utterly on job creation.”
The real-sector capital mismatch
According to Diop, the fundamental barrier to African competitiveness is not a shortage of domestic savings, but the absence of viable financial instruments to intermediate those funds.
Drawing from consultations with private sector operators across the continent, Diop identified five structural distortions handicapping African businesses:
African firms are ‘forced’ to finance long-term capital investments with short-term bank facilities, undermining corporate durability. Enterprises across the continent are excessively leveraged because risk capital remains scarce at scale. “You can lend to a company, but you build a company with equity,” Diop noted.
Companies continue to incur debt in US dollars while generating revenues in depreciating domestic currencies. Subdued corporate bond issuance prevents local institutional capital, including pension funds, from backing domestic firms. Diop dismissed the narrative that domestic investors lack an appetite for African risk, noting that quality issuances are consistently oversubscribed.
Unpredictable regulatory changes continue to deter multi-year capital deployment. Beyond financial mechanics, Diop called for an administrative overhaul of African civil services, arguing that public bureaucracies often view the private sector with suspicion rather than as an engine of job creation.
“In many countries, public administrations still do not see themselves as being there to serve the private sector,” Diop said. “The feeling among the private sector in many countries is that businesses still have to struggle to make civil servants understand that they are there to serve the country and help create jobs. So, there is a cultural revolution that still needs to happen.”
To bridge the gap between statutory legislation and real-world implementation, Diop proposed establishing permanent national “Private Sector Councils.” These bodies would provide heads of state and finance ministries with a real-time feedback loop on how commercial laws are applied on the ground and recommend rapid corrective interventions.
Ditching collateral for cash flow and fintech
A core pillar of the IFC’s African agenda, Diop stressed, involves dismantling traditional collateral constraints for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). Historically, African commercial banks have rationed credit based on immovable assets such as real estate, thereby automatically excluding the majority of informal and emerging businesses.
Diop stated that the IFC is actively shifting its focus toward non-bank financial intermediaries, deploying fintech platforms and digital telematics to underwrite borrowers based on observable revenue rather than fixed property.
“We want to move from lending based on collateral towards lending based on cash flow,” Diop said. “Data is the new gold. That is why the fintech agenda is so important for IFC. By using new technologies and the fintech architecture, we will be able to reach many more MSMEs.”
To shield borrowers from exchange rate volatility, the IFC is also expanding its local-currency exposure. Around 35% of the corporation’s continental commitments are currently disbursed in local currencies, with internal targets to increase that share substantially.
Mobilisation targets
Under its “IFC 2030 Strategy,” the World Bank Group’s private-sector lending arm has re-engineered its balance sheet to act as a catalyst for private co-investment.
Five years ago, the institution managed roughly $33 billion in combined financing, mobilising $0.90 of commercial capital for every $1 of its own funds. Today, annual commitments have exceeded $100 billion, with a global mobilisation ratio of 3.4-to-1.
Africa accounts for approximately 25% of the IFC’s total global portfolio. While the corporation’s African mobilisation ratio has climbed from $0.60 to $1.50 per dollar deployed, Diop set a target to scale that ratio to 5-to-1 in the coming years.
To unlock offshore institutional liquidity, the IFC is reallocating personnel directly into major financial capitals, including London, New York, Tokyo, Frankfurt, and Sydney.
Dedicated investor-relations teams are tasked with channelling international sovereign wealth funds and institutional asset managers into African equity funds, infrastructure corridors, and clean energy projects.
Simultaneously, the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), the political risk insurance arm of the World Bank Group, has met its $25 billion guarantee target years ahead of its 2030 deadline, providing risk-mitigation instruments to reassure private investors entering volatile markets.
Deepening continental partnerships
Domestically, the IFC is backing the consolidation of African commercial banking under its Local Champions Initiative, helping indigenous and regional lenders fill the space vacated by multinational European and American banks that have exited the continent over the past decade.
In the host country, Angola, where the government has curbed public debt and brought inflation down to 8.43%, Diop confirmed he will sign two major direct-financing agreements with domestic agricultural companies this week to advance food security and reduce reliance on imports.
Regionally, the institution is collaborating with African multilateral partners. Diop noted that Ethiopis Tafara, IFC’s Vice President for Africa, is leading a joint initiative with Dr Sidi Ould Tah, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB), to coordinate with domestic sovereign wealth funds and institutional asset managers to mobilise internal long-term capital for trade and regional transport corridors.
As global liquidity tightens, the strategic direction outlined in Luanda signals an end to the reliance on traditional concessionary aid. For the IFC and its institutional partners, Africa’s economic future depends on structuring investable, local-currency instruments that convert domestic savings into real-economy employment.

articles.title: UK Cyber Chief Says the UK Will Face AI Cyberattacks on Critical Infrastructure by 2028
articles.text:
The U.K. will likely face artificial intelligence cyberattacks on its critical infrastructure by 2028 as criminals and states, including China and Russia, increasingly use AI in their cyber activity, Britain’s cyber chief warned Tuesday.
That could include AI-powered malware for ransomware attacks as the technology will allow “vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long” to be discovered and exploited “at a scale that was once unimaginable,” Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Center said.
In a speech marking the publication of the NCSC’s annual cyber report, Horne said the leaders of businesses and organizations of all sizes who have “got away with tech on the cheap” will have to explain why “food isn’t on the shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under,” if they fail to invest in cybersecurity or update out-of-date technology.
Chinese cyber activity is the “most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the U.K.” while both Russia and China will routinely use AI to achieve their geopolitical goals, the report said. Russia is intentionally conducting cyber campaigns which fall below the threshold of armed conflict while Iran is carrying out attacks against the U.K. and targeting individuals who are a threat to the Iranian regime, Horne said.
The use of AI by states and criminals is highly likely to increase the scale and efficiency of hostile operations, but AI is more likely to be used to enhance and scale existing tactics and techniques rather than find brand new vulnerabilities, the report said.
Last week, governments and corporations worked on urgent security updates after the AI-assisted discovery of vulnerabilities in a programming language vital to 70% of websites globally. The two critical flaws identified by AI could allow bad actors to get unauthenticated access to sites which, in theory, could allow them to control a web server remotely without needing a password.
Technology “underpins the automation of physical processes that are vital to modern life,” Horne said. That includes, he said, electricity switching, sluice gates in water facilities, dam operations, manufacturing lines, heating and refrigeration controls. The recent cyberattacks on refrigeration systems in French supermarkets showed how easily hostile actors could exploit civilian infrastructure, Horne said.
Russia has already attacked critical infrastructure in Europe, according to the U.K. and EU member states that said Russia’s FSB security service was behind an attack on Poland’s energy grid in December 2025. If the attack had been successful, 500,000 people could have lost electricity during winter.
In the U.K., malicious cyber activity is costing organizations almost $20 billion every year, the NCSC said. In 2025, the carmaker Jaguar Land Rover suffered more than $260 million in direct losses following a cyberattack which also hit suppliers and dented the U.K. economy.
“We need every organization in the UK to take action now. Not only to protect their customers, services and livelihoods, but because cybersecurity is now part of the front line defense of our nation,” said Anne Keast-Butler, director of GCHQ, Britain’s signals intelligence agency, which the NCSC is part of.
That includes implementing basic but effective cybersecurity measures such as making sure devices are up to date, limiting administrator access to systems and backing up important files and data, the NCSC said.
Related: UK Legal Aid Agency Hack Scope Widens After Forensic Review
Related: US, UK, Dutch Agencies Expose Iranian ‘Chosen Brick’ Surveillance Malware
Related: UK Moves to Block High-Risk Tech Suppliers From Critical Infrastructure

articles.title: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
articles.text:
The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
Plus: Today’s midterms will test AI’s influence on US politics.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.
While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.
Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.
Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave.
—Amit Katwala
Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.”
One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn't caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.”
But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration. Those who don’t become targets for attacks.
—James O'Donnell
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Today’s midterms will test AI’s influence on US politics
Candidates are betting that AI regulation will sway voters to their side. (Axios)
+ Angry constituents could derail Elon Musk’s Republican bets. (BI)
+ Tech investors are on edge about the results. (Reuters $)
+ America is divided over AI regulation. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Nvidia is ordering data centre clients to limit their business with China 
It told providers that the majority of their sales must be non-Chinese. (FT $)
+ The move follows pressure from Washington. (Bloomberg $)
+ Chinese AI has ruptured the White House. (MIT Technology Review)
3 Hackers have turned supermarket fridges into a food security risk
Attacks in Europe have put US supermarket systems on alert. (CNBC)
+ They’ve also sparked concerns over other domestic appliances.(BBC)
+ It’s a good time for doing crime. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Scientists have detected signals at the smallest scale ever explored
The discovery offers clues to a world of exotic new particles. (BBC)
+ It came via CERN's Large Hadron Collider. (The Times $)
5 Zapping part of the brain makes you think harder—at a cost
It can both improve performance and reduce motivation. (New Scientist $)
+ Neuropixels probes are transforming how we study the brain. (Nature)
6 Big tech is splurging on mega gas plants to power data centers
The projectsthreaten to reverse years of climate pledges. (WP $)
7 Google says an Android partner infected 1.3 million devices
The malware infected TV boxes and other Android-based devices. (Verge)
8 Apple is trying to create its first robot
It’s proving a lot harder than expected, though. (Information $)
+ AI robots are still a long way from useful. (MIT Technology Review)
9 China’s biggest shopping festival has a new product to sell: AI
AI tokens have become a major new Singles’ Day category. (Reuters $)
10 A meteorite in the Sahara has revealed new clues about Mars
Its chemistry may help explain how the planet lost its water. (Wired $)
Quote of the day
“Don’t spend money unduly by asking a human expert to enter into a debate with a robot expert.”
—Steven Benmor, a family lawyer, tells the Wall Street Journal that clients increasingly need to pay human experts to correct advice they’ve received from chatbots.
One more thing
The noise we make is hurting animals. Can we learn to shut up?
As human society has expanded, animals have started struggling to hear one another. For many birds, the noise has grown so loud that they’ve begun to sing with faster trills. Now, their mating calls aren’t as effective.
The growing hubbub can also increase bird-on-bird conflict, and entire species that can’t handle urban clamor simply leave town for good. But there are technological solutions to the noises hurting animals—and they could help humans, too.
—Clive Thompson
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

articles.title: Anthropic speeds up Claude Code with message threads. But your token bill stays the same.
articles.text:
Anthropic speeds up Claude Code with message threads. But your token bill stays the same.
Anthropic has announced a new feature that aims to speed up long-running Claude Code sessions by reducing the amount of conversation data repeatedly sent to its API, helping developers get responses faster as their coding sessions grow.
Message threads, as it’s called, is available now in public beta for Anthropic’s Messages API and is already enabled by default for “most” Claude Code users, according to an article published by Anthropic on Monday.
The company says that the feature has reduced median time to first token (TTFT) — the time it takes Claude to begin generating a response — by approximately 35% for Claude Code requests containing between 500,000 and 1 million tokens.
Given that it’s now part of the Messages API, the feature also extends beyond Claude Code to developers building their own AI agents, particularly those handling lengthy conversations, repeated tool calls, and large amounts of data.
How message threads works
To understand what’s changed, it’s worth looking at how the Messages API has traditionally handled conversations.
Every time an agent sends a new request to Claude, it includes the entire conversation history. That means all messages and tool calls must be transmitted again, even though the API has previously received them.
For example, a coding agent working through a complex task will likely entail hundreds of API calls. As it reads files and modifies code, the conversation history grows, and by the time that history reaches 500,000 tokens, every subsequent request requires sending those 500,000 tokens again, along with whatever new information has been thrown into the mix.
The API then has to validate and tokenize the incoming data before Claude can begin responding. This rinse-and-repeat processing can add significant latency, particularly during lengthy coding sessions.
And so message threads switches things up by allowing Anthropic to temporarily retain the conversation history on its servers. The first request still sends the complete conversation, including any system prompts and tool definitions. But subsequent requests need only contain new messages and a reference to the previous response.
Behind the scenes, Anthropic reconstructs the full conversation on its servers before passing it to Claude, negating the need for the client to keep uploading the same information. This detail is important, because Claude still processes the entire conversation on every turn — if the history contains 500,000 tokens, the model still receives that context, even though the client has transmitted only the latest messages.
“While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.”
As such, message threads doesn’t inherently reduce API costs — Anthropic continues to charge for the tokens Claude processes. “While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same,” the company notes.
Developers can, however, combine message threads with Claude’s existing prompt caching feature, which allows previously processed content to be reused at discounted token rates. The two features can work in tandem to reduce latency and processing costs respectively.
Anthropic identifies several use-cases where message threads could be particularly useful. These include long-running coding agents that accumulate file edits and tool results, computer-use agents that repeatedly capture screenshots, and applications handling large volumes of documents or images. In each case, avoiding repeated uploads reduces the amount of data transmitted during a session.
Guillaume Lebedel, co-founder and CTO of AI agent infrastructure company StackOne, took to LinkedIn on Tuesday to illustrate the potential benefits of message threads for computer-use agents, using a simulation to estimate how much data could be saved.
His calculations assume an agent captures one 150 KB screenshot at each step. Without message threads, the 50th request would need to upload approximately 7.5 MB of accumulated screenshots. With message threads, that request would carry just the latest screenshot, approximately 0.15 MB.
Across the entire 50-step session, the cumulative screenshot data uploaded would fall from roughly 191 MB to 7.5 MB — a reduction of approximately 25 times.
While these figures aren’t based on a live API test, they illustrate the potential benefits for agents that repeatedly upload large files. Indeed, Lebedel predicts that computer-use agents could spearhead adoption of the feature, with widespread uptake before the end of the year.
“My bet — computer-use agents adopt it before coding agents do, since a screenshot per step is what makes the resend heavy.”
“My bet — computer-use agents adopt it before coding agents do, since a screenshot per step is what makes the resend heavy, and most have it on by the end of December,” he writes.
How to use message threads
To implement the feature, Anthropic has introduced a new thread parameter to the Messages API. The initial request creates a thread by including thread={"type": "create"}, alongside the full conversation history, system prompt, and any tools being used.
Subsequent requests use thread={"type": "continue", "previous_message_id": first.id}, where first.id refers to the response ID returned by the initial request.
These follow-up requests contain only the new messages. The API retains the earlier conversation and its original system prompt and tool definitions.
Because the feature remains in beta, developers making requests directly must also include the anthropic-beta header with the value message-threads-2026-08-12. In the Python SDK, this can be supplied through betas=["message-threads-2026-08-12"].
Anthropic also provides a simpler approach through its SDK thread helper, which manages the conversation history and API parameters automatically.
Using the Python SDK, developers first create a client with client = anthropic.Anthropic(), before initialising a thread through client.beta.messages.thread(). The latter accepts the model, maximum output tokens and initial system prompt, among other parameters.
Once configured, developers use thread.send() to submit messages. The SDK thread helper automatically creates the thread on the first request, then continues it on subsequent turns, supplying the necessary parameters and retaining a local copy of the conversation history.
The SDK thread helper also adds the required beta header automatically, removing the need for developers to specify it with each request.
Message threads expire
There is, however, one notable limitation in all of this. Message threads expire after just five minutes of inactivity. And as one user observed on X, “Five minutes at the coffee machine and the thread expires.”
Another user went further, writing: “Only 5 minutes for cache expires is almost useless.” The user appears to be referring to the message thread expiry, which is separate from Claude’s prompt caching feature.
“Five minutes at the coffee machine and the thread expires.”
That might seem like an unforgiving restriction for a feature designed to improve lengthy coding sessions, however the implications are perhaps not so dramatic. If a developer steps away for ten minutes, say, the thread will indeed have expired. However, provided the client has retained the conversation history, the SDK helper automatically resends it to establish a new thread when they return. So the first request after a break may therefore take longer, but the coding session can continue without losing its previous context.
For agents operating continuously, the limitation may be even less consequential. Every successful request stored in the thread refreshes the five-minute expiry period, meaning an agent making regular API calls can maintain the same thread throughout a lengthy task.
Developers managing threads directly must handle expiry themselves. An attempt to continue an unavailable thread returns a 404 error, requiring the client to resend the complete conversation and establish a new thread.
There are also some data-handling considerations. Anthropic says thread contents are encrypted and held in server memory without being written to persistent storage. Although threads expire after five minutes of inactivity, their contents may remain in memory for up to an hour after their last use.
The feature is currently ineligible for zero data retention and HIPAA, which could restrict its use in environments with stringent data-handling requirements. Certain context-management capabilities, including on-demand compaction, are also unsupported.
Message threads is available across all Claude models in beta, including through Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and Anthropic-managed Claude Models on Google Cloud.
Learning Path

articles.title: Trump wanted to give No Kings no air. Then, Meta suspended its Instagram.
articles.text:
Mark Zuckerberg in Menlo Park, California on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Donald Trump in Fort Myers, Florida on October 23, 2026.
Credit:
Aurich Lawson | Getty Images | Minh Connors | Alex Wong
Mark Zuckerberg in Menlo Park, California on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Donald Trump in Fort Myers, Florida on October 23, 2026.
Credit:
Aurich Lawson | Getty Images | Minh Connors | Alex Wong
Over the weekend, the No Kings Coalition said Meta declined to commit to taking steps to prevent automated systems from suspending one of Instagram’s most prominent pro-democracy accounts if activity surged around the page during the midterm elections.
A demand for action came after Meta apologized for temporarily suspending the No Kings Instagram account and disabling access for four hours at the peak of an early voting push from the group. In a post on X, Meta’s Andy Stone said the account had been using a Claude AI tool in a way that made it appear to be a bot. But even though automated review detected the error within an hour, Stone acknowledged that additional hurdles kept admins locked out. State and federal lawmakers—as well as a coalition of 14 attorneys general—have asked Meta to further explain its actions.
In a letter to No Kings, Meta offered to arrange a meeting with a technical expert who could better explain the mistake. But No Kings rejected the response, saying it failed to address any of the group’s ongoing concerns and requesting a meeting with Meta senior leadership instead. The group stressed that the issue goes beyond its Instagram account, saying that Americans who rely on Meta’s platforms need assurance that voting content won’t be suppressed ahead of or on election day. Among eight questions, the coalition asked Meta to publicly disclose any communications with the Trump administration about the No Kings account or the historic early voting day event.
On October 30, Meta executives met with No Kings. According to the coalition’s account of the meeting, Meta said it has “no plans” to change policies that lead to harmful over-enforcement, a problem that even the independent Oversight Board, which reviews Meta’s content decisions, worries could result in suppression or censorship of No Kings and other pro-democracy content during this critical period.
“Meta acknowledged that it made a mistake, but an apology without action does nothing to ensure that this kind of censorship won’t happen again,” No Kings said, calling Meta’s laissez-faire attitude “unacceptable.”
Ars has found no evidence that the Trump administration asked Meta to restrict the No Kings account or that anyone at Meta intentionally targeted the account for political reasons. Meta told No Kings that it planned to post a public reply to the coalition’s demands, but the company did not respond to Ars’ request for comment, and Stone has yet to post an update on X. His account did, however, apologize for another accidental enforcement action impacting a Republican-controlled account the day before the No Kings meeting. “We automatically removed the @MOSenateGOP Facebook account because our systems mistakenly assessed the account was impersonating another one,” Stone said.
“This was never simply about a technical glitch or one Instagram account,” No Kings’ press release said. “It’s about whether millions of Americans can rely on these platforms to organize, communicate, and access critical voting information without disruption.”
Meta’s AI explanation seems incomplete
Formed in 2025 after Donald Trump returned to office for a second term, the No Kings Coalition is best known for organizing some of the largest coordinated protests in recent US history. Using social media channels to coordinate nationwide demonstrations against Trump policies viewed as anti-democratic, organizers estimated that more than 5 million people participated in its first protests in June 2025 and say attendance has only increased since. No Kings estimates 7 million people attended the second protests in October 2025, and more than 8 million showed up for the third demonstration last March.
For the fourth event, however, No Kings sought to get more than 9 million people into the streets, and then directly to the polls, by organizing an early voting event on October 17. Unlike the family-friendly protests where Americans held up signs demanding “No Kings in America,” this event focused on driving voter turnout. Although No Kings describes itself as a pro-democracy coalition with no interest in building up the Democratic Party, turnout for its events is driven by those who oppose Trump’s most controversial policies—including domestic ICE enforcement and US military involvement in Iran.
Hundreds of civil rights organizations, including Black Voters Matter and the American Civil Liberties Union, make up the No Kings Coalition. Initially, there was no centralized Instagram account where the groups could coordinate their social media messaging. But as the November 3 election approached, the coalition got more organized, hoping that an official No Kings account with a large following would help it identify and amplify content ahead of the fourth event.
That’s when No Kings decided to use Claude as a “keyword and hashtag search tool to track conversations across social media platforms,” the group’s social media team told Ars.
According to Stone, the Claude tool was “reading profiles, posts, and hashtags,” which “sharply” increased the account’s activity in “intense bursts” that “resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems.”
Ars could not determine what specific Claude-powered tool the coalition was using, how it accessed Instagram, or whether it was an Anthropic service or a third-party integration built using Claude. Ars asked both Anthropic and Meta whether there was anything unusual about the way No Kings was using Claude, but neither company responded.
Ezra Levin, co-founder of Indivisible, a progressive nonprofit in the No Kings Coalition, told Ars that the volume of posting increases because organizers understand a basic principle of advertising: “You’ve got to reach people seven different times in seven different ways, and it’s the seventh time that they hear, and they’re like, ‘Oh right, there is an early vote action going on. I should get out there.’”
The high volume shouldn’t matter, though, Levin said, emphasizing that “it seems pretty absurd that a social media company that doesn’t go down during the Super Bowl or during the World Series or during the Oscars shuts our account down during an early vote push.”
“We’re not using any boutique tools that nobody has developed before,” Levin said. “These are all nonprofits. We’re putting things together with popsicle sticks and glue. We’re not developing our own sophisticated apparatus. So there is nothing that I’m aware of that is unique about how we were using the social media platform that day.”
Meta’s closer ties with Trump fuel suspicion
Levin pointed to a series of episodes dating back to at least 2016 that raised questions about Meta’s role in protecting democratic processes. That year, Facebook acknowledged that it sold election-related ads to a shadowy Russian company. More recently, Meta faced questions from Congress in 2021 after turning off election-related safeguards and failing to detect “Stop the Steal” groups from gaming its algorithm to spread disinformation. After Trump’s 2024 election and shortly before his inauguration, Meta announced that it would end its US third-party fact-checking program. Zuckerberg also said Meta would work with Trump to push back against what he characterized as censorship by foreign governments. Critics warned that the move amounted to Meta declaring that “the truth doesn’t matter.”
To Levin, Meta’s playbook for handling controversies like the No Kings Instagram suspension is to lawyer up, offer technical explanations, and issue “empty apologies.”
Levin also pointed to Meta’s decision to donate $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund and later $5 million for Trump’s ballroom project, which Levin said were blatant efforts to curry favor with the president.
Given what Levin sees as Zuckerberg’s alignment with Trump, he said it’s difficult for No Kings to accept that a technical glitch, rather than deliberate action by someone at Meta, was behind the suspension. Levin acknowledged that some posts that appear to be suppressed on Meta platforms may simply fail to get traction. But given Meta’s history with election content and its failure to make changes to protect pro-democracy content, he said, it’s difficult for outsiders to not be skeptical.
For example, Levin said Meta never acknowledged that at least one No Kings creator’s account was also suspended on the day the No Kings account was disabled. Other No Kings creators have reported that some Instagram posts seemingly receive no views.
“This is why the history does matter,” Levin said. “The context matters here because if I believed Meta to be a corporation that was operating above-board and was stridently pro-democracy and always erred in the defense of people organizing, I would say, ‘Look, it’s Meta. You know Meta, they wouldn’t do that. Probably there’s something else going on.’ But you would have to not have your head screwed on straight to believe that based on the publicly available information.”
Trump seems to shift No Kings tactics
Levin told Ars that one of his biggest remaining questions is whether Meta had any interactions with the Trump administration ahead of the suspension.
To No Kings, the Trump administration had been vocal in its opposition to the protests during the coalition’s first two events. Last October, Trump controversially posted an AI-generated video of a jet labeled “King Trump” flying over protesters while blasting the Kenny Loggins song “Danger Zone.” He has also directly dismissed protesters as an “ineffective” “joke,” echoing comments from others in his administration.
But Trump may have realized that such comments were only drawing more attention to the movement, and there has since been a “notable tactical shift,” Levin suggested. Trump and his supporters now seem to pointedly refuse to discuss No Kings, perhaps hoping to deny the movement oxygen, he said.
“It’s not absurd to think they were also talking to their friends in social media and asking them to not cover this as much or tilt the algorithm a certain way,” Levin said.
Although four hours may not seem like a long time, any disruption that makes it harder for No Kings to reach people has a significant impact, Levin said.
“We are forced to use these platforms that are privately owned in order to reach these folks,” Levin said. “And in using the platforms, we are vulnerable to this kind of pressure, and that directly undermines our ability to reach these people.”
If the same thing happened “in the middle of election day, where pro-democracy accounts are suppressed or shut down,” that could be “cataclysmic,” Levin said.
Lawmakers, AGs probe Meta
David Greene, senior counsel for the digital rights group the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), told Ars that the timing of the No Kings Instagram suspension is “suspicious” and that Meta’s technical excuse is “a really incomplete answer.”
As No Kings continues to demand that Meta release any communications with Trump, Meta also faces increased pressure from lawmakers and state officials to make changes to support accounts like No Kings during election day.
Last week, a coalition of 14 state attorneys general sent a letter to Meta demanding a more transparent explanation of the suspension. By October 29, they asked Meta to “detail its plans to ensure that legitimate election activity on Meta platforms is not disrupted.”
“This is particularly concerning given the proliferation of AI agents marketed to consumers, including by Meta, as compatible with social media accounts,” the attorneys general wrote.
Ars could not confirm whether the coalition’s deadline was met, but the attorneys general weren’t alone in expressing concern that Meta may be “unable to differentiate between legitimate political activity and bot activity that harms users” in the age of AI.
Democratic Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen sent a similar request, The New Republic reported, specifically asking why it took so long for Meta to help admins regain access. In Congress, Robert Garcia and Jamie Raskin, members of the House Oversight Committee and House Judiciary Committee, also probed Meta for answers. Levin noted that these lawmakers could become future chairs of those committees if the elections swing No Kings’ way.
In Levin’s ideal world, “the next Congress” would “take a very different approach” to regulating the tech industry. He believes that could have significant consequences ahead of the next presidential election. Rather than seeing tech CEOs aligned with the executive branch, there could finally be a more “healthy” public debate, where “different presidential candidates” may adopt “different positions of their orientation towards Silicon Valley,” Levin said.
The path Meta is not taking
Greene suggested that Meta could take steps such as requiring human review of election-related content or creating emergency support channels to quickly address automated throttling, inadvertent suspensions, or content removals.
Although Meta has no legal obligation to do so, Greene said, “they certainly have an obligation to their users to anticipate these things and to be ready for them.”
Greene told Ars that he agreed with Meta’s Oversight Board, which directed Meta to take proactive steps to protect election-related content rather than simply waiting to fix problems after an account is automatically suspended. One possible solution, Greene suggested, would be a notification system allowing No Kings to notify Meta when major events are planned so the company can prepare.
“Clearly if it was a technical problem, it’s a technical problem that should have been expected and thought about ahead of time and anticipated and addressed ahead of time,” Greene said. “The No Kings stuff was not secret in any way.”
Like Levin, Greene pointed to Meta’s history of mishandling election content, not just in the US but around the world. Levin noted that No Kings worked with election organizers in Brazil, where Meta also recently faced allegations of electoral interference.
“These are technical glitches that happen around elections all the time, and Meta just needs to have an affirmative plan for this and not just try to respond as they happen,” Greene said. “And I think until they do that, they’re not going to dispel suspicion that things are politically motivated.”
The EFF believes the Trump administration should disclose all its communications with Meta, but so far neither side is clarifying whether Trump may be influencing how Meta handles election-related content, Greene said.
Greene said it’s difficult to determine whether Meta was engaged in “jawboning,” with the Trump administration pressuring the platform to silence dissidents. However, “the explanation they’ve given is so inadequate that it’s hard to discount the [idea] that there was political influence,” he said.
And he agreed that a four-hour admin lockout was too long.
“Because as we know, when you’re organizing a protest, even if you shorten this to a three-minute delay from a three-hour delay, that could be consequential,” Greene said. “And so, the idea is to avoid these things in the first place.”
Kate Ruane, director of the Center for Democracy and Technology’s Free Expression Project, told Ars that Meta must explain not only why its automated systems flagged accounts like the No Kings Instagram account but also why the “mistake prevention systems” it designed to avoid such situations “were not triggered in this circumstance.”
Ruane noted that the CDT supports the JAWBONE Act, which “would require the government to be transparent with the public about communications from the government to online speech intermediaries related to the constitutionally protected speech they distribute.” If the next Congress passes that law, Meta could face greater scrutiny if questions about the No Kings suspension remain unanswered. Levin suggested that “a pro-democracy Congress” would send subpoenas, hold hearings, and use legislative processes to hold Meta accountable.
“Large-scale political speech events are frequently organized using Meta’s services,” Ruane said. “It is critical for users engaged in those activities to understand exactly what happened and how they and Meta can avoid it in the future.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide.
Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking.
This post introduces how Cartesia, an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation.
The rise of conversational AI and latency expectations
The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries:
- Contact centers: AI agents handling millions of customer interactions require instantaneous speech generation to maintain natural dialogue.
- Telehealth: Remote patient consultations demand low-latency voice for accurate, empathetic communication.
- Gaming and virtual worlds: Immersive experiences require real-time voice synthesis for non-player characters (NPCs) and player interactions.
- Accessibility: Screen readers and voice interfaces must respond instantly to serve users with visual impairments.
- Inbound and outbound sales: AI sales agents must respond without awkward pauses to qualify leads, handle objections, and keep prospects on the line.
Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off.
AI for voice: State Space Models (SSM)
State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. Transformers use a mechanism called attention, which compares every element in a sequence to every other element. As a result, the amount of computation grows quadratically as the sequence gets longer. SSMs instead treat a sequence as a system that evolves continuously over time, processing it step by step and carrying a compact internal state forward. This can be converted into a form computers handle efficiently, keeping the cost low for certain long sequences. This efficiency makes SSMs well suited to real-time, streaming data like live speech.
Key advantages of SSMs for audio processing include:
- High-quality long-range dependencies: Structured SSMs are a form of linear recurrence, but their state parameterization preserves information over long audio sequences, avoiding the long-range signal decay that limits classic recurrent neural networks (RNNs) such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks.
- Constant memory footprint: Unlike transformers that cache all previous tokens, SSMs maintain a fixed-size hidden state.
- Native streaming support: The recurrent structure processes input token-by-token, so it supports true streaming without architectural modifications.
These properties make SSMs uniquely suited for real-time voice applications where both quality and latency are non-negotiable.
How it works: SSMs for real-time voice
Cartesia puts these SSM advantages to work in two production voice models: Sonic for speech generation and Ink for transcription.
Introducing Cartesia
Cartesia is a real-time multimodal intelligence company that has built a voice AI application, purpose-built on State Space Model architecture. Founded by researchers who pioneered SSM advances, Cartesia’s application is designed for streaming inference at the edge of human perception.
The application features two core models, Sonic for text-to-speech and Ink for speech-to-text, both optimized for sub-100ms first-byte latency while maintaining studio-quality output.
Sonic (text-to-speech)
Sonic is Cartesia’s flagship streaming text-to-speech model, delivering ultra-realistic speech synthesis with sub-100ms latency:
- First audio byte in approximately 90ms: Users hear the voice respond almost instantaneously.
- Ultra-realistic voice quality: Natural prosody, emotion, and expressiveness across over 44 languages.
- Voice cloning with minimal data: Create natural-sounding custom voices from 10-second audio samples.
- Streaming-native architecture: Audio begins generating before the full text input is received.
- Context-aware synthesis: Maintains consistent tone and style across long passages.
Sonic is recommended for teams that want the fastest time-to-production with minimal operational overhead. Call the API and receive streaming audio in real time.
Ink (speech-to-text)
Ink is Cartesia’s streaming speech-to-text model, purpose-built for conversational AI applications:
- Native turn detection: Automatically identifies when a speaker has finished their turn, alleviating awkward pauses without a separate voice activity detection (VAD) or end pointing model.
- Context-aware end pointing: Uses semantic understanding to distinguish between mid-sentence pauses and true conversation boundaries.
- Streaming transcription: Emits partial transcripts in real time as the user speaks, so a downstream large language model (LLM) can begin forming its response before the turn ends.
- Noise robustness: Maintains accuracy in noisy environments common in real-world deployments.
- Multi-speaker support: Handles overlapping speech and speaker transitions gracefully.
Together, Sonic and Ink provide the complete voice AI stack needed to build conversational agents that feel human.
Deploying Cartesia on AWS
If you need data sovereignty, latency control, or compliance, you can deploy Cartesia models directly into your own AWS account. Sonic is delivered as an Amazon SageMaker AI model package through AWS Marketplace, which you deploy to a SageMaker AI endpoint running entirely within your virtual private cloud (VPC). Inference data doesn’t leave your account.
The deployment patterns in this section cover Sonic. Ink is currently available through the Cartesia API, which you can purchase through the Cartesia Voice AI Platform listing in AWS Marketplace. Two primary patterns are available for Sonic.
Option 1: Amazon SageMaker AI (AWS Marketplace model package)
Deploying on Amazon SageMaker AI is the fastest path to a managed, in-VPC Sonic endpoint. Sonic ships as an AWS Marketplace model package, so there’s a one-time subscribe step that grants your account an AWS Region-specific model-package ARN. You then create the SageMaker AI endpoint from that ARN, either from the console or with the SageMaker or Boto3 SDK. The following steps follow Cartesia’s official deployment notebook.
Prerequisites
Run from an Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instance or SageMaker Studio.
The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role needs AmazonSageMakerFullAccess.
To subscribe, your role (and you) need aws-marketplace:Subscribe, aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe, and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions. Otherwise, the account must already be subscribed to the listing.
Before deployment, choose a supported instance type from the model package’s SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes field:
- ml.g6e.xlarge or larger
- ml.g7e.2xlarge or larger
- ml.g7.2xlarge or larger
- ml.p5.48xlarge
- ml.p5en.48xlarge
If your chosen instance type’s applied value is below your current usage plus your planned endpoint instance count, you may need to request a service quota increase. See SageMaker AI quotas for details.
Deploy Sonic 3.6 to a SageMaker endpoint
In Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, you can subscribe to its AWS Marketplace model package, create a SageMaker model, and host it on a real-time endpoint. The following four steps show the deployment path.
- In SageMaker AI, open AWS Marketplace resources, then All products. Search for Sonic 3.6 SageMaker and choose the Cartesia listing.
- Choose View purchase options, review the pricing and terms, and subscribe. The subscription grants your AWS account access to the model package. It doesn’t deploy resources.
- Open Deployments & inference > Deployable models, choose Create model, select Use a model package subscription from AWS Marketplace, and select Sonic 3.6 SageMaker. Choose an execution role, then create the model.
- Create a real-time endpoint from the model with a supported GPU instance, such as ml.g6e.2xlarge. The endpoint first appears with Creating status. Wait for InService before invoking it.
The model-package ARN is Region-specific. To verify the Sonic 3.6 package in US East (N. Virginia) with the SageMaker API, run:
After the endpoint reaches InService, invoke it with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream API and process the returned audio stream in your application.
Option 2: Self-managed on EC2 GPU instances
Some teams have existing GPU infrastructure, strict networking requirements, or a need to co-locate Cartesia with other services. For these cases, you can run the model container yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) GPU instances. This gives you full control over the runtime, scaling, and network path. It uses Cartesia’s container image, obtained from Cartesia, rather than the AWS Marketplace model package.
Obtain the container image. Request the Sonic container image and licensing terms from Cartesia. Replicate it into your own private Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository so your compute plane can pull it with IAM-scoped credentials rather than reaching out to an external registry at scale.
Choose your GPU instance family. Sonic runs on NVIDIA GPU instances. The G6 (L4) and G6e (L40S) families are the optimal balance for real-time TTS. The earlier G5 (A10G) also works. Match GPU memory and vCPU to your target concurrency and prefer a single-GPU instance per model replica for simplest scaling.
Provision the compute plane (Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)). For ECS: register a GPU task definition (set the container’s GPU resource requirement, for example, resourceRequirements with type GPU) and run it as a service behind an Application Load Balancer. For EKS: create a GPU node group (or Karpenter provisioner) using the EKS GPU-optimized AMI, install the NVIDIA device plugin, and deploy the container as a Deployment fronted by a Service/Ingress.
Configure networking for low latency. Place inference nodes in a cluster placement group to minimize inter-node latency, keep replicas in a single Availability Zone for the tightest path, and use VPC endpoints for ECR/S3 pulls. For hybrid or on-premises callers, terminate traffic over AWS Direct Connect or a private Network Load Balancer to avoid public-internet hops.
Load model weights efficiently. Store model weights on a shared, low-latency volume (Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) or Amazon FSx for Lustre) mounted across replicas so new pods/tasks start without each re-downloading multi-GB artifacts. Warm the model at container start and expose a health check so the load balancer only routes to ready replicas.
Tune batching and concurrency. Set the container’s max batch size and concurrent-stream limits to match your traffic profile. Higher batch size improves GPU utilization but adds first-byte latency, so tune against your sub-100ms target. Benchmark streams-per-GPU to find the replica capacity you will scale on.
Implement custom auto scaling. Scale on a signal that reflects real load, active audio-stream count or GPU utilization, rather than CPU. On Amazon ECS, use AWS Application Auto Scaling with a custom Amazon CloudWatch metric. On Amazon EKS, use HPA/KEDA driven by a GPU or stream-count metric, with Karpenter (or Cluster Autoscaler) adding GPU nodes as replicas grow.
Add observability and resiliency. Emit latency (time-to-first-byte), stream counts, and GPU metrics to CloudWatch. Run at least two replicas across nodes for availability. Set rolling-update or draining policies so deployments don’t drop in-flight audio streams.
This approach is recommended when integrating Cartesia into an existing machine learning (ML) system, meeting networking or compliance requirements not available through managed services, or optimizing cost with Reserved or Spot GPU capacity. The trade-off is that you own provisioning, scaling, patching, and monitoring that SageMaker would otherwise handle for you.
Learn more: See Amazon ECS task definitions for GPU workloads, managing NVIDIA GPU devices on Amazon EKS, and getting started with GPU-accelerated EC2 instances.
Choosing the right deployment pattern
AWS offers two ways to run Sonic, each suited to a different starting point.
The managed path, using the Amazon SageMaker AI model package from AWS Marketplace, is the default for most teams: you subscribe, deploy to an in-VPC endpoint in minutes, and let SageMaker handle scaling and operations.
The self-managed path, running the model container yourself on EC2 GPU instances, is designed for teams with specific constraints: existing GPU infrastructure, strict networking requirements, or a need to co-locate Cartesia with other services. For these teams, full control over the runtime, scaling, and network path matters more than time to deployment.
The following table summarizes how the two compare.
| Criteria | SageMaker (Marketplace) | EC2 GPU (Self-Managed) | 
| Time to Deployment | Minutes after subscribing | Hours to days | 
| Compute | Real-time endpoint. See SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes for supported instances. | EC2 GPU instances | 
| Operational Control | Managed by AWS | Full control | 
| Scaling | SageMaker automatic scaling | Custom scaling policies | 
| Cost Model | Software fee + per instance hour + infra | EC2 (Reserved/Spot savings) | 
| Networking | In-VPC endpoint (network isolation) | Placement groups, Direct Connect | 
| Best For | Fast, managed, in-VPC | Custom infra, max control | 
Beyond deploying Cartesia in your own account, these models are already proven in production inside Amazon services, and few environments are more demanding for real-time voice than a live contact center. Amazon Connect is exactly that proving ground.
In production: Amazon Connect
This section shows how Cartesia’s voice models operate inside Amazon Connect at production scale.
What is Amazon Connect?
Amazon Connect is a cloud-based contact center service that businesses use to set up and run customer support operations that handle inbound and outbound voice calls, chat, and messaging. With pay-as-you-go pricing and deep integration with AWS services, Amazon Connect powers millions of customer interactions daily across industries from financial services to healthcare.
How Cartesia powers the Amazon Connect experience
Cartesia’s voice AI models integrate natively with Amazon Connect to deliver next-generation contact center experiences:
- Instant responsiveness: Alleviate unnatural pauses that erode customer confidence in AI-powered interactions.
- Real-time transcription: Ink provides live transcription with intelligent turn detection for agent-assist workflows.
- Multilingual support: Serve customers in over 44 languages with consistent voice quality and natural prosody.
- Scalable infrastructure: Handle traffic spikes during peak hours without degradation in voice quality or latency.
By combining the omnichannel orchestration of Amazon Connect with Cartesia’s real-time voice AI, you can automate complex customer interactions while maintaining the natural, responsive experience that builds trust and loyalty.
Getting started
Ready to build ultra-low-latency voice AI applications? Here are next steps:
- Deploy Sonic through SageMaker JumpStart: Search for “Cartesia” in the SageMaker JumpStart model hub and deploy a real-time endpoint in minutes.
- Try the Cartesia API: Get started with the Cartesia get-started guide. No infrastructure setup required.
- Explore reference architectures: Visit the Cartesia GitHub repository for sample notebooks, deployment templates, and integration examples.
- Contact the team: Reach out to Cartesia on AWS Marketplace.
About the authors

articles.title: 'It’s the best Android watch yet' — the four-star Google Pixel Watch 5 drops to a record-low price in the early Black Friday sales
articles.text:
The Google Pixel Watch 5 drops to its lowest-ever price on Amazon — 'it’s the best Android watch yet'
The four-star smartwatch is now $100 off for the first time
You can definitely tell that Black Friday season is upon us, as big discounts on brand-new tech are popping up almost every day now. The latest early deal I've spotted is this record-low price for the Google Pixel Watch 5 at Amazon, which brings the latest version of the popular wearable down to $299.99.
Outside of a smaller $50 discount at the start of October, this is only the second time the Pixel Watch 5 has been on sale since its launch in August. And I don't expect it will get any cheaper than this over the next couple of months — even with Black Friday technically still over three weeks away.
The offer I've picked out here is for the standard 41mm model with Wi-Fi support only. However, the larger 45mm version and the watches with LTE support are also discounted by $100 right now at Amazon.
So, if you prefer a bigger screen or want your watch to be able to receive messages and alerts while away from your phone, you can choose between those options as well. For most, though, the standard 41mm version does everything you need in terms of health tracking, fitness tracking, and phone connectivity — and it's excellent value for money.
Google Pixel Watch 5 — record-low price
The Google Pixel Watch 5 drops to its lowest price yet following this $100 discount at Amazon. It's only the second time the smartwatch has been discounted since launch, and it's unlikely to get any cheaper over Black Friday. It's a competent wearable, too, with an accurate GPS, all the essential health and fitness tracking features you need, and an attractive design. If you're upgrading from a Pixel Watch 3 or 4, you won't notice a huge leap, but for everyone else, it's easily the best Android smartwatch right now.
We called the Google Pixel Watch 5 "the best Android watch yet" in our four-star review.
While it does feel like a clear iterative upgrade over the Pixel Watch 3 and Pixel Watch 4, it's definitely a top choice for anyone picking up a wearable for the first time. It focuses on excelling in the key areas that matter, including reliability and accuracy in metric tracking, offering a comfortable fit and attractive design, and adding advanced features for those who need them, like Breathing Emergency Detection and Insulin Resistance Trends.
The updated Google Health app puts a lot of emphasis on AI, so your mileage may vary on how much you appreciate some of the more advanced health and fitness features that rely on your data, but this is a very capable smartwatch for Android users — now at an even better price.

James Pickard is a Deals Editor at TechRadar. After many years of scouring the net for the cheapest games and tech for his personal use, he decided to make it his job to share all the best bargains and coupon codes with you. James also has almost a decade of experience covering some of the biggest sales events of the year at Eurogamer and VG247, including Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Amazon Prime Day. When not deals hunting or stacking coupon codes to get the biggest savings, James can be found on the PS5, watching a classic film noir or cheering on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
