articles.title: Apple aún no sabe cuándo tendrá suficientes iPhone Duo para todos sus compradores
articles.text:
Con la demanda del iPhone Duo superando con amplitud la cantidad de unidades disponibles para la venta, Apple se está moviendo rápido para tratar de mitigar esa escasez. Sin embargo, aún no sabe cuándo tendrá la disponibilidad suficiente para enviar su primer móvil plegable a todos los compradores.
John Ternus, CEO de Apple, le dijo a Reuters que el acceso al iPhone Duo continúa restringido a pesar de que han incrementado su producción. Por lo pronto, el ejecutivo no se ha aventurado a ofrecer algún tipo de ventana objetivo en la que esta situación podría normalizarse.
"A día de hoy, la disponibilidad del iPhone Duo está limitada. El aumento de la producción avanza bien, pero en este momento no podemos predecir cuándo se van a equilibrar la oferta y la demanda", manifestó el jefe de Apple al citado medio.
Así que si todavía no tienes tu iPhone Duo, lo mejor es que sigas cultivando tu costado más paciente. Al momento de redacción de este artículo, la tienda en línea de Apple sigue mostrando una fecha de entrega estimada para el 22 de enero de 2027, así que no se han observado cambios sustanciales en tal sentido.
Apple no sabe cuándo se equilibrarán la oferta y demanda del iPhone Duo
Vale mencionar que Apple ha logrado reducir los tiempos de espera para algunos de los compradores del iPhone Duo. Se han visto casos de personas que inicialmente recibieron una fecha estimada para diciembre, pero que luego se actualizó a noviembre. Aun así, la cosa dista bastante de ser la ideal.
Desde el principio se sabía que el iPhone Duo estaría disponible en cantidades muy limitadas, aunque la situación ha excedido cualquier estimación previa. Según analistas, no solo la demanda por el plegable ha sido muy alta a pesar de su elevado precio, sino que muy posiblemente hubo menos unidades del móvil a disposición de las que se creía.
Por supuesto que los revendedores hicieron de las suyas y Apple ha tomado medidas para evitar que se aprovechen todavía más del panorama. No obstante, las palabras de Ternus dan a entender que la poca disponibilidad del iPhone Duo posiblemente sea un problema hasta entrado el 2027. A lo que hay que sumarle el episodio de las pantallas con fallos, un episodio que la compañía sostiene que es de alcance limitado.
Más allá de lo que ocurre con el iPhone Duo en particular, el CEO de Apple también se pronunció sobre la crisis de la RAM. El ejecutivo le manifestó a Reuters que durante el último trimestre padecieron un marcado incremento en los precios de la memoria. Ternus dijo que lograron morigerar el impacto de la subida, aunque no precisó si esto se sostendrá en el tiempo.
"Observamos un aumento en los costos de la memoria en comparación con el trimestre de junio, lo cual se vio parcialmente compensado por el beneficio de tener inventario y menores costos en ciertos componentes que no son de memoria", explicó. La próxima prueba de fuego para Apple y sus productos, incluyendo el iPhone Duo, será la temporada navideña.

articles.title: Apple's new iPad mini is thinner, lighter and more expensive
articles.text:
I’ve been using the 2026 Apple iPad mini for about a week, and I’m a fan. While it’s not unique or really special, compared to some of the other Apple devices recently released or announced (like the iPhone Duo, HomeView or the touchscreen MacBook) it’s still a worthwhile update.
It’s worth mentioning that I didn’t get to review or ever use the last iPad mini that came out in 2024, so I will be comparing it with the 2021 device. But I don’t think people update their iPad every two years, so this might be more realistic for buyers. And, on the outside, the 2021 and 2024 versions are pretty much the same.
Ahead of the review, I also wanted to mention that the iPad mini costs $949 to start versus the 2024 model, which was initially priced at $679. Is the new iPad mini worth that price jump? I’m not exactly sure, but it’s definitely worth keeping that $270 increase in mind.
Thin boy
The new iPad mini sports an 8.5-inch OLED panel, which is slightly larger than the previous iteration’s 8.3-inch LCD screen. Though the screen is bigger, the package is even smaller with a noticeably lighter and thinner body, and in my week with the tablet this was the biggest and most impactful difference.
The iPad mini is 5.4mm thin, and the 2024 model is 6.3mm thick, which doesn’t seem like a huge difference on paper, but it ends up being everything. The 2026 iPad mini is thinner than the iPhone Air, and only 0.2mm thicker than the iPhone Duo (when unfolded), it’s so nice in that small package.
As someone who travels a lot, I can’t wait to bring the mini on my next trip; it’s going to fit in my carry-on very nicely. Especially considering the mini is also very light, weighing 255g. I don’t mind holding it for long periods before bed, carrying it around, bringing it on commutes; it’s pretty much the same weight as foldables like the iPhone Duo and the Pixel 10 Pro Fold.
I love the iPad mini’s body; it’s so portable and definitely a highlight for someone who’s on the go often. I’m also having this weird experience where I keep trying to fold the mini because I forget it’s not the Duo, which is definitely a good sign.
OLED is a welcome upgrade
The tablet’s OLED panel is a nice switch-up, showcasing a Super Retina XDR OLED with 1,200 nits of brightness. There’s also a 1,512 x 2,316 pixel resolution, so videos, pictures and more look great. I’m not always the best at seeing the difference in resolution between two phones, but the difference between the Super Retina OLED versus the Liquid Retina IPS LCD is clear. Blacks are blacker, brights are truly bright, and colours are fantastic. I’ve enjoyed watching different shows on Crunchyroll and the look of games.
However, I also could tell that the tablet lacks a 120Hz refresh rate. The iPad mini line isn’t known for the higher refresh rate, but when you’re used to looking at your phone all day with the higher refresh rate, switching to a 60Hz refresh rate iPad can throw you off.
I played Oddmar and Marvel Snap on the iPad, and I could immediately tell something was off when playing. The iPad mini has never had a 120Hz refresh rate before, so I didn’t really expect it, but with the price increase it’d be a nice addition.
Speaking of games, the iPad mini played both games very well without a hitch. I played for about 20 minutes straight of Oddmar and a lot of different sessions of Marvel Snap for at least up to 15 minutes, and the iPad mini stayed cool to the touch. And the games looked gorgeous on the screen.
Portable art studio
The iPad mini’s battery life was definitely better than its predecessor. Apple says it’s an all-day battery, but I don’t use the mini all day like my smartphone or laptop (I don’t think most people would), I use it leisurely. While I can say the mini’s battery life is better than its 2021 predecessor, I definitely don’t need to charge it as much with the same amount of weekly usage — where I browse YouTube, watch anime, play Marvel Snap and scroll social media before bed. However, what’s probably more exciting is the fast charging on the iPad mini, as the little tablet can get up to 50 per cent in 30 minutes with the right charger.
The mini also works with the Apple Pencil Pro. While I’m not really a stylus guy, I like that you can quickly write something down in a text field and it changes from my messy writing into text. It’s a nice touch considering the iPad mini isn’t necessarily the best for typing on.
My partner, on the other hand, loves designing, painting and drawing so I let him test out the Apple Pencil Pro with the iPad mini, and he was really impressed. It was the first time he used the Pencil Pro, and he liked that it was pressure-sensitive and that it magnetically attaches and charges super quickly on the side of the tablet, so you never have to worry about it.
He also likes that when you squeeze the Pencil Pro, you can get a menu with different controls. These aren’t necessarily new features, but it’s my first time trying them, and it might be yours as well. Either way, he says the mini and the Pencil Pro are a great combination for artists, especially those who like to create on-the-go.
I liked the iPad mini 2026, anything that can make a commute easier is definitely a pleasure. The slightly larger OLED display is beautiful and a worthwhile upgrade compared to its predecessor. I like the thinner body and lighter casing as well, which is the biggest highlight for the iPad mini 2026.
However, the $270 price hike is hard to swallow, so I wouldn’t blame you for wanting to skip the iPad mini, or for waiting for a sale.
The new iPad mini is available for pre-order now and launches on Nov. 6. It comes in midnight or starlight colours and starts at $949 in Canada for the 128GB version. For students, Apple’s education store offers the iPad mini for $879 — but you’ll need proof to get the discount.

articles.title: Valve is making changes to deal with a ‘significant increase’ in Steam game submissions
articles.text:
In a new post today, Valve acknowledged that it’s seen “a significant increase in submissions for store and page review in recent months” and says it’s “running a little behind” by taking “up to 12 business days” for reviews instead of the typical 3-5 days.
Valve is making changes to deal with a ‘significant increase’ in Steam game submissions
Valve admits that it’s now taking ‘up to 12 business days’ to review games.
Indie developers have recently expressed frustrations over lengthy approval times for Steam games, even causing some games to miss planned launch dates. Valve says that “much” of the delay is having to re-review games, so it’s making some changes to the release checklist for developers to hopefully “cut down on re-reviews for basic functional issues.”
The changes include requiring developers to run games through Steam for at least five minutes. “Believe it or not, sometimes we review builds that have not ever been played through Steam,” Valve says. “This means that even if a game runs smoothly when a dev launches their executable directly, they might have missed basic steps that would impact a user installing and playing via Steam.”
Other requirements include making sure that achievements are ready and confirming any required common redistributables, like DirectX or Visual C++, that Steam may need to install.
Valve also says more improvements are in the works for the build review process.

articles.title: Google Dismantles XCPE Botnet of 1.3 Million Android Devices
articles.text:
Google on Monday announced the dismantling of XCPE (aka X.CPE), a backdoor and botnet of more than 1.3 million Android set-top boxes.
The malware was developed and deployed by Videostrong Technology, a China-based original equipment manufacturer and original design manufacturer (OEM/ODM) of Android devices that also operated the botnet.
Videostrong, Google says, sold access to affiliates and loaded malicious modules on the backdoored devices, which were then abused for ad fraud and data exfiltration, as residential proxies, and for loading additional malware.
“We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” the internet giant says.
As part of the takedown, Google took legal action to take down the botnet’s domains and servers, as well as the command-and-control (C&C) domains behind the additional modules loaded on the XCPE bots.
This likely resulted in severed access to at least 10 million other devices, as the module’s operators had diversified the distribution of their malware beyond XCPE.
Google believes the XCPE botnet was a deliberate operation by Videostrong, not the work of a rogue insider or the result of a development oversight. As such, it banned the company from making devices with preloaded Google apps.
“Google requires OEMs to go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device’s first boot,” Google says.
Videostrong’s pre-installed malware has had a three-stage architecture consisting of the primary backdoor that persisted on the /oem/ partition, a loader and execution engine, and the monetization modules that could execute additional backdoors and load more modules.
The company provided affiliates with access to its backdoor, thus allowing them to monetize the infected devices for a long time.
“While the overwhelming majority of the infected devices in the XCPE botnet are Android TV set-top boxes, we observed a number of other infected Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices,” Google notes.
In XCPE’s disruption, Google received help from Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, Human Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI. Technical details on the botnet and the takedown were published by Plume (PDF), Synthient, and TrendAI as well.
“While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs,” Google said.

articles.title: Evertrue Capital raises €15 million debut fund backed by British Business Bank and Phoenix Court | EU-Startups
articles.text:
British VC firm Evertrue Capital, the debut fund of Yvonne Bajela, has closed at €15 million ($17 million) aiming to invest €299-€599k (£250k–£500k) at pre-Seed in founders building frontier technologies primarily in the UK and Europe.
The fund is backed by Phoenix Court through Basecamp, its fund of funds investing in a global community of emerging managers, alongside the British Business Bank, Better Society Capital, Bootstrap 4F (Invest in Women Taskforce) and Allocator One.
Yvonne Bajela, founder and General Partner at Evertrue Capital, says: “Over the past decade, I’ve backed founders who went on to build billion-dollar companies, and almost none of them looked obvious at the start. The ones I’m drawn to understand a problem deeply, often from lived experience, and have the conviction and discipline to build around it. They don’t always fit a familiar pattern, but their insight gives them an edge others can’t yet see.
“The best moment to invest is before the market has proof. That belief has shaped Evertrue. We make concentrated, early bets and give founders the capital, access and support to build companies of consequence.”
Evertrue’s close follows several European early-stage VC fund announcements in 2026.
In the UK, Nauta secured a €60 million first close to back software and DeepTech startups, while Project Ventures launched a €5.8 million fund targeting AI and research-led businesses.
Elsewhere, Germany’s Vanagon Ventures closed a €20 million debut fund, also backed by Allocator One, while Berlin-based solo GP Robin Capital just today also closed a €15 million second fund.
Spain’s Masia secured €18 million, Belgium’s solo-GP NewSchool VC closed €10 million, and Germany’s ZOHO.VC reached a €7 million first close.
These fund closes represent approximately €130 million in disclosed capital, rising to €145 million including Evertrue.
EU-Startups previously named Evertrue among the British Business Bank’s first microfund recipients in June 2026, having interviewed Bajela about her investment approach in 2021.
Zaki Gabe-Wilkinson, co-founder of YC-backed Revion, adds: “Yvonne was our first cheque and backed us from day zero. Her conviction in us as founders was clear from the start and she immediately got to work, helping us find top talent and opening doors across the UK and US to industry leaders and investors ahead of our Seed round.”
Evertrue was founded on a belief shaped by Yvonne’s career in investing: that insight often comes before the evidence. Yvonne was previously a Partner at Phoenix Court, home of LocalGlobe and Latitude.
After beginning her career at Goldman Sachs and founding her own company, she joined Mitsui & Co., where she became one of its youngest investment managers, investing globally in tech companies including Wise and helping portfolio companies expand into Asia. She later became a founding member and Principal at Impact X Capital, leading its Seed investment in Marshmallow, before joining Phoenix Court as a Partner, where she invested in and supported technology companies including Moove.
According to Evertrue, fundraising for solo GPs has become increasingly difficult, with 67% of new VC funds launched in 2024 targeted under €8.9 million ($10 million).
Rather than pursuing a high-volume portfolio strategy, Evertrue will lead a concentrated number of investments each year.
The fund has already invested in seven companies, including:
- Revion, agentic AI for the automotive sector
- Poindexter Labs, an AI capability and efficiency lab
- Zuba, the FinTech building the infrastructure for global businesses
- Zaro, the shared knowledge layer for enterprises.
Half the portfolio has already launched operations in the US.
Jocelyn D’Arcy, co-founder of Poindexter Labs, says: “Yvonne saw what we were building before it was easy to explain, back when training data was still an afterthought to most investors. That early belief gave us the confidence to go after the partnerships that mattered.”

articles.title: Exclusive: Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away
articles.text:
Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions, TechCrunch has learned.
The project received grant funding from the Shell Foundation, an independent charity established by the British oil and gas giant Shell plc. A section of the Shell Foundation’s website that has since been removed said the project’s goal was to “enable and de-risk global OEM entry into Africa’s EV market by piloting a locally integrated electric two-wheeler platform in Kenya, with potential to scale across East Africa.”
According to the deleted section, Also was expected to work on modular battery designs and distributed EV charging, and planned on “developing a purpose-built electric motorcycle for African riders.”
The opportunity for electric motorcycles seems ripe on the continent, which has a massive two-wheeler market. African mobility company Spiro recently said it has more than 130,000 electric motorcycles operating across seven countries, along with 2,500 battery-swapping stations. This boom has drawn interest from Chinese mobility companies and investors, which are pouring resources into the space.
In a September email, Also told TechCrunch that it had “explored this project” with an unnamed partner, but ultimately “decided to focus on its core roadmap” after completing only “some early-stage work.” Also said the grant funding it received from the Shell Foundation “will follow the project to support its ongoing development,” but declined to offer specifics.
The Shell Foundation told TechCrunch in an email that the project was “intended to generate evidence on driver income uplift potential, operational performance and commercial viability to deepen the company’s understanding of the market opportunity.” But when TechCrunch asked for more specifics, the Shell Foundation declined, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Also. Days later, the project disappeared from the Shell Foundation’s website.
During an interview last month at TechCrunch Disrupt, Also co-founder and president Chris Yu said the Kenya pilot project initially made sense given Also’s mission to build small, purpose-built vehicles that are “first and foremost cost-optimized to do the job that needs to be done in a particular market.”
But other projects took precedence, Yu said, especially the development of small autonomous vehicles — which Also is working on as part of a partnership with DoorDash.
“We piloted and ultimately decided, largely because of just urgency and pace around autonomy, frankly, that our attention would be best, in the near term, served fully focused” on that, he said, adding that he thinks there’s a “high chance that autonomy will show up first, and at a broader scale in these types of purpose-built smaller vehicles than at scale in passenger vehicles.”
Also walked away from the Africa project during a somewhat rocky first year of independence.
Supply chain problems forced the company to repeatedly delay deliveries of its first product, a premium e-bike called the TM-B, frustrating customers who had reserved one. What made matters worse was Also’s relative silence. The company said little for much of 2026 about when the bikes would arrive — a communication failure its leadership now acknowledges was a mistake.
“I think we did a pretty poor job communicating to our reservation holders through the summer when they were all waiting, and we got called out for that,” Yu said in the interview. “But I think it’s actually great. It’s really hard to earn the opportunity for people to care, and to tell us what they think, and to help us improve.”
Getting its first product launch back on track is crucial for Also, which has ambitions far beyond e-bikes. The company plans to sell commercial cargo bikes to companies like Amazon, including four-wheeled models, and has the partnership with DoorDash. These products are next in the company’s pipeline, Yu said, and represent bigger revenue opportunities.
But the TM-B comes first. It’s Also’s most visible product to consumers, and its striking design has drawn plenty of curiosity.
Yu said no single problem was responsible for delaying the bikes, which finally started shipping to customers in early October. Instead, Also spent much of the year playing supply chain Whac-A-Mole, a particularly difficult challenge given the TM-B’s complexity. Yu described the bike as “kind of a computer on wheels.”
At one point, Also found itself competing for the same raw materials used to make printed circuit boards for AI data centers. At other times, the company struggled to navigate certification requirements with different government agencies.
Yu said the scope of these problems, and the pace at which new ones popped up — almost weekly — made it difficult to give customers reliable updates about why their bikes were delayed.
“The entire team is like running at a million miles an hour to get these things produced and shipped to customers, and then it’s also really dynamic as well,” he said. “I think what we could have done better is just [say], straight up: ‘We’re chasing down these things, we’ll have an update shortly.’”
That didn’t happen at first, but Also has steadily improved its communication, earning some goodwill from customers on Reddit. The company will need it as it works through the inevitable kinks that come with a first product. Early customers have already reported problems, including delivery damage and noticeable battery drain.

articles.title: Anthropic quer impedir que empresas escondam qual IA estão usando
articles.text:
A Anthropic está desenvolvendo tecnologia que permite verificar se uma resposta foi realmente produzida pelo modelo de inteligência artificial (IA) que uma empresa afirma utilizar. Batizado de FlashProve, o sistema usa criptografia para criar uma espécie de comprovante matemático da identidade do modelo responsável por determinada saída.
A proposta é dar aos usuários uma maneira de confirmar se estão interagindo com a IA anunciada pelo fornecedor, em vez de uma versão diferente ou menos avançada. Segundo a Anthropic, o mecanismo também poderia dificultar tentativas de empresas de substituir secretamente seus modelos por alternativas mais baratas ou apresentar resultados de desempenho que não correspondem à tecnologia utilizada.
O projeto foi apresentado em publicação da companhia nesta terça-feira (3). A empresa também disponibilizou uma especificação técnica e partes do código em formato aberto para que outros pesquisadores possam examinar e aprimorar a iniciativa.
Como funciona o FlashProve?
- O sistema utiliza o conceito de “inferência comprovável”, que consiste em gerar uma prova criptográfica de que determinada resposta veio de um modelo específico;
- A ideia é semelhante às assinaturas digitais usadas em e-mails para confirmar a identidade de quem enviou uma mensagem. Nesse caso, porém, a verificação serviria para identificar qual IA produziu um conteúdo;
- Para isso, os desenvolvedores de modelos precisariam publicar uma espécie de impressão digital de cada sistema lançado. Posteriormente, essa identificação poderia ser comparada às respostas produzidas pela IA e verificada por meio de mecanismos criptográficos;
- Um aspecto importante é que essas impressões digitais não revelariam os pesos do modelo — os valores internos que determinam seu funcionamento e comportamento. Empresas, como Anthropic e OpenAI, mantêm essas informações privadas, mas poderiam participar de um sistema de verificação sem abrir mão desse segredo comercial;
- A tecnologia também foi projetada para ser leve, permitindo que a verificação seja realizada diretamente em um dispositivo local.
Leia mais:
- Anthropic diz que IA pode acelerar o próprio desenvolvimento
- Modelo de IA da Anthropic ignora aviso e mantém ciberataque em teste de segurança
- Anthropic muda regras do Claude Code para impedir cópias de jogos existentes
Sistema poderia impedir troca secreta de modelos
Um dos problemas que o FlashProve pretende enfrentar é a possibilidade de um fornecedor apresentar um modelo aos clientes, mas utilizar outro durante o funcionamento do serviço.
Uma empresa poderia, por exemplo, anunciar o acesso a uma IA avançada e substituí-la por alternativa mais barata para reduzir custos. O mecanismo também poderia dificultar situações em que uma companhia utiliza um modelo diferente daquele que afirma ter empregado para demonstrar determinado desempenho.
A verificação teria aplicações além dos serviços oferecidos diretamente pelas empresas de IA.
Os pesquisadores citam o exemplo de um desenvolvedor que afirma ter utilizado um modelo avançado de cibersegurança para examinar uma biblioteca de software em busca de vulnerabilidades. Outra possibilidade seria uma empresa declarar que seu plano de negócios recebeu aprovação de uma IA apropriada para a tarefa.
Com o FlashProve, seria possível verificar criptograficamente se o modelo anunciado realmente foi utilizado nesses processos.
Tecnologia ainda não tem previsão de lançamento
Apesar da apresentação pública, o FlashProve ainda é um projeto de pesquisa. A Anthropic disponibilizou uma especificação técnica detalhada e código funcional de diferentes componentes sob uma licença de código aberto, permitindo que a comunidade examine e desenvolva o sistema.
A companhia, no entanto, não anunciou planos para implementar a tecnologia em seus próprios serviços ou em outras plataformas de IA.
Os pesquisadores afirmaram que a publicação representa avanço intermediário do trabalho, e não a conclusão de uma agenda de pesquisa. A intenção é permitir que outras equipes analisem a proposta, aproveitem seus componentes e contribuam para aperfeiçoá-la.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
articles.text:
How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
Borrowing from disciplines like economics could help AI safety researchers control AI models, even if they don’t understand them.
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.
As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.
Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.
The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.
Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.
An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.
In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.
A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).
Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.
The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.
A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”
Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.
During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.
There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.
Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.
Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”
One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.
It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.
“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.
Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)
Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?
“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

articles.title: Tu TV box con Android podría traer malware de fábrica: Google desactiva una puerta trasera en millones de dispositivos
articles.text:
Mucho ojo si tienes un TV box con Android en tu casa. Google descubrió que un fabricante de dispositivos certificados con Android TV y Google TV instaló una puerta trasera que se usó para distribuir malware y controlar la red de bots XCPE. Se calcula que existen millones de aparatos impactados por esta situación, vinculados con una empresa llamada Videostrong.
Según explican los de Mountain View, Videostrong fabricaba modelos de TV box con Android que llegaban desde fábrica con una puerta trasera destinada a fines maliciosos. La empresa indica que los acusados vendían el uso de ese backdoor para cargar malware y controlar los aparatos de forma remota a través de botnets.
Uno de los socios de Google para desmantelar esta operación fue Synthient, que descubrió que la brecha de seguridad en los TV box con Android de Videostrong otorgaba a los hackers privilegios a nivel de sistema. Esto permitía llevar a cabo todo tipo de acciones, desde la gestión de archivos hasta la ejecución de código de forma remota.
La campaña atribuida a Videostrong no se limita a una marca o a un modelo de TV box con Android en particular. Los investigadores han señalado que los registros de la botnet XCPE están presentes en modelos que se venden bajo la denominación Mecool y YokaTV, entre otros.
"Videostrong monetizó la puerta trasera vendiendo acceso a afiliados delictivos e instalando los módulos de malware de dichos afiliados en los dispositivos infectados. Estos módulos secundarios llevaban a cabo fraudes publicitarios, incorporaban de forma silenciosa los dispositivos infectados a redes de proxies residenciales e instalaban malware adicional en los dispositivos comprometidos por XCPE. Asimismo, tomamos medidas para desmantelar los dominios de comando y control (C2) que operan estos módulos de los afiliados", indica Google.
Google desmantela una puerta trasera en millones de TV box con Android TV y Google TV
El uso de dispositivos tipo TV box con Android para distribuir malware no es nuevo. Los actores maliciosos suelen aprovechar esta plataforma debido a su popularidad para acceder a servicios pirateados, tanto de streaming como de eventos deportivos. El caso de Videostrong es una mancha particularmente notoria para Google. Esto, porque la empresa era tanto un fabricante de equipos originales (OEM) como un fabricante de diseños originales (ODM) con Android.
Al producir equipos con Android TV o Google TV certificados, Videostrong podía precargar las apps de Google en los aparatos. Esto le daba una legitimidad mayor a los productos que comercializaba y que en los últimos años se hicieron especialmente conocidos en el mundo. Algunas de las marcas de TV box con Android impactadas por esta puerta trasera se volvieron populares en países como México, Brasil, Alemania, Malasia, Estados Unidos y China, indica Synthient.
Si bien Google habla de que alrededor de 1,3 millones de TV box con Android de Videostrong fueron infectados y utilizados en la botnet XCPE, el número de dispositivos afectados sería mucho mayor. Los californianos calculan que serían más de 10 millones los aparatos comprometidos por esta puerta trasera.
Todas las miradas sobre Videostrong
Al ser Videostrong el fabricante de dispositivos con Android certificados, sus TV box tienen que pasar por un proceso de evaluación de Google. De acuerdo con la compañía, los actores maliciosos tomaron medidas para ocultar la puerta trasera durante las pruebas de seguridad.
"Google exige a los fabricantes de equipos originales (OEM) que se sometan a un conjunto exhaustivo de pruebas de compatibilidad y seguridad para garantizar una experiencia de usuario coherente y segura en todo el ecosistema Android. Sin embargo, Videostrong empleó técnicas de ofuscación para aprovechar una laguna en nuestras pruebas y cargar código malicioso tras el primer arranque del dispositivo. Como resultado, Google ha introducido cambios en su proceso de revisión actual para protegerse mejor frente a actividades similares en el futuro. Que un fabricante de dispositivos infecte deliberadamente a sus usuarios con software malicioso constituye una ruptura de la confianza inaceptable y representa un grave riesgo para dichos usuarios. Sin el conocimiento ni el consentimiento de los usuarios, los dispositivos infectados se utilizaron como mecanismo de distribución para diversos actores delictivos. Esto dio lugar a una serie de actividades maliciosas llevadas a cabo en los dispositivos (o a través de ellos), tales como el fraude publicitario, la exfiltración de datos y el enrutamiento de tráfico de red malicioso a través de dichos dispositivos".
Google
Google ha tomado varias medidas para desactivar la puerta trasera de Videostrong en sus TV box con Android. Entre ellas, el desmantelamiento de los servidores y los dominios que se usaban para instalar malware y controlar la botnet XCPE, como también para manejar las acciones de comando y control, al igual que la distribución de otras familias de software malicioso.
Asimismo, los de Mountain View han vetado a Videostrong y a cualquier filial o subsidiara (existente o futura) de fabricar y comercializar dispositivos Android certificados. Pero esto no es todo: la empresa tampoco podrá vender software a otros fabricantes certificados.
Tanto Synthient como Google Threat Intelligence han publicado reportes técnicos que abordan en profundidad esta campaña y sus implicaciones. Los investigadores instan a los usuarios de estos TV box con Android a inspeccionarlos y/o dejar de usarlos, aunque la realidad puede ser más compleja. De hecho, aún no se sabe qué sucederá con las unidades de las marcas involucradas que se estén comercializando a través de revendedores.

articles.title: Privacy commissioner says Bill C-22 must change to protect Canadians | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada’s privacy commissioner is recommending that the Senate make changes to Canada’s controversial proposed lawful access legislation, Bill C-22.
The news: Speaking before the Senate’s standing committee on national security on Monday, privacy commissioner Philippe Dufresne told senators that his office had drafted several proposed changes to Canada’s proposed Bill C-22, also known as the Lawful Access Act.
If passed into law, Bill C-22 would give law enforcement, as well as national security agencies like the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS), more power to monitor and collect personal communications and data.
From the source: “The current bill incorporates significant improvements over previous versions,” Dufresne told the committee. “These are positive measures, but in spite of these improvements, extra amendments are still necessary to better protect the privacy of Canadians.”
The context: Recommendations from the privacy commissioner included narrowing the definition of which information can be collected and the range of people it could be obtained from, as well as more clearly defining what constitutes publicly available information. Dufresne also recommended a carve out for healthcare-related data or privileged information, and asked that electronic service providers be able to “trigger a preemptive, arm’s length assessment” on how a particular access order would impact their operations.
Notably, Dufresne advocated for legal principles around proportionality and necessity to be integrated into the bill. In the legal field, those terms refer to core legal principles that limit state power and evaluate the legality of rights-restrictive actions. Dufresne told senators that right now “there is no overarching requirement that all obligations imposed under the Act be both necessary and proportionate.”
Final thought: Bill C-22 has earned the ire of both civil liberties organizations and much of Canada’s tech ecosystem, prompting companies like Signal to say they would halt operations in Canada were it to become law. The Munk School’s Citizen Lab and the Electronic Frontier Foundation have argued that the bill infringes on privacy rights and creates a de facto surveillance state.
Bill C-22 passed the House of Commons earlier this year and is currently before the Senate. Some senators, such as Senator Yuen Pau Woo, have expressed doubts about passing the bill in its current form.

articles.title: 10 SA founders selected for One Young World job creation programme - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ten South African entrepreneurs have been selected for a new initiative run by global youth leadership organisation One Young World, which aims to support young founders in scaling their businesses.
With the Ichikowitz Family Foundation as its founding partner, the National Programme for Job-Generating Entrepreneurs supports founders aged 18-35 whose businesses show the potential to create meaningful employment. It is part of the legacy of the One Young World Summit, taking place in Cape Town from November 3-6.
The selected entrepreneurs come from sectors including technology, education, agriculture, transport, fashion and employment services. They include Christiaan van den Berg, co-founder of JOBJACK, a platform connecting unemployed South Africans with entry-level work. It has more than six million users and over 5,000 employer sites, and has placed more than 65,000 people into jobs.
Also selected are Ntwenhle Linda of rural poultry enterprises Qandalami and Bunye Qanda; Merishka Harilall of Alter Ego Promotions and Spenda Holdings; and Mandla Mazibuko of Jobox, which links young people with employers, educational institutions and funders.
The other six are:
- Akhil Boddu of Zaio Institute of Technology, which trains unemployed youth in software, data and AI.
- Bonolo Matjila of skincare brand Golden Hour.
- Huzaifa Khan of Resolute Education, which offers coding, robotics and future-skills education.
- Navhani Tshikosi of student logistics business HRA Transportation.
- Thapelo Nthite of Botlhale AI, which builds digital services in African languages.
- Thobey Cooper of Thobey Cooper and Fierce Creative Academy, which works in fashion and creative education.
The founders will attend the Cape Town summit, and then join One Young World’s network of more than 20,000 young leaders in over 190 countries and receive mentorship from established figures in South Africa’s startup ecosystem.
The programme ends with a Demo Day, provisionally planned for late May 2027, where participants will pitch to prospective investors and partners. The initiative does not provide direct funding, but instead focuses on networks, partnerships and market access.
“South Africa’s youth unemployment challenge demands more than preparing young people to find jobs. We must also support the entrepreneurs who have the vision and potential to create them,” said Kate Robertson, co-founder of One Young World.

articles.title: 1,3 million de boîtiers TV Android piratés : Google démantèle un botnet chinois, installé dès l’usine par un fabricant
articles.text:
Google vient de démanteler un vaste réseau d’appareils compromis. Baptisé XCPE, le botnet regroupait plus de 1,3 million d’appareils Android. Il y a quelques jours, le géant de Mountain View a pris le contrôle de tous les serveurs qui pilotaient le réseau criminel. Google a mis un terme aux activités du botnet avec l’aide de la police nationale japonaise et de plusieurs entreprises de cybersécurité. Selon les investigations menées par le Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), la branche de Google dédiée à l’analyse des menaces, c’est le fabricant des boîtiers qui est à l’origine de l’opération malveillante. Google pointe du doigt Videostrong, une entreprise chinoise basée à Shenzhen.
À lire aussi : 2 millions de TV et de boîtiers Android ont été piratés, mais Google contre-attaque
Une porte dérobée installée dès l’usine
D’après l’enquête de Google, Videostrong a glissé une porte dérobée, intitulée x.cpe, directement dans le système de ses propres boîtiers. De facto, le logiciel malveillant, sur lequel repose toute l’offensive, était déjà présent sur le boîtier au moment de l’achat. En clair, l’acheteur ne pouvait rien faire pour échapper à celui-ci. Le virus, enfoui dans le code de l’appareil, disposait des privilèges les plus élevés du système. Même supprimé, il se réinstallait automatiquement au redémarrage de l’appareil.
« Nous avons trouvé ce logiciel malveillant intégré directement dans de nombreux modèles et marques d’appareils, sur plusieurs années. Nous pensons que cette campagne n’était pas le fait d’un employé isolé ni d’une erreur de développement », explique Google, évoquant une opération de grande ampleur.
Au moment du premier allumage, la porte dérobée commençait par désactiver Play Protect, le système de sécurité intégré à Android. Les cybercriminels pouvaient ensuite installer des applications à l’insu du propriétaire, exécuter des commandes, faire des captures d’écran ou encore simuler des frappes sur le clavier. Les pirates se sont servis de la porte dérobée pour dérober des identifiants, des données sur les appareils et des journaux système.
« Un abus de confiance inacceptable »
Surtout, Videostrong vendait l’accès à la porte dérobée à des groupes criminels. En passant par la porte dérobée, glissée à dessein par Videostrong, les pirates pouvaient installer leurs propres modules malveillants sur les boîtiers. C’était évidemment la porte ouverte à tous les abus. Certains pirates se sont mis à utiliser les boîtiers compromis pour commettre des fraudes publicitaires. En l’occurrence, les appareils compromis par le botnet servaient à générer de fausses vues sur des publicités en ligne. Ce procédé permettait aux truands de gagner rapidement des revenus publicitaires.
D’autres modules identifiés par Google transformaient les boîtiers en proxys résidentiels. Concrètement, les pirates louaient la connexion Internet des victimes à d’autres cybercriminels. Les hackers pouvaient ainsi faire transiter leur trafic malveillant par le réseau Internet des victimes, ce qui leur permettait de camoufler leurs activités.
« Un fabricant d’appareils qui infecte intentionnellement ses utilisateurs avec un logiciel malveillant constitue un abus de confiance inacceptable, et représente un risque sérieux pour ces utilisateurs », dénonce Google.
Impliqués dans l’enquête initiée par Google, les chercheurs de TrendA ont recensé près de 1,5 million d’appareils infectés, répartis sur 206 modèles, entre juin et octobre. La Malaisie, le Brésil, l’Irak, le Mexique et Taïwan sont les pays les plus touchés. Pour faire tomber les serveurs du botnet, Google s’est tourné vers les tribunaux. Avec l’accord de la justice, l’opération va couper l’accès des pirates à au moins 10 millions d’appareils supplémentaires, infectés par d’autres moyens et d’autres virus, mais reposant sur la même infrastructure.
« Une action collective comme celle-ci interrompt l’infrastructure nécessaire à la monétisation, augmente le coût d’exploitation de ces réseaux et affaiblit les incitations qui les font vivre », souligne Gavin Reid, responsable de la sécurité chez HUMAN Security.
Des boîtiers piratés, mais certifiés par Google
Une partie des boîtiers fabriqués par Videostrong ont été certifiés Android TV par Google. Cette certification indique que l’appareil est passé par une batterie de vérifications de sécurité. Elle doit théoriquement permettre aux acheteurs de trier le bon grain de l’ivraie, au moment de l’achat d’un nouveau boîtier TV sous Android. Il s’avère que Videostrong a trouvé le moyen de contourner tous les contrôles de Google. Le groupe chinois avait pris l’habitude de charger le code du malware après le premier démarrage de l’appareil, ce qui lui a permis de passer sous le radar. À la suite de la découverte des pratiques de Videostrong, Google a revu de fond en comble son processus de vérification d’appareils. Sans surprise, Google a aussi cessé de collaborer avec Videostrong. Le fabricant n’est plus autorisé à produire des appareils certifiés Android TV.
 Residential proxies, ad fraud, and credential theft have flourished through sophisticated pre-infected device schemes. This research, in partnership with the @motionpictures and in collaboration with @Google, @trendaisecurity , @BlackLotusLabs , and @SecureWithHUMAN, disrupts one of these operators.
Synthient’s Research Team documents its findings in this report, showing how the operators distributed over 1.3 million devices to unsuspecting consumers and how this supply chain pushed numerous backdoors from APSolo to Honeygain.
Read more here: https://t.co/qOR4fx9xzr
— Synthient (@synthient) November 2, 2026
Les propriétaires d’appareils conçus par Videostrong se retrouvent donc avec un boîtier compromis par un botnet inopérant. Privé de son infrastructure, le botnet ne peut plus recevoir d’ordre de la part des pirates. Bien que le botnet soit hors service, la société Synthient, qui a identifié 182 modèles de boîtiers compromis, recommande tout simplement de jeter les appareils concernés, par mesure de sécurité. La plupart des références piratées proviennent de petites marques chinoises, comme MECOOL, Dreamstar, Cruze TV, Switron, ou Showbox. De notre côté, on vous recommande d’éviter les marques low cost méconnues. Tournez-vous plutôt vers des marques de référence, dont la réputation n’est plus à faire.
Ce n’est pas la première fois que des appareils Android sont infectés par un logiciel malveillant dès la sortie de l’usine. Ces dernières années, plusieurs virus de ce type ont fait parler d’eux. C’est le cas de Badbox, un botnet chinois qui s’est propagé sur des Smart TV, des boîtiers TV, des tablettes et des projecteurs Android, avant même leur mise en vente. Selon le FBI, Badbox est parvenu à compromettre près de dix millions d’appareils à l’été 2025. Citons aussi Triada, un virus retrouvé dans le micrologiciel de milliers de smartphones contrefaits, ou encore Keenadu, un malware planqué dans le firmware de plus de 13 000 smartphones et tablettes de marques chinoises low cost, présentes sur Amazon ou AliExpress.

articles.title: Vodafone issues a warning to Australians about the latest frightening call scams - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Vodafone has issued a warning to Australians about three new convincing scams with scammers posing as law enforcement officers, clone Australian voices with AI and disguising calls with legitimate phone numbers.
Scammers are always trying to come up with new ways to fool you and win your trust before running their fraudulent schemes.
Vodafone has already been hard at work and has blocked more than 60.5 million scam calls and 43.8 million scam texts just this year.
So the telco knows what it’s talking about when it comes to spotting scams and the new most frightening scams to keep an eye out for.
These include:
AUSTRALIAN FEDERAL POLICE IMPERSONATION SCAM
A call comes in from someone pretending to be an Australian Federal Police officer investigating an arrest.
The scammer tells you your ID has been found on a suspect’s devices but to help you lower your guard they repeatedly say they won’t be asking you for information.
Instead they say they may send an email appearing to be from the AFP it says you’re welcome to visit a police station if you don’t believe them.
This elaborate scam is designed to build your trust so you would potentially share personal information and verify credit card and other financial details that they allegedly found on that suspect’s devices.
POLICE NUMBER SPOOFING
One of the most worrying tricks a scammer has in their criminal toolbox is the ability to manipulate caller ID so that an incoming call appears to be coming from a legitimate number – in this case a legitimate police phone number.
If you Google that number, you’ll find that it is actually a number used by police so it appears legitimate and that you’re talking to police.
From here the frauds to then attempts to extract personal and financial or cryptocurrency information.
This scam became a big enough problem for the Western Australian Police Force to issue a statement and warn people about it.
AI CRYPTO SCAM
In this scam people receive a call from an Australian number and talk to a person with an Australian accent and are told that there has been an unauthorised withdrawal from their cryptocurrency wallet.
The scammer is posing as a crypto support staffer and builds a sense of urgency with the target to pressure them into handing over details to secure their account.
But the catch is the voice is AI-generated and the number can be manipulated.
Vodafone has recommended three simple steps to stay scam safe:
Keep security credentials strictly to yourself: Never share passwords, one-time codes, account access, or crypto recovery phrases over the phone.
Never transfer money to a “safe” account: Don’t move money or cryptocurrency to a “safe” or “secure” account at a caller’s request. Legitimate organisations will not ask you to do this.
Hang up and verify independently: If you receive a suspicious call, hang up immediately and check the claim yourself. Use official channels to speak with someone and verify the request.

articles.title: Gartner Predicts SOCs Will Have 50% More Engineers Than Analysts by 2028
articles.text:
By 2028, security operations teams will have 50% more engineers than analysts. That is one of the predictions in The Roles Required for the AI-Enabled Security Operations Center (SOC), a 2026 Gartner report by analyst Pete Shoard.
If the prediction holds, the people who build and tune a SOC's systems will outnumber the people who work its queue.
Gartner starts its reasoning with alert handling. The report finds that AI SOC agents already cut alert-handling work significantly for common and traditional detection use cases. It describes this as the end of alert processing as the SOC's primary function.
From there, the report works through what that means for the people in the SOC. Analysts move from triage to case ownership, and entry-level roles need a new way in.
Detection engineering grows into a broader engineering job, the metrics shift from alerts to cases and decisions, and exposure management becomes a standing SOC function.
Prophet Security is offering the full report as a free download.
Analysts move from alert triage to case ownership
Gartner's recommendation for analysts is direct: "Human analysts must transition from alert triage roles to end-to-end case ownership and effective response option communication." In practice, the agent investigates the alert, and the analyst owns what happens next.
That means confirming what the agent found, choosing the response, and explaining the options to the people who have to act on them.
The report also holds that AI-assembled case files still need meaningful human validation before a team can rely on them,so analysts spend more of their time judging whether a conclusion holds up and less of it producing verdicts from scratch.
None of this shrinks the team, in Gartner's view. "The SOC will not shrink by 2030," the report states. The people who worked alert volume get redirected toward detection engineering, threat expertise, offensive testing, and exposure management.
Practitioners expect the same. Prophet Security's State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey asked more than 250 CISOs, SOC leaders, and practitioners about this. Of those respondents, 57% expect their team size to stay the same, and 9% expect it to grow.
Entry-level roles need a new way in
Many analysts learned the job in Tier 1 triage, and AI is flattening those tiers. Working a high alert volume taught them what normal looks like in their environment. Gartner's report addresses how L1 and L2 roles change and the training and staffing changes SOC leaders should make now. If agents take over triage, junior analysts lose the repetitions that built their judgment, unless the team replaces those repetitions on purpose.
Three practices can do that:
- Study the agent's work. When an agent records every question it asked, every query it ran, and the evidence behind its determination, each closed alert becomes a worked example. Junior analysts can check whether they would have run the same queries and reached the same conclusion. At JBPCO, the team was able to onboard a new analyst to senior level proficiency within months.
- Own cases early. Gartner's shift to case ownership applies to new analysts too. Giving them end-to-end ownership of lower-risk cases, with a senior reviewer, lets them practice the decisions and response communication the report puts at the center of the analyst role.
- Feed corrections back. Gartner lists "operational feedback management" among the responsibilities of the future detection engineer, and expects analysts to give more feedback to improve AI accuracy. Among Prophet Security's customers, some analysts have already moved from handling alerts to curating the guidance the AI platform uses in its investigations. The same work suits a new hire who is still learning the environment.
The risk to manage is an analyst who only confirms what the agent says. One control is to have analysts work a sample of cases on their own before they see the agent's determination, then compare the two.
Gartner: The Roles Required for the AI-Enabled SOC
As AI SOC agents take on a rapidly growing share of alert triage and investigation, the role of SOC analysts and the necessary skillsets are changing.
Download Gartner's 2026 report on the roles required when moving towards an agentic SOC
Download Now
Detection engineering grows into SOC engineering
The 2028 prediction rests on a wider definition of engineering work. Gartner describes detection engineering expanding into a broader SOC engineering discipline.
The report tells SOC leaders to "redefine detection engineering role descriptions and hiring requirements." The new descriptions should go beyond rule writing to include prompt design, workflow testing, and AI output validation. The report also calls for software engineering practices such as versioning, testing, and rollback.
Each of those maps to work that exists once agents run in production:
- Prompt design and guidance: writing the instructions and context an agent uses to investigate in your environment, such as asset criticality, VIP users and known-benign admin activity.
- Workflow testing: checking an agent workflow against past incidents before it goes live, the way a detection is backtested before it ships.
- AI output validation: sampling the agent's determinations on a schedule and measuring how often a reviewer agrees with them.
- Versioning and rollback: managing guidance and detection changes as code, so a bad change can be traced and reverted.
The analyst hours that agents return also go into threat hunting. In the State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey, 49% of teams that hunt weekly or more said a hunt had surfaced malicious activity their detections missed.
Among teams reporting the lowest hunting frequency, the figure was 8%. A confirmed hunt finding often gives the engineers a new detection to write for their own environment.
The metrics move from alerts to cases and decisions
Gartner's guidance on measurement is short: "Stop recording alert metrics and run the SOC on cases and decisions." The report points SOC leaders away from alert volume, closure rates and mean time to detect, and toward case accuracy, cycle time and decision confidence.
One way to put a number on each:
- Case accuracy: review a fixed sample of closed cases each week, from agents and analysts alike, and track how often the reviewer agrees with the determination.
- Cycle time: measure the time from the first signal to a decision on the case, including the response.
- Decision confidence: record how much evidence supports each determination and how often one is overturned later.
Alert counts still help with capacity planning, but they say little about whether a determination was right. The new measures can sit alongside the SOC metrics a team already reports, such as mean time to respond.
Exposure management becomes a standing SOC function
Gartner's report calls exposure management "the emerging SOC capability to invest in before anything else." It calls for continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) to run as a standing SOC function, rather than as an annual or quarterly exercise.
It also predicts that by 2030, SOCs will be largely offensively driven, testing their own business the way an attacker would.
Many security teams have wanted to run this kind of continuous testing for years and rarely had the hours for it. Once agents handle the alert queue, the analysts and engineers who move into exposure work can validate exposures as they appear.
What they find goes to the people writing detections and planning hunts.
Planning the transition
The report's recommendations translate into decisions that are easier to make before an AI SOC rollout than after it:
- Map today's roles against the work Gartner expects to grow: case ownership, SOC engineering, hunting and exposure management.
- Rewrite the detection engineering job description to include prompt design, workflow testing, and AI output validation, as the report recommends.
- Design the entry-level path, including case ownership and feedback work, before triage volume drops.
- Record a baseline for case accuracy and cycle time, so the rollout has a before and an after.
- Choose one exposure management practice to run continuously instead of once a year.
How Prophet Security helps
Prophet Security is a leading agentic AI SOC platform, recognized in Rising in Cyber 2026, an honor voted on by more than 150 CISOs and security leaders. Its platform, Prophet AI, uses specialist AI agents to investigate alerts, hunt for threats, and build and tune detections on the stack a team already runs.
Here is how it maps to the shifts described above:
- Case ownership. Prophet AI SOC Analyst investigates every alert and records every question, query, and piece of evidence behind its determination, so analysts can own the case and check the reasoning. It groups related investigations into one incident and takes only the response actions a team has approved.
- SOC engineering. Prophet AI Detection Engineer keeps a live MITRE ATT&CK coverage map built from a team's own investigations, then builds and tunes detections from what investigations, hunts, and coverage gaps reveal. Each change is backtested against the team's own history and arrives as a reviewable, version-controlled proposal, and by default nothing reaches production until the team approves it. Guidance that changes an investigation step is versioned and testable too.
- Threat hunting. Prophet AI Threat Hunter runs hunts automatically when a severe new threat emerges. Scheduled hunts against coverage gaps, and hunts a team writes as plain-language questions, run on the cadence the team sets. Suspicious findings go to Prophet AI SOC Analyst for a full investigation, and validated ones become candidates for new detections.
- Case accuracy. Prophet Security measures the quality of Prophet AI's determinations through a continuous QA program with ISO 2859-1 sampling audits. When the evidence does not support a verdict, Prophet AI SOC Analyst returns an inconclusive determination instead of guessing.
Read the full report

articles.title: 1 400 km d'autonomie et propulsion : la future Renault Mégane prépare une vraie révolution contre Tesla
articles.text:
Ca turbine sévère chez Renault. Le Losange a bien lancé ces derniers mois les Mégane et Scénic restylés avec quelques évolutions leur permettant de progresser en douceur, il est vrai. Mais l’avenir s’annonce autrement plus palpitant avec la plateforme RG EV Medium 2.0, promise d’ici 2028. Et il sera alors question de révolution en commençant par la Mégane, qui jure de tout changer.
Déjà, la nouvelle plateforme RG EV Medium 2.0 pourra accueillir des véhicules allant de 4,30 à 4,80 mètres, ce qui signifie que la compacte verra inévitablement sa longueur augmenter. Elle en profitera alors pour offrir un meilleur espace intérieur grâce à un empattement rallongé qui permettra en parallèle de loger des batteries plus conséquentes. Renault promet en ce sens 750 km d’autonomie au minimum sur une charge et une masse sous les 2 tonnes.
Autonomie record : jusqu’à 1 400 km pour oublier le diesel
Une inédite version à prolongateur d’autonomie se joindra aussi à la fête avec un rayon d’action porté à 1 400 km pour satisfaire les propriétaires de Mégane diesel. L’architecture technique sera d’autre part chamboulée, en passant de la traction à la propulsion. Ce changement est inévitable afin de mieux accommoder l’unique bloc électrique, qui développera 275 ch et 350 Nm de couple.
Dans un entretien accordé à Auto Express, Philippe Brunet, le directeur de l’ingénierie mécanique chez Renault, a admis que « la traction avant pose problème en termes d’agrément de conduite, de confort et de tenue de route […]. Il a effectivement été très difficile de régler les Scénic et Mégane actuelles ». Cette architecture laisse également derrière elle un autre bienfait : une intégration facilitée de l’électronique de puissance et du câblage.
Un style inédit pour faire plier le Tesla Model Y
Côté style, la future Mégane entamera un virage radical permis par la plateforme RG EV Medium 2.0. Laurens van den Acker, directeur du design du groupe Renault, confirme que ces nouvelles bases « offriront d’emblée des silhouettes inédites. Des empattements plus longs, des roues plus grandes et des porte-à-faux plus courts. [De cela résultera] des voitures ni aussi hautes qu’un SUV, ni aussi basses qu’une berline ».
La Mégane pourrait alors tendre vers un SUV coupé comme l’a fait Nissan avec la Leaf. Elle constituera de fait une alternative plus pertinente au Tesla Model Y, quand le Scénic hésite encore trop entre le monospace et le SUV. Le coup de crayon devrait cependant être plus raisonnable. Van den Acker évoque « une allure un peu plus sérieuse et un peu moins de superficiel », concluant un juste milieu entre la « froideur des Allemands et la chaleur des Italiens ».

articles.title: Elon Musk aconseja a niños y jóvenes: “Obtén una educación lo más amplia posible: artes, ciencias, ingeniería y un amplio conocimiento general”
articles.text:
Elon Musk recomienda que los jóvenes mezclen sus estudios. Así podrán desenvolverse, según él, en un mundo de inteligencia artificial y robots. En concreto, deben recibir “una educación lo más amplia posible: artes, ciencias, ingeniería y un amplio conocimiento general”. La clave es saber plantear las preguntas. Cuanto más sabemos, mejor podemos decirle a la máquina qué queremos.
En una entrevista se le pregunta por un joven de 20 años que quiere desarrollar todo su potencial. ¿Qué debería hacer para no quedarse atrás en esta transición tecnológica? Musk apuesta por combinar los estudios de artes con los científicos. No recomienda qué carrera elegir o qué garantiza un puesto de trabajo.
“Para saber qué pedirles a los robots, necesitas ser capaz de formular la pregunta”. Esto está relacionado con la llamada ingeniería de prompts (preparación de las instrucciones para que la IA entienda qué tiene que hacer). Los conocimientos generales nos ayudan a concretar nuestras peticiones.
En un mundo con muchos robots e inteligencia artificial, tenemos máquinas a nuestro servicio. Podemos pedirles cosas y ellas las harán de forma inmediata. Así lo anticipa Elon Musk.
Sin embargo, no es que baste con tener conocimientos superficiales para controlar sistemas complejos. Musk habla de ampliar nuestra formación. No es un plan de estudios. Y no compara qué resulta mejor en educación. ¿Qué es lo que tengo que aprender para poder usarlas de manera independiente?
Ya en febrero de 2020, Musk se mostraba a favor de que los títulos académicos no fueran el filtro clave en algunos casos de contratación de Tesla. Como hemos contado en su momento (búsqueda de programadores e ingenieros), Musk pedía que supieran de inteligencia artificial (y que pudieran aplicarla) y que pasaran un test de programación.
Saber evaluar las respuestas de la IA
En la investigación sobre el uso de IA en el trabajo, es importante saber juzgar lo que nos devuelve la máquina. En un estudio de Microsoft Research (2025) de Hao-Ping Lee y otros seis investigadores se ha encuestado a 319 trabajadores del conocimiento. Se han recogido 936 ejemplos de uso de IA generativa en sus tareas.
Por ejemplo, los participantes que tenían más confianza en la IA declaraban realizar menos pensamiento crítico. Por otro lado, cuanta más confianza tenían en ellos mismos, más pensamiento crítico declaraban hacer. Sin embargo, en este trabajo se describen percepciones y asociaciones. No se puede concluir que usar un chatbot lleve a una pérdida de capacidad intelectual. La comprobación de información está entre las actividades donde sigue siendo necesario el humano.
En educación se ha medido otro problema concreto. Hamsa Bastani y sus colaboradores han publicado el resultado de un experimento en estudiantes de matemáticas en un instituto turco. Casi mil alumnos. Comparan dos asistentes diferentes (basados en GPT-4) con un grupo de control (que no tiene acceso a estos asistentes). Hay dos tipos de asistentes. Uno es similar a un chat general y el otro tiene unas instrucciones que han sido diseñadas con los profesores para proteger el aprendizaje.
Con el chat general se observa una mejora de las calificaciones en la práctica del 48 % respecto al grupo de control. Sin embargo, en el examen (sin ayuda), las calificaciones son un 17 % peores que en el grupo de control. Con el tutor con protecciones se evita prácticamente este efecto negativo, pero en el examen sin asistente tampoco se certifica una mejora frente a los que estudiaron sin IA.
Resolver una tarea no siempre significa aprender
Esta distinción es recogida por la Organización para la Cooperación y el Desarrollo Económicos (OCDE) en su informe sobre educación digital (2026). Alerta de que puede haber casos en los que el uso de una IA generalista para delegar en ella las tareas conduce a un mejor resultado sin que ello implique un aprendizaje equivalente. También recoge usos que tienen fines pedagógicos y que sí ayudan a aprender.
Para el usuario que está estudiando, es importante considerar más aspectos que el resultado de la respuesta. Por ejemplo, si el asistente le pide que piense. También es relevante que use sus intentos para guiarle; de esta forma ayuda a detectar errores. La OCDE describe tutores que hacen preguntas y van ajustando sus indicaciones en el proceso de diálogo. Para ello es necesario que el estudiante continúe entrenando en las habilidades que tendrá que usar posteriormente de manera autónoma.
