articles.title: Solo VC Robin Capital closes €15 million second fund to back AI, robotics and space startups | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Berlin-based VC firm Robin Capital has closed its second €15 million fund, bringing total commitments across its two early-stage funds to €30 million.
The new fund, Robin Capital Fund II, follows the firm’s first €15 million vehicle closed in 2024. It has already made 17 investments, including SkySpy.ai, Marble Imaging and Helicity Space, which operate across intelligence, defence, Earth observation and space technology.
Robin Haak, Founder and General Partner at Robin Capital, says: “They call it a Solo GP, but nothing about building Robin Capital has ever been solo. Our limited partners, founders, and venture partners are what make this possible. We believe the best venture capital partnerships are built on trust, conviction, and a genuine willingness to help one another succeed.”
Robin Capital’s latest close joins several European early-stage VC fund announcements in 2026.
In Germany, Munich-based Vanagon Ventures closed a €20 million fund targeting pre-Seed AI and DeepTech startups, while Berlin-based Angel Invest and Auxxo secured €40 million and €33.3 million, respectively.
Elsewhere, Barcelona’s Masia closed €18 million, Monaco’s Monte Carlo Capital reached a €13 million first close for its second DeepTech and SpaceTech fund, and Belgium’s Solo GP-led NewSchool VC closed €10 million.
Together with Nuremberg-based ZOHO.VC‘s €7 million first close, these announcements represent €141.3 million in reported fund capital, rising to €156.3 million including Robin Capital’s new fund.
Robin adds: “We want to build a home for exceptional founders, and stay with them long enough to help build exceptional companies.”
Founded in 2023 by entrepreneur and investor Robin Haak, the firm focuses on pre-Seed and Seed-stage investments in European startups, with a particular interest in AI, enterprise software, robotics, defence, space and DeepTech.
Robin Capital typically invests between €100k and €600k in early-stage companies, primarily across Europe. Rather than following strict sector boundaries, the firm looks for founders addressing large markets with the potential to build scalable businesses.
The firm’s investor base includes entrepreneurs, unicorn founders, technology executives, family offices and investors with experience in venture capital and private equity. Its limited partner community includes entrepreneurs and families associated with businesses such as Ferrari, Moratti, Adyen and FTMO, alongside investors connected to Permira, Macquarie and FJ Labs.
Robin Capital operates under a Solo General Partner (Solo GP) model, with Haak leading investment decisions while drawing on a network of venture partners, limited partners and more than 100 experienced operators.
Its first fund has backed European technology companies including Simsalasim, Uvionix, Paypercut and Xaver. Meanwhile, Fund II is building a portfolio with a stronger emphasis on emerging technologies, particularly applications of AI, autonomous systems and space infrastructure.
Beyond its two early-stage funds, Robin Capital has established three dedicated growth Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) to support ARX Robotics, Almetra and Ground A. These investment vehicles enable its investor community to participate in additional financing opportunities beyond the firm’s typical pre-Seed and Seed-stage investment strategy.
Before establishing Robin Capital in 2023, Haak built a career spanning entrepreneurship, corporate operations and venture capital. In 2013, he co-founded Jobspotting, which subsequently became part of SmartRecruiters, where he served as Global COO and Managing Director. SmartRecruiters was later acquired by SAP.
Earlier in his career, Haak worked in mergers and acquisitions at Axel Springer and co-founded Axel Springer Plug & Play. He also made the first institutional investment in German fintech N26 and subsequently served as a General Partner at European growth investment firm Revaia.
Over the past decade, Haak has invested in more than 60 companies, including seven unicorns, among them N26, Algolia, Aircall and Coralogix.
Looking ahead, Robin Capital plans to establish a third €15 million early-stage fund, with the ambition of managing three such vehicles and backing approximately 80 to 90 startups in total. The firm is also considering a dedicated growth continuity fund as part of its medium-term strategy, which would allow it to continue supporting selected portfolio companies as they scale.

articles.title: Big techs reforçam combate a conteúdos falsos gerados por IA nas eleições dos EUA
articles.text:
OpenAI, Anthropic, Google e Meta reforçaram suas estratégias para impedir que ferramentas de inteligência artificial (IA) sejam usadas para manipular as eleições legislativas dos Estados Unidos, que estão sendo realizadas nesta terça-feira (3). As empresas montaram equipes especializadas para monitorar atividades suspeitas e tentar conter campanhas de desinformação capazes de comprometer a confiança no processo democrático.
Na OpenAI, mais de uma dúzia de funcionários trabalha em uma central de operações instalada em escritório da companhia em São Francisco (EUA). A estrutura representa ampliação significativa dos esforços adotados pela empresa durante a eleição presidencial de 2024, quando os recursos de IA eram menos avançados e o ChatGPT tinha apenas um quinto da base de um bilhão de usuários que possui atualmente.
“Em 2024, a tecnologia mais acessível era o texto. Agora, não estamos monitorando apenas textos”, afirmou Josh Lawson, responsável pela área de riscos cívicos e estratégicos da OpenAI e líder da operação, ao The New York Times.
O cenário atual inclui ameaças que vão de vídeos deepfake e ataques cibernéticos a operações de influência estrangeira e doméstica. Com ferramentas de IA, esse tipo de campanha pode ser produzido e colocado em circulação a partir de uma sequência de comandos.
Anthropic também monta central de monitoramento
- A OpenAI não é a única empresa a reforçar suas defesas. A Anthropic, responsável pelo chatbot Claude, criou pela primeira vez uma sala de operações dedicada ao tema, reunindo equipes de analistas em São Francisco, Nova York (EUA) e Washington (EUA);
- Google e Meta também prometeram ampliar os esforços para impedir que suas ferramentas de IA sejam usadas para enfraquecer a confiança no processo democrático;
- Na OpenAI, a central eleitoral começou a funcionar na quinta-feira anterior à votação. A equipe de São Francisco trabalha em conjunto com uma unidade em Washington e reúne dezenas de pessoas, segundo representantes da companhia;
- Os funcionários analisam comandos enviados ao ChatGPT que são sinalizados automaticamente por possíveis tentativas de produzir textos ou imagens falsas sobre as eleições;
- Um exemplo seria o uso do chatbot para elaborar uma campanha de influência baseada em alegações falsas de fraude eleitoral, como acusações de manipulação de cédulas. O material poderia ser distribuído em redes sociais por meio de contas falsas;
- Quando identifica atividades maliciosas destinadas a circular em determinadas plataformas, a OpenAI afirma que notifica as empresas responsáveis por esses serviços.
IA amplia riscos de manipulação eleitoral
Um levantamento do Brennan Center for Justice, organização ligada à Faculdade de Direito da Universidade de Nova York, identificou cenário contraditório.
Os chatbots mais populares geralmente resistem a solicitações relacionadas a teorias conspiratórias sobre eleições. Ao mesmo tempo, as ferramentas de IA produzem regularmente textos, imagens e vídeos que podem ser utilizados para enfraquecer a confiança na votação.
A preocupação também está relacionada à redução das equipes de segurança e moderação das redes sociais nos últimos anos. Após a interferência russa nas eleições presidenciais de 2016, a Meta criou uma central de operações para as eleições legislativas de 2018.
Desde então, porém, a Meta e outras plataformas reduziram equipes responsáveis por segurança e combate à desinformação eleitoral. A decisão ocorreu em meio à pressão de republicanos e, a partir de 2025, do governo Donald Trump, que acusaram as empresas de censurar opiniões conservadoras.
Esse recuo coincidiu com a expansão das ferramentas de IA, aumentando os receios sobre o impacto da tecnologia nas eleições. Especialistas e ex-integrantes do governo estadunidense também alertaram para a capacidade desses recursos de tornar campanhas de manipulação mais convincentes, enquanto o governo Trump desmontou equipes federais que anteriormente atuavam no combate a ameaças ao processo eleitoral.
“Seria imprudente pensar que essa ameaça desapareceu e que a tecnologia não está tornando essas ameaças mais poderosas e convincentes”, afirmou Lauren Protentis, ex-integrante do Conselho de Segurança Nacional dos Estados Unidos, onde supervisionava questões relacionadas à influência estrangeira maliciosa durante o governo de Joe Biden.
OpenAI já identificou operações ligadas a outros países
A OpenAI já havia divulgado tentativas de Rússia, China e Irã de utilizar o ChatGPT em operações de influência estrangeira. A empresa afirma ter interrompido duas campanhas desse tipo no mês anterior à eleição estadunidense.
Até o momento, porém, a companhia não havia divulgado nenhuma operação específica relacionada às eleições legislativas de novembro.
O investigador-chefe da OpenAI, Ben Nimmo, afirmou que o objetivo é identificar essas iniciativas antes que consigam alcançar um público significativo.
“Estamos tentando detectar as operações antes que tenham a oportunidade de ganhar força”, declarou.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: The Founder Summit agenda is only half the reason to be in Boston on Nov. 4 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
You can learn a lot from a great founder session. But sometimes the conversation that changes what you do next happens five minutes after the session ends. And with the event happening tomorrow, there is another reason to make sure you are in the room: The format is designed to help founders learn in different ways throughout the day.
On November 4, TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 brings founders and investors together at SoWa Power Station in Boston for one day of practical learning, candid conversations, live pitching, smaller roundtables, and networking.
Register now to save up to $100 on your pass, plus get a second for free. Or save up to 30% on group bundles.
All-day founder bootcamp
Start with the Build Stage: Practical lessons for building what comes next
The Build Stage focuses on the decisions founders make while they are still shaping, testing, and growing the business. These sessions get into the mechanics behind building a company, from distribution and fundraising to team building and pitching.
Hunter Worland of NEA opens the conversation on why distribution can become a startup’s next competitive advantage, especially when strong technology alone is not enough to win customers.
Kristen Craft of Fidelity Private Shares brings a current view of fundraising trends, helping founders understand how the capital environment is shifting and what that means for the way they approach their next raise.
The stage also gets tactical about building high-performing teams and sharpening the story you tell investors, customers, and potential hires.
Dave Balter of True Ventures and Edisyl takes on a deceptively simple question: Does your pitch earn the next conversation?
The value of the Build Stage is straightforward: These are lessons founders can take back to their companies immediately.
Use the Impact Stage to think about what happens after something starts working
If the Build Stage is about creating momentum, the Impact Stage is about what happens once that momentum becomes real. This is where founders can step back and think about bigger decisions around product-market fit, scaling, enterprise relationships, leadership, and long-term growth.
Steve Fredette, president, co-founder, and director of Toast, brings the perspective of building and scaling one of Boston’s most recognizable startup success stories.
Rudina Seseri, founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures, explores the tension every founder eventually faces: when to scale and when hitting the brakes may actually protect the business.
Kent Bennett of Bessemer Venture Partners tackles product-market fit before scale, helping founders think more critically about whether the signals they are seeing truly justify the next phase of growth.
Chase Garbarino, CEO and co-founder of HqO, brings the conversation home with the Boston Founder Playbook and a perspective on building ambitious companies outside the Bay Area.
The Impact Stage is valuable because it creates space for founders to get out of the weeds for a moment and ask whether they are scaling the right things, in the right way, at the right time.
Go deeper in the roundtables
Main Stage sessions can give you perspective. Roundtables give you room to get specific.
Founder Summit’s smaller roundtables are built around highly focused problems that many founders are actively solving right now, from entering difficult verticals and building enterprise trust to creating lean teams and opening doors with major customers.
Chirag Shah of Define Ventures digs into what happens when your first vertical is also one of the hardest to enter.
A technical session with Shishir Tewari of Procore Technologies moves the AI conversation from broad hype to the practical challenge of reducing hallucinations with better enterprise context.
Merve Kitapci of ADIN.AI gets highly specific about enterprise selling and what it takes to land major global customers before Series A.
Andy Tang of Draper Associates opens a different kind of founder conversation: What if you are building something the market does not even have a name for yet?
Linden Tibbets of IFTTT explores how AI may change the assumptions founders make about team size, productivity, and what a smaller company can realistically accomplish.
The value here is participation. Instead of simply hearing how someone else approached a problem, founders can bring their own questions, compare experiences with the people around the table, and leave with ideas that are much closer to their actual business.
Watch the startup pitch advice get tested live
Founder Summit also gives attendees the chance to see what happens when founders put their stories in front of investors in real time.
During “So You Think You Can Pitch?,” founders make their cases in front of investors, including Dave Balter, Chirag Shah, and Simran Suri of Maveron.
This is one of the most interactive parts of the day because it turns advice about pitching into something founders can actually watch: what gets an investor’s attention, where a story loses momentum, and which questions come up immediately.
For anyone preparing to raise, sell, recruit, or simply explain their company more clearly, seeing those reactions live can be incredibly useful.
Spark meaningful connections with Braindate networking
The Networking Lounge powered by Braindate gives attendees another way to connect intentionally throughout the day.
Schedule a one-on-one conversation. Join a small group. Find someone who wants to talk about the exact challenge you are working through.
Hear a session on product-market fit, then find another founder working through the same issue. Watch the pitch competition, then compare notes with someone preparing for their own fundraise. Hear the Boston Founder Playbook, then meet other founders doing exactly that. Braindate helps turn the content into conversation.
Keep it going at the closing reception
The day wraps up with a closing reception presented by Fidelity Private Shares, giving attendees time to keep the conversations going without rushing to the next session.
That matters because some of the most useful connections at an event happen after you have already shared a room, a question, or a conversation earlier in the day.
One day, several ways to learn
Founder Summit is not built around one type of conference experience. The Build Stage gives founders practical lessons they can apply now. The Impact Stage creates room for bigger growth and leadership decisions. The roundtables let you ask questions and go deeper. The live pitch competition puts founder storytelling to the test. Braindate makes networking intentional. And the reception gives those conversations somewhere to continue. That mix is what makes the day valuable.
Bring a partner and cover more ground
TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 takes place November 4 at SoWa Power Station in Boston. There is still time to join us in Boston. Current Founder Summit passes include breakout sessions, roundtables, Braindate networking, the Expo Hall, and access to session materials after the event.
Even better, buy one pass now, and you can get a second pass free. Bring your co-founder. Bring a partner. Bring the person you’d be texting session takeaways to all day anyway. Get your pass, bring someone with you for free, and join the founder community in Boston.

articles.title: AIs Hacking the Law - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
AIs Hacking the Law
In both a 2021 essay and my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind, I talk about AIs finding vulnerabilities and exploits—hacking—the legal system.
Here’s some demonstrations of this from Germany:
Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language. Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation.1 Courts absorb most exploits through interpretation, and such vulnerabilities rarely surface in the first place. With highly capable AI systems enabling the discovery of vulnerabilities at unprecedented scale, we believe the latter could change.
In testing this hypothesis, we have identified a substantial number of vulnerabilities in the German legal system using LLMs. To our knowledge, none of these have been previously recorded. We share a selection of vulnerabilities below, and present potential exploits for each. We share only those vulnerabilities whose exploitation we believe would not cause serious harm.
We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems. In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves.
Still in its early stages, but definitely something that’s coming.
Rontea • November 3, 2026 8:44 AM
I wonder if our society, worshipping procedure with the zeal of a monk and the memory of a bureaucrat, can endure the laughter of logic when the letter devours the spirit.

articles.title: „Vielleicht verschwenden wir komplett unsere Zeit“: Forscher geben die Suche nach Dunkler Materie nicht auf
articles.text:
Auf der Jagd nach Dunkler Materie: Wie Physiker sie endlich finden wollen
Unter einem Apennin-Massiv, unterhalb des Jinping-Gebirges in Sichuan und am Grund eines Bergwerks in South Dakota ist eine kosmische Jagd im Gange. Tief unten, isoliert von diesen felsigen Schutzschilden, sollen riesige Detektoren, gefüllt mit flüssigem Xenon, Dunkle Materie nachweisen – jene hypothetische Substanz, deren Schwerkraft dafür sorgt, dass das Universum nicht einfach auseinanderfliegt. Und die gleichzeitig so beschaffen ist, dass wir sie mit unseren Instrumenten bisher nicht erfassen können, sie also für uns „dunkel“ bleibt.
Die Hoffnung war, dass eines Tages ein Baustein Dunkler Materie, ein sogenanntes schwach wechselwirkendes massives Teilchen (kurz: WIMP), mit einem Xenonatom kollidiert und dabei einen Lichtblitz sowie elektrische Ladung erzeugt. Und tatsächlich registrieren die Detektoren seit Kurzem vereinzelte Signale. Nur leider stammen die nicht von Dunkler Materie. Stattdessen registrieren die Detektoren etwas für Physiker:innen weitaus Alltäglicheres, aber ähnlich Substanzloses wie WIMPs: Neutrinos, federleichte subatomare Teilchen, die Sterne in riesigen Mengen produzieren.
Dieser Text erscheint in der Ausgabe 8/2026 von MIT Technology Review. Darin beschäftigen wir uns mit den Folgen des Klimawandels und wie wir uns an Hitze, Dürre und Überschwemmungen anpassen sollten. Das Heft erscheint am 06.11.2026 im Zeitschriftenhandel und lässt sich auch in unserem Online-Shop bestellen.
Neutrino-Nebel bedeutet nicht das Ende der Suche nach Dunkler Materie
Physiker:innen wissen schon seit Jahrzehnten von diesem Neutrino-Hintergrundrauschen, hatten allerdings gehofft, zuerst WIMPs für Dunkle Materie zu entdecken. Aber offenbar sind die heutigen WIMP-Detektoren einfach so groß und empfindlich, dass sie in dem „Neutrino-Nebel“ stecken bleiben und – so die Vermutung – jedes andere Signal übertönen. Auch gibt es keine Möglichkeit, diese Detektoren vor Neutrinos abzuschirmen, die mühelos sogar durch die Erde selbst gleiten. Das nächste Experiment, das diesen seit Langem verfolgten Ansatz zur Suche nach Dunkler Materie nutzt, könnte also das letzte sein.
Der Neutrino-Nebel bedeutet jedoch nicht grundsätzlich das Ende der Suche. Die Forschenden müssen lediglich den Fokus ihrer Suche verlagern. Wissenschaftler:innen hätten auch noch keine neuen Teilchen im Large Hadron Collider (LHC), der leistungsstarken Protonenbeschleunigeranlage, die sich über die Grenze zwischen Frankreich und der Schweiz erstreckt, gefunden, sagt Kathryn Zurek, theoretische Teilchenphysikerin am California Institute of Technology. „Und wir haben eben noch keine WIMP-Dunkle Materie gesehen.“ Also erweitern sie ihren Suchhorizont. Dabei würden noch zahlreiche weitere Kandidaten in den Startlöchern warten, sagt Zurek.

articles.title: Por qué la segunda oleada de ‘hackeos’ a las neveras en supermercados avisa de los riesgos que vienen
articles.text: Trabajadores de un supermercado de la cadena sueca ICA, en la ciudad de Sjobo, retiran productos estropeados tras el ciberataque que alteró la temperatura de las cámaras frigoríficas. Decenas de supermercados de al menos siete países europeos amanecieron este lunes con parte de su género estropeado. Un ciberataque subió la temperatura de las cámaras frigoríficas de varios establecimientos, en algunos casos hasta los 50 grados, echando a perder productos frescos y congelados. Los países más afectados fueron Bélgica y Suecia, pero también se registraron problemas en Luxemburgo, Países Bajos, Irlanda, Estonia y Finlandia. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished.
AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure.
To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire: a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next.
How it works
Zero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section.
Each briefing brings together a plain-language explanation of the vulnerability, who should investigate it, recommended actions, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance. The format is deliberately simple: an index card with what you need to know, without the drama. A CISO should be able to understand the issue quickly and ask the right questions. An engineer should be able to follow the same briefing to the technical guidance needed to investigate and remediate it.
We also offer a pre-compiled prompt you can use with your agent to assess the impact on your infrastructure. Cloudflare contributes security research, observations from our network, and practical knowledge of the controls that can help reduce exposure. The information is useful whether or not you are a Cloudflare customer.
Zero Wire brings that context together with authoritative external sources, giving readers a starting point for assessment and a place to return as an issue develops.
Our focus
Rather than a catalog of every CVE, Zero Wire complements vendor advisories and vulnerability databases, linking readers to the evidence and technical guidance needed to act. Zero Wire focuses on critical CVEs in Internet-facing software, such as vulnerabilities in web applications, the runtimes and libraries they depend on, and services exposed to the Internet, where a proxy can help mitigate exploitation.
We select significant issues that security teams need to understand and assess. Each briefing explains the potential impact, which deployments should be investigated, what is known about exploitation, and the available mitigation and patching guidance. A vulnerability’s severity and evidence of active exploitation are distinct: readers need both to make informed decisions.
A dedicated Cloudflare protection, such as Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules, is not a prerequisite for inclusion. Some issues require vendor updates or changes beyond the traffic Cloudflare can inspect. Where Cloudflare controls can help, we explain their scope and configuration requirements.
A walk through Zero Wire
Start on the Zero Wire homepage. Each card introduces an issue, identifies associated CVEs where applicable, and summarizes why it matters and what to do. You can search for a published briefing using a CVE or issue name, and follow technology tags to related entries. One briefing can cover several related CVEs when understanding them together makes the response clearer.
Find what needs attention
The homepage separates briefings into two categories. “Needs attention” brings together issues requiring active assessment or action, including those with known exploitation or developing guidance. “Reference” keeps briefings available when guidance has stabilized. Moving to “Reference” does not mean every affected system has been patched: an older vulnerability can still matter to an organization that has not completed remediation.
The status and last-checked date help you interpret each card. Known exploitation, an ongoing investigation, and an available vendor fix describe different things. Read them alongside the briefing’s evidence rather than treating them as a verdict on your own environment.
Understand what happened and who should investigate
When you open a briefing, the overview tells you what happened, why it deserves attention, and which teams should investigate. The explanation connects the technical issue to its practical consequences, such as service disruption or risk of data exposure.
For example, the recent php2shell vulnerability concerns flaws in the PHP runtime. That distinction matters for teams running applications such as WordPress or Magento: updating application code or a plugin alone does not repair the underlying runtime. The briefing helps readers identify the right system owners and directs them to the PHP security guidance for affected versions and remediation.
Turn the briefing into an action plan
What to do now gives your team a short set of next steps. Depending on the issue, that can mean identifying affected deployments, checking versions with a hosting provider, applying vendor updates, reviewing suspicious activity, or keeping compensating controls in place while patching.
The purpose is to make the next conversation concrete. For a PHP deployment, ask which runtime is actually running, whether the vendor’s fix has been applied, and who owns the update. Follow the linked vendor advisory for detailed applicability and remediation instructions, which can change as the investigation develops.
Assess your exposure with an AI agent
In this section, we share a prompt that can be used with your AI agent to quickly assess the impact on your infrastructure. The prompt asks for a read-only assessment of deployed software, relevant vendor fixes, exposure, and compensating controls, with per-asset evidence, unknowns, and next actions. It helps your team investigate its own environment; copying the prompt does not itself scan or change systems.
Check the evidence and follow what changed
To help you learn more about the vulnerability, each briefing links to external documents such as CVE records, research, and relevant exploitation evidence, including CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. These sources answer different questions. A vendor advisory establishes affected versions and remediation guidance. An exploitation report provides evidence of attacker activity.
If applicable to a briefing, Cloudflare can add context about traffic seen on our network, for example by showing traffic matching WAF rules that indicates exploitation attempts. Those distinctions matter. Observing an attack attempt does not establish that a particular organization was compromised. Equally, a lack of observed attempts on Cloudflare’s network does not establish that exploitation is absent elsewhere. Briefings distinguish what the sources establish from what remains unknown.
Where available, charts add context to that evidence. The php2shell briefing shows the volume of HTTP requests matching Cloudflare WAF managed rules over time. Note that requests matching these rules are not a count of compromised systems or successful exploits; the chart aims at providing practitioners a sense of what the focus level is by threat actors on a particular vulnerability.
Finally, update chronology records important developments, such as new advisories or changes to the evidence and response guidance. Together with the last-checked date, it helps returning readers understand what has changed since their previous visit.
Understand Cloudflare’s role
The Cloudflare section provides links to whether we offer compensating controls or provide a way to mitigate the vulnerability impact on your infrastructure.
If a particular CVE can be addressed with a WAF rule, the briefing reports its availability and essential configuration requirements. When applicable, paid Plans and free Plans links take customers to the relevant dashboard configuration. The next step is explicit: “Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected”. A link allows you to review your security posture, it does not automatically enable a rule or verify a deployment.
Note that a WAF mitigation is a compensating control for the traffic it covers, it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Blocking the requests can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. The security teams should always follow the vendor remediation guidance.
Stay informed with Zero Wire
A useful vulnerability briefing should leave you with a clearer understanding of the issue and a concrete next step. Day Zero brings those essentials together: what happened, who should investigate, what to do now, and where to find the evidence.
Visit Zero Wire vulnerability intelligence, share the relevant briefings with the teams responsible for your systems, and return for new entries and updates. When the next disclosure arrives, we want you to spend less time assembling the basic facts and more time acting on them.
Follow Cloudflare Radar on X @CloudflareRadar and Bluesky @radar.cloudflare.com for updates.

articles.title: Inside Côte d'Ivoire's next retail opportunity
articles.text:
3 novembre 2026
Hello 👋,
Sorry about the break in transmission last week. Moonshot by TechCabal happened. Welcome back to Francophone Weekly by TechCabal, your weekly deep dive into the tech ecosystem across French-speaking Africa. For readers who want to understand Francophone Africa beyond headlines—through markets, startups, and systems. New editions of the newsletter will land directly in your inbox every Tuesday at 12 PM WAT.
By default, this newsletter is in French. If you’re reading this in your email inbox, click the “Read in English” button below to switch to the English version. If you’re reading on our website, you can either click the button below or toggle the language selector at the top right-hand side of the page to view the English edition.
Une nouvelle génération de marques et de plateformes découvre que la route vers le consommateur ivoirien passe par la boutique de quartier et de plus en plus, par l’écran.
Le commerce électronique africain traverse une période de turbulences. Jumia a quitté l’Afrique du Sud et la Tanzanie, se repliant sur les marchés où ses équilibres économiques tiennent réellement. La Côte d’Ivoire n’a pas figuré sur cette liste de départs. Elle a figuré sur la liste opposée. Le pays est l’un des quatre plus grands marchés de Jumia à l’échelle mondiale — aux côtés du Nigeria, du Maroc et du Kenya — et en 2024, plus de 67 % des commandes passées sur la plateforme ne provenaient pas du Plateau ou de la Zone 4 à Abidjan, mais de villes secondaires et de zones rurales dispersées à l’intérieur du pays.
Bouaké et Yamoussoukro arrivent en tête de ces volumes. Jumia opère désormais depuis un nouvel entrepôt de 5 500 m² inauguré au PK24 en avril 2025, et son réseau d’agents JForce — des conseillers commerciaux indépendants de terrain, plus de 19 000 actifs en Côte d’Ivoire seulement — a mené plus de 120 activations marketing à travers le pays en 2024. Jumia double la mise sur un marché qu’elle construit depuis 14 ans.
La question pour les marques de produits de grande consommation (FMCG) — locales, régionales ou internationales — est de savoir comment utiliser intelligemment cette infrastructure. Et la réponse, il se trouve, exige de comprendre quelque chose de contre-intuitif sur le fonctionnement du marché ivoirien.
1. Les chiffres d’abord
            Source de l’image : Jumia.
       
        
    
Le secteur FMCG en Côte d’Ivoire renoue avec la croissance après une période de pression sur le pouvoir d’achat. Les données d’audit de distribution de Maverick Research couvrant le premier semestre 2026 montrent une progression des volumes d’environ 3 % et de la valeur de 2 % dans les catégories alimentaire, soins à domicile et hygiène-beauté. La part de l’alimentaire dans le volume total FMCG s’est élargie à 34,2 %, portée par les huiles comestibles, la tomate concentrée, les produits laitiers, les nouilles et les condiments — des produits de première nécessité achetés en petites quantités, fréquemment, à travers le réseau de distribution capillaire du pays.
Ce réseau est informel dans une proportion écrasante. Environ 85 % des transactions commerciales en Côte d’Ivoire transitent par le commerce informel — l’épicerie de quartier, l’étal de rue, la table de marché — et non par Carrefour ou Prosuma. La grande distribution est une vitrine de prestige. Ce n’est pas là que vit le volume.
L’économie numérique évolue en parallèle, à vive allure. Le secteur e-commerce ivoirien a progressé de 30 % en 2023, et le gouvernement a depuis engagé 32 milliards de FCFA dans une stratégie nationale de structuration du commerce électronique à horizon 2028. Une loi-cadre sur le e-commerce est en cours d’élaboration, avec des décrets d’application validés fin 2025. Le gouvernement a lancé Tradepost, une plateforme de commerce numérique destinée aux PME ivoiriennes, et recense activement les vendeurs informels en ligne — notamment les dizaines de milliers de marchands opérant sur Facebook et TikTok — en vue de leur formalisation. L’économie numérique représente déjà environ 9 % du produit intérieur brut (PIB).
Près de la moitié de la population (~47,5 %) vit hors des centres urbains. Ce chiffre n’est pas un obstacle. Comme le démontrent les données de Jumia, c’est un marché.
Jumia comme infrastructure marketing, pas seulement comme canal de vente
Le réflexe de la plupart des marques FMCG qui entrent sur le marché ivoirien est de traiter Jumia comme un canal de vente. Le cadre d’analyse plus utile est de le considérer comme un moteur de notoriété et une couche d’infrastructure marketing, en particulier pour les produits qui n’ont pas encore gagné la confiance des grossistes qui contrôlent l’accès au marché de masse.
Cela tient à la façon dont la distribution fonctionne réellement en Côte d’Ivoire. Les grossistes, les intermédiaires essentiels qui acheminent les produits des fabricants vers les réseaux d’épiciers qui desservent la majorité des consommateurs, ne référencent pas les produits inconnus. Ils stockent ce que les consommateurs demandent déjà. La conversation de référencement avec un grossiste n’a lieu qu’une fois que la marque est déjà connue. En s’associant aux marques FMCG, Jumia vise à construire cette reconnaissance préalable.
Une marque qui mène une campagne soutenue sur la plateforme construit une notoriété consommateur avant même que toute conversation de distribution ne commence sur le terrain. Le format Sponsor Brand de Jumia — visibilité en page d’accueil, payé mensuellement, entièrement focalisé sur la présence de marque — fonctionne comme un panneau publicitaire numérique : il ne génère pas de conversion immédiate, mais il dépose le nom de la marque dans la conscience du consommateur. Le format Sponsor Point, plus proche de la logique de Facebook Ads, déclenche une bannière lorsque les utilisateurs recherchent des mots-clés spécifiques. Pour une marque alimentaire, des mots comme piment, sauce ou accompagnement sont des points d’entrée à fort trafic qui redirigent les acheteurs potentiels vers la boutique de la marque à ~4 000 FCFA pour 1 000 impressions.
Pour la conversion au niveau produit, le Sponsor Prodax va plus loin : un produit spécifique propulsé en tête des résultats de recherche, payé au clic entre 80 et 250 FCFA (0,14 et 0,43 dollar), capturant des utilisateurs dont l’intention d’achat est avérée plutôt qu’un défilement passif. La qualité du signal est sensiblement supérieure à celle d’une impression.
Deux outils supplémentaires sont plus tangibles. Le premier est l’insertion d’échantillons ou de flyers dans les colis Jumia : un contact physique avec le produit au moment de l’achat, filtrable par zone géographique ou catégorie de panier. Pour un produit nutritif cherchant à s’implanter à Bouaké avant de tenter une distribution de masse, glisser un échantillon de 50 ml dans une commande Jumia dans cette ville revient moins cher et s’avère plus ciblé que n’importe quelle activation marketing traditionnelle.
Le second est le réseau JForce lui-même : les agents de terrain qui passent des commandes pour le compte de consommateurs qui ne peuvent pas ou ne souhaitent pas utiliser l’application directement. Dans les zones hors Abidjan, ces agents sont souvent le seul point de contact entre une marque et son client potentiel.
Le consommateur ivoirien : curieux, aspirationnel, et pas entièrement lisible
Une tension persistante sur le marché ivoirien réside dans l’écart entre les préférences déclarées et le comportement d’achat réel. Les consommateurs disent systématiquement préférer les produits locaux. Ils achètent fréquemment des produits importés. Les ressorts en sont la perception de la qualité (Abidjan a une tendance de marché à lire le prix élevé comme un signal de qualité), le prix et l’ubiquité de la distribution. Les produits que l’on trouve partout inspirent confiance. Les produits difficiles à trouver semblent risqués, quelle que soit leur qualité réelle.
L’analyse de Maverick Research sur le rebond FMCG du premier semestre 2026 formule une observation franche : les marques doivent mettre à profit l’amélioration du contexte économique pour élargir leur distribution et leurs volumes, non pour relever leurs prix sans discernement. La reprise en Côte d’Ivoire repose explicitement sur l’accessibilité. Les consommateurs qui sont revenus sur le marché l’ont fait parce que les prix et les formats de conditionnement correspondaient à leur seuil. Mal évaluer ce moment en montant trop tôt en gamme, c’est perdre le volume avant qu’il ne se consolide.
Cela pose un défi particulier aux produits à positionnement naturellement premium — une histoire d’origine, une revendication nutritionnelle, un récit d’authenticité. Le consommateur ivoirien est sincèrement réceptif à la nouveauté.
Le marché répond plus vite à l’activation par des influenceurs et au bouche-à-oreille que la plupart des autres marchés ouest-africains. Mais la nouveauté sans accessibilité, c’est un jeu de niche, pas de masse. Les marques qui gagnent sur les deux canaux — Jumia pour la notoriété, le réseau de grossistes traditionnel pour le volume — sont celles qui résistent à la tentation de se positionner exclusivement en haut de la fourchette de prix avant que la distribution soit suffisamment large pour le justifier.

2. La tech comme tissu conjonctif
            Source de l’image : The Africa Report.
       
        
    
La couche manquante dans la stratégie Côte d’Ivoire de la plupart des marques, c’est la donnée. Jumia, correctement structuré, n’est pas seulement un partenaire commercial — c’est un outil de veille. Des réunions hebdomadaires avec l’équipe commerciale de la plateforme permettent de suivre les impressions, les clics, les taux de conversion, les retours produits et les ruptures de stock.
Ces données, lues avec attention, révèlent quels unités de gestion des stocks (SKU) sont recherchés sans être trouvés, quelles zones génèrent de la demande sans offre correspondante, et quels niveaux de prix convertissent ou font fuir. Pour une marque encore en train d’apprendre le marché, cette boucle de retour vaut plus que la marge sur les premières ventes.
Au-delà de Jumia, l’opportunité tech dans le FMCG ivoirien reste embryonnaire. Les plateformes de distribution B2B (business-to-business) — comparables à ce que Maad construit au Sénégal ou à ce qu’OmniRetail déploie au Nigeria et au Ghana — n’ont pas encore atteint la même échelle en Côte d’Ivoire. L’entrée récente d’OmniRetail sur le marché ivoirien laisse entendre que cela est en train de changer.
Quand ce sera le cas, les marques qui auront déjà construit leur notoriété sur Jumia et ouvert des discussions avec le réseau de grossistes seront les premières à obtenir un référencement sur une plateforme de distribution numérisée.
L’infrastructure se met en place. La loi sur le e-commerce, la plateforme Tradepost, la formalisation des vendeurs Facebook et TikTok, l’initiative d’interopérabilité BCEAO-CEMAC facilitant les flux de paiement transfrontaliers — chacune de ces mesures, prise séparément, est une étape réglementaire modeste.
Ensemble, elles décrivent un marché qui évolue délibérément vers une architecture commerciale numérique. La question pour toute marque active en Côte d’Ivoire aujourd’hui est de savoir si elle est en train de construire sa présence dans cette architecture dès maintenant, ou si elle attend que le coût d’entrée ait augmenté.
Ce que cela signifie pour la région
La Côte d’Ivoire n’est pas un cas isolé. C’est le modèle. Le pays contribue à 40 % du PIB de l’Union Économique et Monétaire Ouest-Africaine (UEMOA), accueille les sièges régionaux de la plupart des multinationales opérant en Afrique de l’Ouest francophone, et donne le tempo commercial du bloc. Ce qui fonctionne ici — en termes de construction de notoriété numérique, d’activation du commerce traditionnel et du séquençage entre les deux — tend à se répliquer au Sénégal, au Mali, au Burkina Faso et au Bénin, avec des ajustements tenant compte des infrastructures locales et du taux de pénétration du mobile money.
La leçon centrale tirée de la résilience de Jumia en Côte d’Ivoire est plus simple qu’il n’y paraît : la plateforme a survécu en devenant indispensable à des marchés que le commerce formel n’avait jamais atteints.
Les marques FMCG qui gagneront dans cette région au cours de la prochaine décennie sont celles qui apprendront la même leçon. Pas en courant après la classe moyenne abidjanaise avec un positionnement premium. Pas en attendant que la grande distribution monte en puissance.
En allant là où se trouve le volume — rural, péri-urbain, informel — avec le bon prix, le bon format, et la bonne présence numérique pour rendre possible la conversation avec le grossiste avant que le premier camion ne quitte l’entrepôt.

articles.title: AI Is Changing How Semiconductor Fabs Work — and Engineers Are Moving Faster Because of It
articles.text:
Demand for advanced chips is rising. The processes to build them are getting more complex. And the margin for error is shrinking.
For engineers, understanding how a process change will behave, how a material will interact with a new step, how a defect maps back to a root cause are critical, challenging steps in semiconductor manufacturing — and these analyses can take days. Physical experiments on a fab line are slow and expensive. A wrong call on yield or process quality has real consequences.
AI is transforming semiconductor manufacturing, impacting what engineers can do — and how fast.
Accelerated computing shortens simulation time, allowing engineers to evaluate more alternatives before committing to physical trials.
Physics-based AI helps engineers predict process behavior without running a full simulation every time.
AI agents handle sequences of engineering tasks that once consumed hours.
And digital twins let teams test changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials.
Together, these capabilities describe an AI-defined fab: a semiconductor manufacturing factory where AI helps engineers optimize processes, catch problems earlier and make better decisions across the full manufacturing chip lifecycle. Engineers direct the work and make decisions based on their expertise while spending less time waiting for answers.
Shorter Simulation Cycles Change What Engineers Can Explore
Accelerated computing doesn’t just speed up individual calculations — it changes how many alternatives engineers can test before committing.
Multiphysics simulations model interactions among physical effects, such as heat transfer, electrical behavior and mechanical stress.
Using the NVIDIA cuDSS library, multiphysics software provider COMSOL is accelerating such simulations for semiconductor manufacturing by up to 10x. This helps engineers optimize equipment and processes, compare alternatives and decide which changes to test physically.
Applied Materials and NVIDIA are collaborating to accelerate atomic-scale materials discovery and process development. By integrating NVIDIA cuDSS, Applied’s Ginestra simulation platform runs up to 10x faster than CPU-only approaches. And with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo, Applied’s ACE+ multiphysics platform delivers topography simulations up to 35x faster.
In some cases, acceleration doesn’t just shorten the calculation — it enables it altogether. Computational lithography — which defines how circuit patterns are printed onto silicon — involves calculations too intensive to complete on CPU at production scale. Siemens is integrating NVIDIA cuLitho into its Calibre lithography software, delivering up to 17x acceleration on key simulation workloads. That expands what engineers can verify before a wafer goes to print.
As such, faster calculations can help researchers explore material behavior and reaction pathways that influence next-generation semiconductor processes.
Predicting Process Behavior Without Running Every Simulation
In addition to accelerating simulations, AI trained on physics can predict how materials and processes will behave — without running a full simulation each time.
The payoff is most visible in complex calculations that are expensive even on accelerated hardware.
Plasma — the electrically charged gas used in semiconductor etch processes — is one example. Modeling plasma behavior requires solving equations that capture how electrical, chemical and thermal processes interact, making repeated simulation costly. Lam Research demonstrated that the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework can predict plasma behavior in milliseconds, compared with days for a full simulation — giving engineers a faster way to explore process conditions without rerunning the full model each time.
Agents Handle the Steps Between Decisions
Engineers turn analyses into decisions — revising a design, investigating a test failure, adjusting a production process and more.
AI agents can help carry out the steps between those decisions.
Evaluating which AI model to apply to a given task is one example: a sequential, manual process that can consume hours on the test floor.
Advantest is using NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard AI agents to automate that selection, reducing response times from hours to minutes.
Testing Factory Changes Before They Reach the Line
Digital twins let teams simulate equipment configurations, layouts and process changes in a virtual environment before committing to physical trials. This reduces experimentation costs, especially as fabs become more complex and the stakes of a wrong change get higher.
Applied Materials uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build physically accurate digital twins of entire fabs. Teams can simulate material movement, identify bottlenecks and evaluate layouts and operating strategies — extending virtual experimentation beyond individual processes to how the factory works as a whole.
The Connected Loop
The future of semiconductor manufacturing lies in connecting these capabilities: using production data to inform models and models to evaluate changes, then bringing those findings back to the engineers making production decisions.
That’s the promise of the AI-defined fab: where AI helps people learn from each production cycle and act on that knowledge sooner.
Explore how NVIDIA is working with semiconductor leaders across the chip lifecycle.

articles.title: PowerUp Money raises $10M to expand AI-led wealth management
articles.text:
PowerUp Money raises $10M to expand AI-led wealth management
The Bengaluru-based company plans to use a significant portion of the capital to develop its AI-powered wealth management platform and expand its managed advisory business.
PowerUp Money, a wealthtech platform offering mutual fund advice and digital wealth management services, has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Flourish Ventures, an early-stage investment firm.
Existing investors Peak XV Partners, Accel, Blume Ventures, Kae Capital, 8i Ventures and DeVC also participated.
The Bengaluru-based company plans to use a significant portion of the capital to develop its AI-powered wealth management platform and expand its managed advisory business.
PowerUp claims more than 1.5 million users track mutual fund portfolios worth over Rs 2.5 lakh crore on its platform. Its paid subscription service, Elite, provides research-backed mutual fund advice and is said to have crossed 1,00,000 paid members in less than a year.
The company has now introduced Elite Prime, an AI-enabled digital wealth advisory service designed to provide a more comprehensive financial planning experience. It assesses investors’ financial goals, risk appetite and existing holdings to suggest asset allocation, systematic investment plans (SIPs), lump-sum investments, portfolio rebalancing and withdrawal strategies. It can also identify gaps in portfolios and suggest diversification into assets such as gold, silver and international investments.
An AI wealth coach and personal assistant are intended to help users understand recommendations and make informed decisions.
Founder and chief executive officer Prateek Jindal said, “AI makes it possible to deliver a much more comprehensive, wealth-manager-like experience digitally”, bringing personalised guidance within reach of investors who may not be able to afford traditional wealth management services.
PowerUp is also looking to expand Infinite, its managed wealth advisory offering. The service combines financial planning, portfolio construction, multi-asset allocation and ongoing portfolio management with dedicated human advisers.
According to the company, Infinite has accumulated nearly Rs 500 crore in assets under management (AUM) within around nine months of launch, despite being available to a limited customer base. Making the service accessible to more investors is another priority for the new funding.
The expansion comes amid sustained growth in India’s mutual fund market. According to the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), industry AUM stood at Rs 82.64 lakh crore at the end of September 2026, up from Rs 15.8 lakh crore a decade earlier. Monthly SIP contributions also reached Rs 32,490 crore in September, reflecting the growing adoption of regular, long-term investing.
Investor interest has encouraged further funding across the wealthtech sector. Debt investment platform Wint Wealth raised Rs 250 crore in a Series B round in January, while wealth management firm Centricity secured Rs 280 crore in August. AI-focused advisory startup Novelty Wealth also announced a $1.4 million seed round in March.
However, growth brings its own challenges. Digital advice must remain suitable, transparent and compliant as platforms expand their customer base. SEBI issued an updated Master Circular for Investment Advisers in February, reinforcing the regulatory framework governing investment advice.
The opportunity, as Flourish Ventures’ Asia head Ravi Kaushik noted, lies in helping investors manage increasingly complex financial lives.

articles.title: Anatel acumula dívida de R$ 30 milhões com seu próprio data center
articles.text:
A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) enfrenta dificuldades para pagar o próprio data center que sustenta serviços digitais oferecidos a cidadãos e empresas do setor. A agência já acumula R$ 30,76 milhões em notas fiscais pendentes relacionadas à aquisição da estrutura, instalada em Brasília (DF), e pediu ao governo federal o desbloqueio de R$ 30 milhões para honrar compromissos financeiros.
O pedido foi feito na semana passada pelo presidente da Anatel, Carlos Baigorri, ao Ministério do Planejamento. A solicitação ocorreu depois de tentativas anteriores de antecipar recursos que não foram atendidas pela Secretaria do Tesouro Nacional, vinculada ao Ministério da Fazenda.
O centro de dados reúne sistemas utilizados pela agência em atividades de fiscalização e dá suporte a serviços digitais destinados à população e às empresas de telecomunicações reguladas pelo órgão.
Bloqueio orçamentário reduziu verba da Anatel em 19%
- A Anatel atribui a pressão financeira ao bloqueio de R$ 51,83 milhões determinado pelo governo em maio. A medida reduziu o orçamento discricionário da agência — destinado a custeio e investimentos — de R$ 275,37 milhões para R$ 223,54 milhões, queda de 19%;
- Em dezembro de 2025, a agência havia assinado contrato de R$ 44,95 milhões com prestadores de produtos e serviços de tecnologia. O acordo inclui equipamentos, programas de gerenciamento, conectividade e serviços de implantação, migração, suporte, manutenção e garantia. A vigência vai até dezembro de 2030;
- Os R$ 30,76 milhões pendentes estão classificados como “restos a pagar”, categoria que reúne despesas de anos anteriores ainda não quitadas;
- Em manifestação citada pela Folha de S.Paulo, Baigorri afirmou que as projeções indicam risco de insuficiência de limite financeiro para o pagamento integral dos compromissos previstos, especialmente no último trimestre de 2026.
Leia mais:
- Ligações suspeitas agora podem ser barradas antes de o celular tocar
- Anatel libera frequência para futura internet da Starlink no celular
- Operadoras terão de bloquear chamadas abusivas a partir de 12 de novembro
- Biometria será obrigatória para usuários de celular; veja os prazos
Agência tenta evitar multas e novos cortes
A dificuldade não é recente. Em agosto, a Anatel pediu a antecipação de R$ 23,3 milhões, que estavam originalmente previstos para dezembro.
A agência afirma que revisou contratos, projetos e despesas para se adaptar à restrição orçamentária. Também busca evitar a cobrança de multas, juros e outros encargos contratuais.
O Olhar Digital entrou em contato com a Anatel e aguarda posicionamento.
O Ministério da Fazenda, por sua vez, afirmou que as restrições orçamentárias e financeiras dos órgãos do Poder Executivo decorrem da necessidade de contingenciamento e bloqueio de recursos, conforme os relatórios de avaliação de receitas e despesas e os decretos de programação orçamentária.
Segundo a pasta, a situação é reavaliada a cada dois meses. A próxima análise está prevista para 24 de novembro, quando a Junta de Execução Orçamentária deverá examinar o espaço fiscal disponível para eventual redução dos cortes.
A Fazenda também explicou que os pedidos de antecipação de recursos são analisados pelo Tesouro Nacional, considerando a capacidade de pagamento futura de cada órgão, para evitar problemas na execução orçamentária ao longo do ano.
Empresas pedem autonomia financeira para agências reguladoras
A situação ocorre em meio à mobilização de entidades empresariais em defesa da autonomia financeira das agências reguladoras.
Cerca de 40 organizações do setor apresentaram um manifesto em apoio à medida. Intitulado “Regulação não é gasto, é investimento”, o documento busca sensibilizar parlamentares sobre a necessidade de garantir recursos no Orçamento de 2027 para que essas instituições funcionem normalmente, sem sofrer novos cortes.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Learn the rules: The hacker mindset - Microsoft Research
articles.text:
For some, rules pose limitations. For others, like Microsoft Research Manager Mike Walker, they’re opportunities.
Walker’s fascination with rules and their role in the social order has allowed him to find success professionally and personally, from uncovering weaknesses in networked systems to redefining how computers are trained to fend off cyberattacks to pushing the limits of a reliable mode of transportation—the bicycle—in ultra-endurance racing.
In this conversation with Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu, Walker describes how his participation in hacker culture led him to a career building next-generation cyber defense, including his work developing the first all-machine hacking tournament. Along the way, he reflects on why effective security depends on understanding trust and context, what competitive hacking taught him about teamwork and collective intelligence, and how an early lesson reshaped his understanding of leadership. He also tackles an important question: are today’s networked systems any safer than they were a decade ago?
Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast:
Transcript
[MUSIC]
MIKE WALKER: Well, you have to understand the rules if you want to be able to do what you want. So I have, I have a definite fascination with the rules, [LAUGHTER] but the thing you have to understand about the rules is that rules are a social construct. And I think that a lot of … in the computer security field, when, when people hear the word “security” and they think about the rules that the security system is imposing on them, every time a security system asks something of users, then you’re asking for their trust. And that trust is a precious commodity. And so when you squander user trust, then the security regime falls down. So I think it’s really important to understand the social context of rules instead of just having instant adjudication.
[THEME MUSIC]
STANDARD INTRODUCTION: This is the Microsoft Research Podcast, where Microsoft researchers—driving advancement through fundamental science and technology research—explore the who, how, and what’s next in computing and AI.
[MUSIC ENDS]
WEISHUNG LIU: Hi, and welcome. My name is Weishung Liu, and I’m a principal technical program manager here at Microsoft Research. And today, I’m joined by Mike Walker, who is a research manager here in MSR, or Microsoft Research, where he leads projects at the intersection of AI, cybersecurity, and large distributed systems.
Before Microsoft, Mike led DARPA’s Cyber Grand Challenge, the pioneering program that demonstrated autonomous AI systems capable of finding and patching software vulnerabilities. And CGC actually just celebrated its 10th anniversary this year in 2026.
Mike’s work spans groundbreaking efforts that include cloud native memory analysis, automated malware analysis, and next-generation cyber defense technologies.
Mike, thanks for joining me.
MIKE WALKER: Good to be here, Wei.
LIU: All right, so, Mike, we have known each other for a couple of years now. And I’ve heard, like, bits and pieces of your story over time as we’ve gotten to talk. But before I really knew who you were, sort of, as a person, I, kind of, knew you as, like, “Mike Walker, the hacker guy that’s working over there,” which I’m sure you love. And I know you love that, when I call you “The Hacker.”
But you’ve worked on so many things that I’ve never really thought about before. Like, new words have entered my vocabulary as a result of knowing you and working with you, like threat intelligence, nation states, and I think there are a couple other ones that I think would have never been in my lexicon had I not known you.
So I’m hoping we can spend this time to also have the audience get to know you, as well. So we’re going to start at the beginning then. And the beginning is, I believe, Mike, you grew up in Ohio.
WALKER: Columbus, Ohio.
LIU: Columbus, Ohio. What kind of a kid were you in Columbus, Ohio?
WALKER: I think I was a kid who spent a lot of time in the woods. [LAUGHTER] I was a skateboard kid. I was a basketball kid. But I think mostly I was a kid who read books and lived in a world of their own imagination.
LIU: Were you on a farm in Columbus, Ohio, or were you in, like, or is this more suburban, rural, urban?
WALKER: It was halves and halves. I spent my … most of the year in Columbus, Ohio, and then every summer, I would go out to the town of Tappahannock on the Rappahannock River in Virginia. And I lived completely on the farm.
LIU: So what was the lifestyle in what you were doing different between, like, Columbus, Ohio, and the farm?
WALKER: So, like, some things that I was doing in Columbus, Ohio, is that my father, who was sort of half scientist, half venture capitalist, would bring me home industrial equipment and say, “See what you can make out of this,” and drop it in my room. [LAUGHTER] Really dangerous stuff. And he would always give me safety warnings, right, like, “This is a helium neon laser.” You know, “This is … this tube is made out of glass. Don’t break it.” And then, “This is a really, really high-voltage power supply driving it, and it can arc and kill you,” right. And I knew what that meant. [LAUGHTER] And then he would leave me with it. And what can you make out of this, right.
So I would do stuff like, like try to replicate the Michelson-Morley experiment, you know, because I had the, had the table and the mirrors and I could do that. And then also I spent a lot of time with the Apple II, which was this just incredible machine from some other universe that I had never gone to. I later found out that was, you know, hackerspace and, and information technology culture, but it came from nowhere and there was nobody I could talk to about it. And so I spent a lot of time trying to hook the Apple II up to stuff in my life and, and try to control it with that thing.
LIU: OK, so you brought up some hacker stuff, so I have to ask. There was farm stuff. There was, you know, “dad brought home interesting tools and equipment.” How did all of that get you interested in cybersecurity?
WALKER: I think I was always in cybersecurity. I just didn’t know.
LIU: Explain.
WALKER: You know, there’s this idea that you live two lives: the one before you find out your purpose and the one after you find it. This was, sort of, life before purpose, where I didn’t know why I was so interested in how these things worked.
So, you know, I ran a bulletin board system. Before the internet, this was how computers communicated with each other. Dial-up modems, not even backbone linked. Each, each BBS—bulletin board system—[LAUGHTER] was, was a universe unto itself, you know, architected by its creator. And so there were all these little universes you could dial into. And then at some point, all these things I’d been doing my whole life, sort of, got connected to a career.
When you say, you know, somebody could, right, somebody could listen to every single badge swipe event on the network, on campus, and then replicate them and badge themselves into any building they wanted because this is all in a broadcast LAN [local area network] and somebody should change that, there was a time when if you said things like that, the people you told it to would just be like, “Well, don’t do that,” [LAUGHTER] right? And then …
LIU: Did you listen to them?
WALKER: No. [LAUGHTER] I was young.
Um, and then at some point, the world started getting serious about imposing rules onto networked computers, and they started hiring people who are interested in that. And that’s … suddenly it was a career, right. I was like, “Oh, I was always here, but now it has a name.”
LIU: So I have to ask then, like, you brought up the notion of rules. I feel like cybersecurity and rules has a relationship there. How much of a rule follower were you growing up versus how much do you think you are a rule follower now, and was there a difference or have you always been some version of “rule following”?
WALKER: Well, you have to understand the rules if you want to be able to do what you want.
LIU: Yes.
WALKER: So I have a definite fascination with the rules, [LAUGHTER] but the thing you have to understand about the rules is that rules are a social construct. And I think that a lot of … in the computer security field, when, when people hear the word “security” and they think about the rules that the security system is imposing on them, every time a security system asks something of users, then you’re asking for their trust. And that trust is a precious commodity. And so when you squander user trust, then the security regime falls down. So I think it’s really important to understand the social context of rules instead of just having instant adjudication.
LIU: OK. I’m going to have to ask you then about a game that we played recently called No Vehicles in the Park (opens in new tab).
WALKER: No Vehicles in the Park is … it’s a game about content moderation is one way to look at it. I think it’s a fascinating thought experiment. But it just takes the thesis that rules are simple and challenges it with putting the player in the position of judge. And so the name of the exercise is the name of the rule, which is no vehicles in the park.
And then it asks you some very simple commonsense questions about, is this a violation of the rule no vehicles in the park? Like if the International Space Station overflies the park, is that a vehicle in the park, and is it against the rules?
LIU: Mike, do you think the ISS flying over the park is a violation of the rules?
WALKER: No. [LAUGHTER] But it’s important that we have a resilient way to adjudicate things that, that bridges social norms.
LIU: OK. How much did you agree with the population, by the way, of No Vehicles in the Park?

LIU: So in thinking about, sort of, capabilities of models then, some terms that, that I’ve heard used are things when we’re testing models, for example, is––we call it––red teaming. And then, of course, if you’ve taken primary colors or understood kindergarten primary colors, if you put red and blue together, you get purple teaming. Can you explain to the audience a little bit about those differences?
WALKER: Yeah. Red team and blue team is sort of an artificial separation between being an attacker and being a defender, and it’s also, sort of, an oversimplification and an abnegation of capability, right. Attackers attack; defenders defend. But if you, if you take that simplification away and you look at what’s going on under the hood, you’ll see that the difference between offense and defense most of the time is, sort of, who’s in control or who’s driving.
If you were to give a name to a program that encrypted every file in your computer and then unlocked it when you needed it, that is either a cryptography utility or it’s ransomware depending on who holds the key. If you were to give a name to a program that, that allows you to log in to your computer remotely and control it, maybe your home automation setup, that is either malware or remote administration utility [LAUGHTER] depending on who holds the key, right? Who holds the key.
So there’s, there’s this, sort of, blurring of offense and defense where computer security capabilities at their most atomic basic level aren’t offensive or defensive. They’re dual use. And so the idea of red teaming and blue teaming is sort of this idea that we can impose single use onto dual-use capabilities, and purple team is the acknowledgment that that’s not true, right.
Attackers, as soon as they break into a network, they have an intrusion that they need to defend. You’ll hear all these terms like moving laterally, which just means breaking into more computers, or exfiltration, which means taking data. But the whole time they’re doing that, they’re trying not to get caught, right. So they are defending their attack, right.
LIU: Mm.
WALKER: And at the same time, when defenders are doing things like log analysis or really any—or traffic analysis—their tools themselves can be broken into, right. They have a duty to defend their own tooling, and they also need to, in order to prevent attackers, they need to be able to find vulnerabilities, find weaknesses, and then grade weaknesses in their own software. And the way that you find vulnerabilities is vulnerability research, and you grade weaknesses by writing exploits or at least proof of vulnerability, and that’s offense, right. So purple team is just this idea that attack and defense are the same skill set. They’re the same tooling. They’re blended. And it’s really a contest to control the logic of memory of networked computers run all the time.

WALKER: You know, I thought I was going to be a musician, but when you’re a … when you go out and you start getting into a music scene, you, kind of, find out if you were a natural or not. So I think science fiction writer is still the thing where I wish I’d kept at it a little more.
LIU: All right, I’m going to, I’m going to break my own rule, which is not … which is a social construct, and ask you one more, which is, can you recommend to the audience a really good—your favorite or one of the best sci-fi books you’ve ever read?
WALKER: Oh, sure. Easy. It’s The Forever War (opens in new tab). Haldeman’s Forever War. And it’s, I think, it’s about coming to hand in the key except the challenge’s already solved, except sort of writ large in a, in a universe governed by relativity.
LIU: OK.
WALKER: No spoilers.
LIU: No spoilers. All right. Fine.
Thank you so much, Mike—this was a great time—for joining me.
To our audience, thank you for listening. If you want to learn a little bit more about any of my colleagues in Microsoft Research and their work, check out the Microsoft Research website at aka.ms/research (opens in new tab) [MUSIC] or listen and watch other episodes of the podcast on YouTube and major podcast platforms.

Un design futuriste

Un nettoyage en toute fluidité

articles.title: Jurassic Park : le trailer d'un projet secret qu'on pensait perdu à jamais a été retrouvé
articles.text:
Déterrée sur Reddit via une vente aux enchères d’objets de tournage oubliés, cette bande démo de Jurassic Park d’une minute et quinze secondes secoue la communauté des fans.
Entre l’hystérie collective des nostalgiques et les accusations immédiates d’arnaque générée par l’intelligence artificielle, le retour de ce projet fantôme sort les griffes et fait l’effet d’une déflagration.
Une série hybride des années 1990 : quand la 2D croise la 3D pour le dessin animé Jurassic Park
Ce qui frappe dès les premières secondes de ce teaser conceptuel, c’est son audace visuelle. À une époque où les séries d’animation du samedi matin régnaient en reines, Évasion de Jurassic Park tentait un pari esthétique fou : marier une animation 2D traditionnelle, qui rappelle immédiatement le style léché de Don Bluth ou de We’re Back!, avec des images de synthèse encore balbutiantes pour les véhicules et les créatures. Un mélange qui annonce ReBoot, première série entièrement en images-de synthèse, ou les décors en 3D de la série Spider-Man, toutes deux lancées en 1994.
Malgré les accusations de trucage par IA lancées par certains internautes, la vidéo a été authentifiée : le site de fans Jurassic Outpost l’a comparée au matériel de production déjà connu, rapporte FirstShowing.
L’illustrateur William Stout, qui a dessiné les personnages et les dinosaures de la série, avait d’ailleurs publié ses dessins préparatoires en août 2015. La série faisait revenir les personnages du film, dont Tim et Lex, les petits-enfants de John Hammond. Elle prévoyait aussi des créatures absentes du film, comme le Lycaenops, un prédateur à crocs de sabre.
Pourquoi Steven Spielberg a-t-il enterré le projet ?
Les documents Kenner diffusés avec la vidéo, dont une lettre datée du 18 juin 1993, rattachaient la série à la deuxième vague de figurines Jurassic Park. Pourquoi, alors, n’a-t-elle jamais vu le jour ? La légende veut que Steven Spielberg, totalement essoré par le tournage titanesque de Jurassic Park et le travail éprouvant sur La Liste de Schindler mené en parallèle, ait refusé de visionner la cassette de démonstration.
Selon Stout, il était lassé du merchandising et de l’exploitation commerciale de son film. D’autres récits, relayés par Inside the Magic, évoquent plutôt son agacement de voir la série commandée sans lui. Faute de feu vert, Universal a abandonné le projet en 1994.
Il a fallu attendre la fin des années 2010 pour voir la saga en série animée, d’abord en Lego, puis avec La Colo du Crétacé et sa suite La Théorie du chaos sur Netflix. Cette bande-annonce montre ce qu’aurait pu donner, dès 1993, une série pensée pour le public du film. Une capsule temporelle brute, imparfaite et fascinante qui rappelle une époque où la 3D était tout juste balbutiante, mais où l’émerveillement était total.
